checked.name: NEISS (CPSC National Electronic Injury Surveillance System), Product_1 code
checked.one_line: NEISS is large, public and dated, with a code list of about 1,000 products, and nobody has published product-code classification on it. But the same trained coder writes the narrative and picks the code, the narrative must name every product (close to a lookup task), Product_1 order is arbitrary when several products are involved, the 2026 year will not be public until about April 2027, and I could not check the per-code tail without a download.
checked.access: Opened the CPSC NEISS overview (cpsc.gov/node/38022), FAQ, Coding Options, the NEISS-Injury-Data page and the NEISS-R release of 22 July 2026. Yearly files come as Excel, tab-delimited or SAS through the NEISS Query portal, covering the last 20 years. A year usually appears in April of the following year. None of the pages I opened has a terms-of-use or licence statement; the only restriction stated is that CPSC does not release data collected for other agencies. These are de-identified US federal data, and the manual forbids PII in the narrative. I found no clause about LLMs. Sending text to an API looks allowed but is not stated anywhere. Public NEISS holds only the CPSC product cases; CDC all-injury (NEISS-AIP) cases go to WISQARS. Direct CPSC file and PDF URLs return 403 to curl (WAF). The scout was right about that. A third-party mirror on Hugging Face (Layered-Labs/neiss-injury-data, licence 'other', ungated, opened via the HF API) has 7,326,429 records for 2005-2024 in one 415 MB parquet file, with a Product_1-3 and Narrative_1 field. HF filter counts gave 323,343 records for 2022 and 338,265 for 2023; the 2024 query failed. Note: I fetched the January 2025 NEISS Coding Manual (4.4 MB PDF) with WebFetch to read it. That is above the 2 MB guideline; it is a documentation file, not data.
checked.who_labels: Source: Coding Manual Jan 2025 rev.1 (opened, text extracted), Coding Options page and FAQ (opened). A NEISS coder, either hospital staff ('surveillance coding') or a third-party coder under contract to CPSC, reviews the ED records for each treatment date. The coder abstracts the chart into coded variables plus a short narrative ('comment'), and must be formally trained by CPSC first. So the label is chosen by the person who writes the text, not by the patient or a manufacturer. Neither comes from an independent second reader. The manual requires every product involved to be named in the comment. CPSC replies to a 9999 ('cannot find') code with the correct code. That is the only documented case of CPSC changing a code. Other checks: software edits at entry and after transmission, and CPSC analysts screen the data on the morning it arrives. A NEISS representative visits once a year to re-review a portion of ED records and writes a data-quality report for the hospital or coder. I found no published product-code agreement or error figure on any CPSC page I opened.
checked.label_space: Up to three product codes per case (Product_1-3), 4-digit codes. The manual states 'When multiple products are involved, it does not matter in what order you enter them', so Product_1 is not a primary label. A clean single-label task needs only single-product cases (Product_2 = 0), or a multi-label setup. The code list is flat with a few catch-alls: 9999 means unassigned, and 5555 is for unknown poisonings in children under 5. Some codes are only allowed under special studies. A NEISS-formats.xlsx from the hadley/neiss GitHub repo (50 kB; I parsed it, date unknown, probably several years old) lists 1,114 PROD codes, including old ones. The scout's figure from the 2023 Comparability Table (1,756 codes ever, 871 deleted, about 885 current) is unverified because the PDF returns 403. Codes are fairly stable year to year, and CPSC publishes a comparability table.
checked.tail_shape: Not verified. Yearly volume is verified from the HF mirror: 323,343 records (2022) and 338,265 (2023), about 366k a year on average over 2005-2024. I wrote per-code count queries for 2023 (HF datasets-server /filter on year and Product_1, over the 1,114 codes). The first two yearly totals worked, after which the server kept returning 'Authentication check ... failed' for every query, so I got no per-code counts. To verify, someone has to fetch either CPSC's yearly tab-delimited file (NEISS Query portal, browser only, tens of MB; size unconfirmed) or the year and Product_1 columns of the 415 MB HF parquet. Then count Product_1 among single-product cases. With about 330k cases a year, about 900-1,100 codes and very skewed products (floors, stairs, beds, basketball), many codes with 1-5 cases a year are very likely, but that is not established. The single-product restriction will cut the count noticeably (multi-product share unverified).
checked.text: Narrative ('comment') of up to 400 characters since 1 Jan 2019 (142 before), confirmed in the FAQ. English, written to a fixed template: the age and sex token first (e.g. '86YOF'), then the event sequence with products, and the clinician's diagnosis at the end ('DX: ...'). The manual requires every product involved to be named in the comment, and asks for a specific description (e.g. 'gas oven', not 'oven'). So the code word or a close synonym is nearly always in the text. Many codes reduce to matching a phrase against the manual's alphabetical product index, which coders themselves search with CTRL-F. The hard part is splitting look-alike codes (e.g. washer subtypes) and the 'not elsewhere classified' codes. Boilerplate is high (age-sex prefix, 'DX:' suffix); duplication across reports was not checked.
checked.time_split: Dated by Treatment_Date. Train 2023, dev 2024, test 2025 is possible if 2025 was released in April 2026. The FAQ promises April release, but I did not confirm the 2025 file exists. The project's plan (2024/2025/2026) does not work yet: 2026 data would appear about April 2027. NEISS-R (CPSC release, 22 July 2026) replaces manual review and coding with electronic health-record exchange and is to be 'fully effective by the beginning of 2027'. The release does not say how products or narratives will be coded. So 2026 may be partly transitional and later years may not be human-coded. That ends the series for this purpose, but it also makes a timely use case.
standing: Burford KG et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024 (doi 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.25981; opened PMC11322845): GPT-4 classified helmet status in 54,569 NEISS 2019-2022 micromobility records against text-string search. Products were selected with NEISS codes plus string search, not predicted.

Omaki E et al., Inj Prev 2023 (doi 10.1136/ip-2023-044858; opened PMC10528494): a BERT/FLAIR pipeline coded fall circumstances (fell-from and fell-onto categories guided by product codes, about 12 and 9 classes) in NEISS-AIP 2012-2016, trained on 4,546 hand-coded 2015 narratives. No classifier metrics reported.

Ye J et al., AMIA Jt Summits 2024 (PMC11141806; opened): predicts the injury diagnosis (24 classes) from NEISS narrative plus structured fields with BERT/RoBERTa fusion. Stratified random 80/10/10 split, with no per-class and no LLM analysis.

Vichare, Nanda, Sundararajan, AI (MDPI) 5(3) 2024, doi 10.3390/ai5030082 (abstract only, via Crossref; the MDPI page returned 403): RF/KNN/LR ensembles predict 'injury codes' from NEISS narratives; which code field is not stated in the abstract.
Bhatt H et al., Injury 2026, doi 10.1016/j.injury.2025.112927 (abstract only, PubMed): NEISS-trained models predict body part and diagnosis for Reddit posts.
Zhou W et al., Inj Prev 2026, doi 10.1136/ip-2025-045761 (abstract only): rule-based vs TF-IDF+XGBoost for helmet use in triage notes, including NEISS.
Computerized 'Learn-As-You-Go' TBI classification on NEISS, Accid Anal Prev 2016, doi 10.1016/j.aap.2016.01.012 (PubMed title only).
Venkatesh, Jaiswal, Nanda, Sci Rep 2024 (abstract only): ML vs zero-shot LLM vs humans on 204 injury narratives in 6 cause codes. The data source is not stated as NEISS in the abstract.

Hundreds of epidemiology papers select cases by product code (e.g. PubMed 2025-2026 lawnmower eye injuries, go-karting, ENDS burns). Reviewers know the data well, but as an epidemiology source, not as an NLP benchmark.
prior_like_ours: None found. No paper I could find predicts the NEISS product code from the narrative with a fine-tuned model or an LLM, let alone compares them by code frequency, routes between them, or tests at natural prevalence. The work closest in task is Ye 2024 (diagnosis, 24 classes, encoder only, random split, no per-class results), Omaki 2023 (a dozen product-guided fall categories, BERT, no metrics) and Burford 2024 (GPT-4 for a 3-class helmet field).

The scout's 'gmcirco 2025 blog uses gpt-4o-mini with retrieved candidates to pick NEISS product codes' was not confirmed. I listed every post in the gmcirco/blog GitHub repo and grepped all .qmd posts for 'product code': no hits. The NEISS posts are retrieve-and-rerank of NEISS 2022 narratives (Jan 2025), LLM calibration for classifying the primary injury on 500 NEISS 2024 narratives (Apr 2026), and the repo 'neiss-injury-classifier', whose README says it classifies the primary body part.

Search effort: WebSearch was unavailable (the shared session budget was used up before my first query), and OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar returned rate-limit errors. Queries actually run: arXiv 'all:NEISS' (12 hits, no product-code work; only e-bike/traffic LLM agent papers), arXiv 'injury narratives', arXiv 'emergency department AND narratives AND classification' (0). PubMed: NEISS AND (machine learning OR NLP OR language model OR deep learning OR text classification OR GPT OR BERT) (6); NEISS AND narrative* AND (classif* OR coding OR automat*) (15); 'consumer product' AND narrative* AND classif* (8); NEISS AND (large language OR ChatGPT OR GPT-4 OR LLM) (2); NEISS AND (natural language OR text mining OR autocod* OR machine learning) (10); 'injury narrative*' AND (large language OR BERT OR transformer) (1). Also the HF dataset search for 'neiss' and 'injury narrative', and the GitHub blog search. Google Scholar, ACL Anthology, SSRN and conference proceedings (e.g. IEEE, AMIA full text) were not searched. Grey literature and CDC/NIOSH autocoding reports could have been missed.
checked.open_ground: All three claims would be new on NEISS product codes: (1) a frozen selector between encoder, zero-shot LLM and retrieval-LLM, with gains over the best single coder on a later year; (2) LLM vs fine-tuned encoder by training-count bin, using a natural tail (if the tail exists); (3) evaluation at natural prevalence with a review queue. NEISS also offers something MAUDE lacks: labels from a CPSC-trained abstractor under an annual re-review, not from a manufacturer, plus a real operational context, since NEISS-R ends manual coding from 2027. The catch is that the narrative must name the product, so a reviewer may see the task as phrase lookup against the manual's index. A string-match or retrieval baseline against the code list would have to be included, and the LLM's long-tail advantage may simply be lexical lookup.
risks: The label is not independent of the text: the same trained coder writes the narrative and picks the code, and must name the product in the narrative. Criterion b is bent. Quality control exists (annual partial re-review, software edits, CPSC screening, 9999 corrections), but there is no published agreement or error figure.

Product_1 is not a primary product: per the manual, order does not matter when several products are involved. The task must be limited to single-product cases or treated as multi-label, and the share of single-product cases is unverified.
The task is close to string matching, since the narrative names the product and coders look codes up by CTRL-F. Strong lexical baselines may close the gap, and the selector's value may shrink.
The tail is unverified (per-code counts need a download; the HF count API failed). The code list is about 900-1,100 codes, partly retired, plus catch-alls (9999, 5555) and special-study-only codes.
Test year: 2026 will not be public until about April 2027, and NEISS-R changes collection by the start of 2027. The 2026 data may be transitional, and there will be no human-coded years after it.

There are no explicit terms of use. CPSC states none, and the HF mirror says licence 'other'. Use the CPSC files rather than the mirror. US federal works are normally public domain, but there is no explicit LLM clause.
The direct CPSC download URLs are behind a WAF (403 to curl), so files must be fetched by browser.

Hospital count discrepancy: the FAQ and overview say about 100 hospitals, Burford 2024 says 96, and the NEISS-R release says the legacy system covers about 70 EDs. That suggests the sample has shrunk; the effect on volume is unverified.
scout_errors: The 'prior_like_ours' claim about a gmcirco 2025 blog post using gpt-4o-mini to pick NEISS product codes was not confirmed. No post in the blog repo mentions 'product code'. The NEISS posts classify the primary injury or body part, or do retrieval.
'The most natural single label is Product_1' is misleading: the Coding Manual says the order of multiple products does not matter.

'Both groups are trained by CPSC and follow the NEISS Coding Manual' is right, but the scout missed that the manual requires every product to be named in the narrative. That makes the label almost literally present in the text, which matters more than the scout's point (3) suggests.
'Yearly volume is a few hundred thousand cases' is roughly right: the HF mirror gives 323,343 (2022) and 338,265 (2023).
'About 96 sampled hospitals': CPSC pages say about 100, and the July 2026 NEISS-R release says about 70 EDs for the legacy system. The figure is stale or inconsistent.
The 2026 test year is not just 'partly transitional': it is not public yet (April 2027 at the earliest), so the project's 2024/2025/2026 split cannot be used now.

checked.effort: Download: one yearly CPSC tab-delimited file per year (tens of MB each, by browser) or the 415 MB HF parquet for 2005-2024. Cleaning: about 1-2 days (restrict to single-product cases, map retired codes with the comparability table, drop or handle 9999/5555, strip the age-sex prefix and the 'DX:' suffix if wanted). Items: about 330k cases a year; single-product cases are probably most of them (unverified), so encoder training would have a few hundred thousand a year. LLM coding at natural proportions on a test year would cost about 300k calls, so a stratified sample plus a natural-proportion slice is more realistic. Narratives are short (at most 400 characters), so a prompt with about 1,000 codes dominates the cost, and caching the code list would matter.

checked.name: CPSC NEISS (National Electronic Injury Surveillance System), Product_1 code on single-product cases
checked.one_line: Large, public, dated and long-tailed: there are about 805 product codes, and roughly a fifth of the codes I sampled have 1-5 single-product cases in 2024. A CPSC-trained coder assigns the code, not the clinician who wrote the chart, and nobody has published a frequency-binned LLM-vs-fine-tuned study, a routing study or a natural-prevalence test on it. Two problems: the same coder writes the narrative and picks the code, with no published agreement figure, and the manual requires every product to be named in the narrative, so many codes can be read off the text by keyword.
checked.access: Confirmed live (opened 2026-11-11): https://www.cpsc.gov/Research--Statistics/NEISS-Injury-Data offers annual files (Excel, tab-delimited, SAS) for the most recent 20 years. The latest year usually appears the following April. The 400-character narrative limit applies to treatment dates from 1 Jan 2019, up from 142. Access goes through a NEISS Query page where the user picks a 'User Affiliation'. I saw no registration requirement and no data-use agreement. Neither the data page nor the FAQ states terms of use or a licence. The FAQ says only that CPSC does not release data it collects for other agencies, so NEISS-AIP all-injury cases are not in the public product files. These are US federal, de-identified files, and the manual forbids PII in the comment, so sending the text to a local LLM or a commercial API looks permissible, but no page grants that explicitly. Hugging Face mirror Layered-Labs/neiss-injury-data (API opened): unofficial, licence field 'other', not gated, 7,326,429 rows for 2005-2024, about 415 MB parquet download. Its fields include Treatment_Date, Product_1/2/3, Narrative_1, Stratum, PSU, Weight and year. The mirror has no 2025 data yet, so a 2025 or 2026 test year needs the official CPSC files. I did not test the scout's 403-on-curl claim.
checked.who_labels: NEISS Coding Manual, January 2021 (PDF opened; text extracted and read, pp. 1-3 and 22-23): 'the coder must be formally trained by CPSC staff' before coding. ED staff document the injury in the medical record. A NEISS coder at the hospital then reviews every ED record for each treatment date, abstracts the eligible cases, and enters both the coded variables and a short narrative comment on a CPSC-supplied laptop. The same person writes the narrative and picks the product code. After transmission the data go through 'several reviews and data checks', and CPSC analysts check them for quality control from the same morning. The FAQ (opened) adds interactive software edits at entry that require every field and accept only valid entries, plus a second computer edit after transmission. The manual says code 9999 is a temporary code for a product the coder cannot find; CPSC NEISS staff review such cases and reply with the correct code. The manual says 'Other / not elsewhere classified' codes exist in several product groups (TOC, p. 26), and the order of products across Product 1 and 2 is the coder's free choice. A 2004 CDC WISQARS archive page (opened) says CPSC headquarters QA coders reviewed all data elements and the narrative and assigned cause codes. That applies to NEISS-AIP cases, which are not in the public product file. Neither the FAQ nor the manual reports a re-coding rate, an audit or an inter-coder agreement figure for the product code. Label independence is therefore partial: better than MAUDE (a CPSC-trained coder rather than a manufacturer picks the code, and CPSC staff review the data), but the code and the text come from one person at one time.
checked.label_space: 805 distinct 4-digit codes appear in dotted-leader index lines of the January 2021 manual (my regex over the extracted text; approximate). This matches the scout's count. It includes underlined codes outside CPSC jurisdiction, which are coded only during special studies, plus 9999 (temporary) and 5555 (unknown poison or chemical, under 5). The task is single-label after keeping cases with Product_2 = 0000; the manual confirms that a single product goes in Product 1 with zeros in 2 and 3. The codes are flat 4-digit numbers. The manual groups them into families with 'other / n.e.c.' and 'not specified' residuals, but there is no formal hierarchy field. Codes change over time (the scout cites a comparability table, which I did not open). The 2024-to-2026 split will meet a few code additions or retirements; their number is unverified.
checked.tail_shape: Measured through Hugging Face dataset-server filter counts on the unofficial mirror. The service was intermittently down ('Authentication check ... failed'), so I could not count all 805 codes. Year 2024, single-product cases (Product_2 = 0): 302,324 records. The scout's total for all 2024 cases was 372,357; I did not re-verify it. Per-code single-product 2024 counts for 23 codes, chosen as every 20th code in the manual list plus the first four: 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 6, 6, 6, 11, 11, 16, 28, 38, 49, 57, 98, 138, 150, 176, 201, 240, 277. By bin: 2 codes at zero, 5 at 1-5, about 5 at 6-20, about 5 at 21-100, and 6 above 100. Extrapolated very roughly to about 805 codes, that suggests on the order of 150-200 codes with 1-5 cases in a year, but the interval is wide. Some zero codes are probably retired codes or special-study codes outside CPSC jurisdiction. The scout's own 14-code sample gives a similar shape. The full table needs the 2024 annual file from CPSC (tens of MB, tab-delimited) or the Product_1, Product_2 and year columns of the 415 MB HF parquet. I did not download either. Rare-code share of cases at natural proportions: unverified, but clearly well under 1%, as on MAUDE.
standing: Nanda G, Das, Vallmuur K, Niven 2025, Proc. HFES Annual Meeting, 'Examining the Efficacy of Large Language Models for Injury Surveillance', doi 10.1177/10711813251357913. Abstract only (Crossref): ChatGPT-3.5 against logistic regression and an MLP on cause, product-involved and nature-of-injury codes for 100 randomly chosen NEISS cases. Qualitative strengths are reported; the abstract notes ML is limited on 'rare causes of injury'.

Chakravarty, Ahmad, Nanda 2026, Proc. HFES, 'Automated Injury Diagnosis Coding Using LLMs: Performance and Privacy Trade-offs', doi 10.1177/10711813261485840. Abstract only (Crossref): 100 NEISS narratives, diagnosis code. GPT-5 reached recall 0.82 and precision 0.81, Llama 4 was similar, and Mistral 7B reached recall 0.62 and precision 0.71. All three beat LSTM/RNN baselines trained on NEISS.

Vichare, Nanda, Sundararajan 2024, AI (MDPI) 5(3):82, 'Probabilistic Ensemble Framework for Injury Narrative Classification', doi 10.3390/ai5030082. Abstract only (Crossref; MDPI returned 403): KNN/RF/LR ensembles predicting the top two injury codes from NEISS narratives, with 90.47% top-1 accuracy. The abstract does not say which code.

Divya Venkatesh J, Jaiswal, Nanda 2024, Sci Rep 14:14295, doi 10.1038/s41598-024-65080-7. Abstract read (PubMed): 204 injury narratives in 6 cause codes. An ML model trained on 120,000 pre-labelled narratives beat a zero-shot LLM and humans; eye-tracking study. The abstract does not say the corpus is NEISS.
Omaki E et al. 2023, Inj Prev 29(5):384-388, doi 10.1136/ip-2023-044858. Abstract partly read (PubMed): ML analysis of fall circumstances in paediatric NEISS narratives. Not product-code prediction.
Bertsimas-style 'Learn-As-You-Go' TBI classification of NEISS narratives, Accid Anal Prev 2016 (PMID 26851618). Title only (PubMed listing).

arXiv 2412.02173 (Dec 2024), 'Keeping Experts in the Loop: Expert-Guided Optimization for Clinical Data Classification using LLMs'. HTML full text read: 17,888 NEISS micromobility narratives from 2023, a 3-class helmet-status label from two physicians on 2,000 notes, gpt-4o-mini with DSPy-style prompt optimisation. F1 0.986. No fine-tuned encoder, no product code.
Zhou W ... Mooney SJ 2026, Inj Prev, doi 10.1136/ip-2025-045761. Abstract read (PubMed): helmet-use extraction from 1,206 notes including NEISS. Rules (F1 0.95-0.96) beat TF-IDF+XGBoost (about 0.80).
Europe PMC also lists Burford et al. 2024 JAMA Netw Open, doi 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.25981: generative AI for helmet status on NEISS micromobility cases. Title only.
Hugging Face hobby models: DevJGraham/neiss_clf_bert_uncased (v1-v3) and Tpan6/NEISS_Llama-3.1-8b. The cards are empty or boilerplate, with no task description. Seen via the HF API only.
prior_like_ours: Nanda et al. 2025 (HFES): the only work found that puts an LLM against trained models on the NEISS product-involved code. It uses 100 random cases, ChatGPT-3.5, logistic regression and an MLP. From the abstract there is no frequency-binned analysis, no routing between models, no natural-prevalence or out-of-time test, and no full 800-code tail evaluation. The full text is paywalled and was not read.
Chakravarty, Ahmad & Nanda 2026 (HFES): LLMs against LSTM on the diagnosis code, 100 cases. Not the product code. No frequency bins and no routing, per the abstract.
arXiv 2412.02173 (2024): an LLM on NEISS with 2,000 physician-labelled notes, a 3-class helmet label. No fine-tuned comparison, no tail and no routing (full text read).
Nothing found that combines or routes between an LLM and a fine-tuned classifier on NEISS, compares them by code frequency, or tests at natural prevalence on a later year.
checked.open_ground: All three claims appear open on NEISS. (1) A per-report selector between an encoder and LLMs, frozen on 2024 and tested on later years: nobody has done it. (2) LLM vs encoder by training-count bin over the full ~800-code product list: only 100-case pilots exist (Nanda group); there is no binned comparison at scale. (3) A natural-proportion evaluation of rare-code answers and a ranked review list: not found. The NEISS setting may also help the owner's 'labels are untrustworthy' problem: the coder is CPSC-trained and is not the product's maker, and CPSC staff review the data and correct 9999 cases. NEISS is also a human-coding operation that CPSC already runs daily, so 'automation versus people' is a real operational question there. The likely reviewer objection is that product words are required in the narrative, so the 'every bin minus its own keyword' control used for SDR is essential here.
risks: The label is not independent of the text: the hospital coder writes the comment and picks the code together, and no agreement or audit figure is published.

The manual requires every product to be mentioned in the comment, so many codes are keyword lookups. LLM gains on rare codes may then reflect lexical matching to the code-list names, and a keyword baseline plus a no-own-keyword subset are needed.
Multi-product cases (about 70k of about 372k in 2024 by the HF counts) must be dropped. The order of Product 1 and 2 is the coder's free choice, so single-product filtering also changes the case mix.

Hospitals are a stratified probability sample and cases carry weights. 'Natural proportions' means sample proportions, not national ones, and hospital turnover across years can shift the distribution.

There is no 2025 or 2026 data in the HF mirror, and CPSC releases each year in April. 2025 should be out (April 2026; not verified). 2026 will not be out until April 2027, so the test year must be 2025 with training on 2023-2024, which breaks the project's 2024/2025/2026 design.
There are no explicit terms of use. The data are federal and de-identified, but API use rests on the absence of restrictions rather than on an explicit grant.
Some codes are outside CPSC jurisdiction or used only in special studies, and some are retired, so the effective label space is below 805.
Codes cover products and activities (e.g. sports), not failures. That fits the owner's 'it does not have to be failures' question, but it leaves the maintenance framing and its venues (RESS, Part O).
scout_errors: No substantive error found in the access, labeller, code-count or narrative-limit claims; each matched the sources I opened.

Minor: the scout says the hospital coder is 'not the ED clinician who wrote the chart'. That is correct, but the manual also says ED staff document the injury first and coders are told to 'work closely with ED staff', so the narrative is an abstract of clinician notes, not independent text.

Minor: the CDC 2004 headquarters QA review the scout cites covers NEISS-AIP cases. The FAQ says CPSC does not release data collected for other agencies, so that QA statement may not describe the public product-file cases.
Unverified rather than wrong: the scout's total of 372,357 for 2024. I verified only 302,324 single-product records.
checked.text: The narrative is a short comment of at most 400 characters since 2019 (142 before). It starts with age and sex (e.g. '10YOM'), describes what the patient was doing, and ends with the clinician's diagnosis. Abbreviations are heavy and the text is in English. The manual requires that 'all products involved' be mentioned in the comment, so the product word nearly always appears, though often in a non-standard wording different from the code-list name. Boilerplate: the age/sex prefix and the 'DX:' suffix are templated. Duplication across cases was not measured.
checked.time_split: Treatment_Date is on every record; annual files run on calendar years. The HF mirror covers 2005-2024. The official site holds the last 20 years, adding the new year in April, so 2025 should now be available (not verified). A workable split is train 2023, dev 2024, test 2025, or train 2024 and test 2025. A 2026 test year is impossible until about April 2027.
checked.effort: Download: one CPSC annual tab-delimited file per year (tens of MB each, size unverified), or the 415 MB HF parquet for 2005-2024. Cleaning: about 1-2 days (single-product filter, mapping retired and special-study codes, a keyword-baseline table from code names). Items: about 300k single-product cases a year for encoder training. For LLM coding, the short texts make a stratified sample of 10-20k test reports cheap, but a natural-proportion run over a full year (about 300k) costs as much as MAUDE work.
unverified: The full 2024 per-code frequency table: HF dataset-server failures stopped me after 23 codes. It needs the CPSC 2024 file or the parquet columns.
The exact official annual case count, and whether 2025 data are already on cpsc.gov.
Terms of use for API or LLM processing: none were found on the pages opened.
The comparability table of code changes (not opened).
Full texts of Nanda 2025, Chakravarty 2026 and Vichare 2024 (abstracts only), and which code Vichare 2024 predicts.
Whether the 120,000-narrative corpus in Divya Venkatesh et al. 2024 is NEISS.

Searches that could not run: WebSearch budget exhausted, OpenAlex daily budget exhausted, Semantic Scholar rate-limited (429), arXiv API returned empty. Searches done instead: PubMed E-utilities (4 queries), Europe PMC full text (2), Crossref (5), arXiv web search ('NEISS', 'injury narratives'), HF hub search ('neiss' datasets and models). Ten distinct queries in all, but no general web engine and no Google Scholar, so grey literature and conference papers outside PubMed and Crossref may be missed.

checked.name: US patents: first (inventive) CPC symbol on USPTO grants/applications (PatentsView / USPTO bulk data / HUPD / USPTO-70k)
checked.one_line: Patents are a well-known public-domain dataset, and on granted patents the code is checked by an examiner. But at the subclass level there is no real 1-5-item tail, the main-group tail is still unverified, and Emer et al. 2026 have already published the encoder-vs-LLM long-tail split and an uncertainty router on USPTO-70k. Our learned per-item selector and the natural-prevalence false-positive analysis would still be new.
checked.access: PatentsView data is US government data and public domain, but the bulk-download location has moved. The scout's URL patentsview.org/download/... now returns 301 to data.uspto.gov/support/transition-guide/patentsview. That page is rendered by JavaScript and came back empty to me. The old S3 links (s3.amazonaws.com/data.patentsview.org/download/g_cpc_current.tsv.zip, g_cpc_at_issue, g_patent_abstract, g_cpc_title) all returned HTTP 403 on a HEAD request today. So I could not confirm where the CPC tables are now, how large they are, or whether the new USPTO Open Data Portal requires an API key; all of that is unverified. HUPD: I opened the Hugging Face card. Its metadata licence is cc-by-sa-4.0, but the card text says CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial), so the two conflict. The data is 125 GB and covers applications filed January 2004 to December 2018, so it has no 2024-2026 years. Its fields include main_cpc_label, main_ipcr_label, cpc_labels, filing_date and decision. The dataset viewer and statistics are off because the dataset runs a loading script; I checked datasets-server is-valid and splits. I did not check the EPO text-analytics licence or size. Patent text itself is public, so sending it to a local or commercial LLM raises no terms problem; that is my inference, and I opened no terms page that says so.
checked.who_labels:
Read in full: Commerce OIG-23-026-A (PDF fetched, text extracted locally). USPTO relies on contractors for initial classification and reclassification. The contracts set a maximum allowable error rate of 10 percent, measured across several error categories. From March 2021 to December 2022 the two vendors averaged 19 and 27 percent error on CPC classification. The report also analysed 87,384 examiner-challenged items from 886 examiners and found that many challenges lacked adequate explanations. These figures apply to the INITIAL classification of applications, and the error is not specific to the first symbol.

Opened: MPEP 905.03(a)-(b). Symbols are attached to patent families, and there is exactly one first-position (invention) symbol per family. Before an application issues, the primary examiner must personally review its classification and sign the Issue Classification form. So the CPC on a granted patent at issue is examiner-checked, which is stronger than MAUDE or SDR. I found no published agreement or audit figure for the first symbol at grant.

Emer et al. v2 (opened) cite non-negligible disagreement among expert examiners (Burke and Reitzig 2007, not opened). Current CPC (as opposed to at-issue CPC) is reclassified as the scheme is revised, so the first symbol of an old patent can change. I could not open the joint EPO-USPTO quality-assurance programme or the EPO remark on AI pre-classification, so both remain unverified.
checked.label_space: The code is the CPC first symbol: one per family under MPEP 905.03(a), so the task reduces to single-label. It can be used at subclass level (scout: about 655 subclasses; I could not confirm the number because the CPC 'about' page gives no counts) or at main-group level (thousands of groups; the count is unverified). The hierarchy is section, class, subclass, main group, subgroup. The scheme is revised continually (the CPC site lists Notices of Changes), so codes drift between a 2024 training year and a 2026 test year. Using the current-CPC table remaps them, and the at-issue table would leave stale codes. In Emer et al. and USPTO-70k the label is multi-label (mean 1.98 subclasses per patent in training, 2.32 in test), not the first symbol.
checked.tail_shape: Subclass level, partly verified: in USPTO-70k (50,250 training patents, 2006-2017, multi-label), the rarest training subclass is C12L with 4 instances. C06C, A44D, B28C and C10C have 9 each, and G06F has 6,272 (Emer v2 appendix, Table 8, opened). So even a sample pooled over 12 years has almost no subclass with 1-5 items. A full natural year of US grants (scout's figure: about 300k or more; I could not open USPTO statistics pages, which returned 404) would have even fewer subclasses that rare. At subclass level the 1-5 tail is therefore close to empty, and claim 2's rare bin cannot be formed there. Main-group level: a real tail is plausible but unverified. Counting it needs the PatentsView/ODP g_cpc_current (or g_cpc_at_issue) table plus g_patent for dates. The scout says the zip is about 462 MB (snippet only; I could not reach the file even with HEAD). HUPD (125 GB) has no stats endpoint. No published per-year main-group distribution was found.
standing: Emer, Lippi, Mina & Vandin, arXiv 2601.23200 (v1 30 Jan 2026; v2 Aug 2026, retitled 'Large Language Models, Encoder Architectures and Hybrid Approaches for Patent Classification'; preprint, cs.CE). Opened the v2 HTML in full and the v1 abstract. USPTO-70k, title and abstract as input, CPC subclass multi-label, chronological split. https://arxiv.org/html/2601.23200v2

Suzgun et al., HUPD, arXiv 2207.04043 (the scout says NeurIPS 2023 D&B; the abstract page I opened lists only arXiv). More than 4.5M applications 2004-2018; tasks include acceptance prediction and multi-class subject-area classification. Opened the abstract and the HF card only. OpenAlex lists 28 citing works, 13 from 2025 or later, none of them an LLM-vs-encoder by-frequency study.

Yoshikawa & Krestel, 'Do large language models understand patents? Enhancing patent classification through AI-generated summaries', World Patent Information 2025, doi 10.1016/j.wpi.2025.102353. Title and authors only, from OpenAlex; no abstract was available.
Pujari et al. 2021 (USPTO-70k origin): cited by Emer et al., not opened.
IPBench, arXiv 2504.15524: abstract opened. It does not mention CPC/IPC classification, so the scout's claim that it tests CPC is unconfirmed.
Yousefiramandi & Cooney, arXiv 2605.24297 (patent embedding benchmark with classification): abstract page opened; arXiv admin withdrew it for quality reasons.
prior_like_ours: Emer et al. arXiv 2601.23200 v1 (abstract opened). Encoders do best overall, driven by frequent subclasses; LLMs do relatively better on infrequent subclasses. The authors call the two complementary and motivate hybrids.

Emer et al. v2 (HTML opened). Encoders: BERT, SciBERT, PatentSBERTa, BERT-for-Patents, plus long-tail variants trained with focal or asymmetric loss and oversampling. LLMs: Phi-3, Mistral-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-12B, run zero-shot, few-shot (TF-IDF-retrieved examples), with RAG over CPC definitions, and as a LoRA-tuned Qwen. Macro-F1: standard BERT-for-Patents 0.208, Qwen few-shot 0.320, long-tail BERT-for-Patents 0.410, Qwen-LoRA 0.379. Results are not reported by frequency bin; instead they report correlations between per-subclass F1 and training frequency (rho about 0.24-0.29) and a 'rare F1' on the bottom 20% of subclasses. Hybrid: the most uncertain 2/5/10/20% of patents by encoder uncertainty go to Qwen-LoRA, which picks among encoder or retrieval candidates. At 5% the full set scores 0.614 micro / 0.412 macro, barely different from the encoder alone; the routed subset rises from 0.298 to 0.378 micro. They do not use a learned per-item selector, frequency features, a frozen selector across years, a rare-label false-positive or precision analysis at natural prevalence (only count-deviation errors), or frontier API LLMs.
Citation lookups of Emer et al. (OpenAlex: 7 citing works; Semantic Scholar: 3) found no follow-up that routes or selects between an LLM and an encoder on patents.
checked.open_ground: Claim 1 would still be new: a learned per-item selector over frequency and agreement features, fitted on one year and frozen for a later year. Emer et al. use a fixed uncertainty threshold, report a negligible full-set gain, and did not compare against a cascade, a frequency rule or a majority vote. Claim 2 is largely taken at subclass level by Emer v1. It would be new only at main-group level, with the single first-CPC label, a training-size sweep, and frontier API LLMs, and the main-group tail must first be verified. Claim 3 (rare-code precision and a review queue at natural prevalence) has not been done on patents. One caveat: a strong long-tail encoder (asymmetric loss plus oversampling) beats every LLM on macro-F1 there, so the 'LLMs win the tail' premise is weaker on this data.
risks: The subclass level has no 1-5 tail (the rarest subclass has 4 items even in a 12-year sample), so the project would have to work at main-group level, where the code list is far longer than several hundred and zero-shot prompting with the full list becomes hard (it needs candidate retrieval).
Emer et al. have already published the frequency split and a router on USPTO-70k, so reviewers will see our work as incremental unless the selector clearly beats their uncertainty routing.
CPC revisions make codes drift between training and test years, and current-CPC reclassification rewrites old labels.
Label noise: initial contractor classification had 19-27% error. Grants are examiner-signed, but no first-symbol agreement figure exists.
Access is in flux: the PatentsView S3 links return 403 and downloads moved to the USPTO Open Data Portal, which may need an API key. HUPD has a licence conflict (NC vs SA) and stops at 2018.
The text is long (claims or descriptions), which raises LLM cost at natural proportions over hundreds of thousands of patents a year.
scout_errors: The PatentsView download URL the scout gave now redirects (301) to data.uspto.gov, and the old S3 bulk links return 403. Availability as described is out of date.
IPBench testing CPC/IPC is not supported by its abstract (the scout had it from a snippet only).
HUPD as NeurIPS 2023 D&B: the arXiv abstract page lists no venue; unconfirmed.

The scout implies that a natural tail at subclass level is plausible for some dozens of codes. In fact USPTO-70k's rarest subclass has 4 items over 12 years, which suggests a 1-5 tail barely exists at subclass level.

The scout's 'who labels' framing (contractors with a 19-27% error rate) applies to initial application classification. It omits that MPEP 905.03(b) requires the primary examiner to review and sign the issue classification of grants, which makes the labels on granted patents more trustworthy than the scout implies.

Emer et al.'s USPTO-70k label is multi-label subclasses, not the first CPC; the scout says 'multi-label in their set', which is correct, but the scout's dataset framing assumes the first CPC is what prior work used.
unverified: The number of CPC subclasses (about 655) and main groups in the current scheme.
US grant and application counts per year for 2024-2026.
The per-year count distribution of first-CPC main groups, which needs g_cpc_current or g_cpc_at_issue plus g_patent (the scout says about 462 MB; I could not reach the file).
The current USPTO Open Data Portal bulk access terms and whether an API key is needed.
The joint EPO-USPTO CPC quality-assurance programme and AI pre-classification at the EPO.
The EPO full-text licence and size.

Search coverage: the shared web-search budget for this run was already used up when I started (my first WebSearch was refused). So I did not run eight search-engine queries. Prior work was checked by opening the known papers and by OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar citation lookups of Emer et al. and HUPD. Patent LLM-classification papers from 2025-2026 that cite neither could have been missed.
checked.time_split: Filing, publication and grant dates are available, so a 2024 / 2025 / 2026 split is possible with PatentsView or ODP data (HUPD stops at 2018). Emer et al. already use a chronological split (train 2006-2017, validation 2018, test 2019). CPC scheme revisions complicate the split.
checked.text: Title and abstract (about 100-250 words, the input Emer et al. used), claims, or full description (pages). English. Boilerplate is moderate; the same family can appear several times (an application and its grant), so deduplication by family is needed. The code word itself rarely appears in the text, but CPC titles overlap with technical vocabulary.
checked.effort: The data download is hundreds of MB for the PatentsView CPC and abstract tables, or 125 GB for HUPD. About 3-5 days of cleaning: family deduplication, choosing at-issue vs current CPC, and mapping across scheme revisions. Encoder training on one year of grants would use a few hundred thousand items. LLM coding at natural proportions on a full test year would be hundreds of thousands of calls, so a sample would be needed.

checked.name: MIMIC-IV with MIMIC-IV-Note: ICD-10 coding of discharge summaries (MDACE as an audited subset)
checked.one_line: This is the best-known long-tail coding benchmark, and the codes are assigned by billing coders rather than by the note writers. Against our criteria it bends three ways: access is credentialed under a data use agreement that blocks commercial APIs unless zero retention is verified; dates fall only in 3-year bins, which makes a yearly split impossible; and the rare-vs-frequent split between LLMs and fine-tuned classifiers is already published on this data. A per-note selector and a test at natural proportions still look unpublished.
checked.access: Opened https://physionet.org/content/mimiciv/3.1/ and https://physionet.org/content/mimic-iv-note/2.2/. Both need a credentialed PhysioNet account, CITI 'Data or Specimens Only Research' training, and a signed Credentialed Health Data Use Agreement 1.5.0 (licence: Credentialed Health Data License 1.5.0). Both pages say only credentialed users who sign the DUA can get the files. Bulk download is possible once credentialed. MIMIC-IV-Note has 331,794 deidentified discharge summaries from 145,915 patients, plus 2,321,355 radiology reports. MIMIC-IV (v3.0 figures on the 3.1 page) has 364,627 patients and 546,028 hospitalizations covering 2008-2022. I also opened the PhysioNet post of 2025-09-24 (https://physionet.org/news/post/llm-responsible-use/). It says the DUA forbids sharing data with third parties, including sending it through APIs. A cloud LLM is allowed only after the user verifies zero retention, no training use and no human review, and the post adds that zero-retention claims may not be enough. Local LLMs are 'Strongly Recommended'. So the two open ~30B models are fine, while Claude Opus 5.5 would need a verified zero-data-retention arrangement, which in practice is a real obstacle.
checked.who_labels: Opened the MIMIC documentation page for hosp/diagnoses_icd (https://mimic.mit.edu/docs/iv/modules/hosp/diagnoses_icd). Codes are billed at discharge, and 'trained personnel' assign them after reading the signed clinical notes. So the person who codes is not the person who wrote the note, which meets criterion b better than MAUDE or SDR. seq_num is the billing priority. The page says the ordering is only loosely reliable, especially for the 5th to 10th codes, and that the codes reflect what was billed, not a complete clinical record. No agreement figure or audit exists for MIMIC-IV codes as a whole. The only audit is MDACE (opened https://aclanthology.org/2023.acl-long.416/): 302 inpatient and 52 profee charts from MIMIC-III (not MIMIC-IV), annotated by professional medical coders with evidence spans. The abstract gives no agreement figure. The Code Like Humans paper (HTML opened) evaluates on the MDACE test split and studies codes that are systematically left off ('blind spots'), so the billing labels are known to be incomplete.
checked.label_space: ICD-10-CM has 70K+ codes (Motzfeldt 2025, abstract opened). Edin et al. 2023 (PDF opened, Table 1) counts 7,942 unique codes in its MIMIC-IV ICD-10 split of 122,279 documents, after dropping codes seen fewer than 10 times. ICD-9 has 6,150 codes over 209,326 documents. The task is natively multi-label: Edin reports a median of 14 codes per document (IQR 9-20). It reduces to one code per item by keeping the principal diagnosis (seq_num 1). That is a legitimate single label, but it is not the benchmark task anyone reports. ICD-9 is used before Oct 2015 and ICD-10 after, so the code list changes partway through the data. Within ICD-10-CM the list changes a little each fiscal year (not checked here).
checked.tail_shape: Only partly checked. Edin 2023 gives 7,942 ICD-10 codes left after removing codes with fewer than 10 occurrences across the whole 122k-document set. So many more codes exist below that cutoff, and the extreme tail is real and natural rather than made by subsampling. The 69.6%-below-10 figure the scout attributed to arXiv 2605.17755 does not appear in its abstract (opened), so it stays unverified. How many distinct principal-diagnosis codes appear per year, and how many have 1-5 items, cannot be had without the data. That needs hosp/diagnoses_icd.csv.gz (roughly 30-35 MB compressed, from memory, unverified) plus hosp/admissions and hosp/patients for the anchor_year_group, all behind credentialing. Items per year: about 331,794 discharge summaries over roughly 2008-2019 suggests on the order of 25-30k a year (my arithmetic). The ICD-10 part, 122,279 documents, covers only about 2015-Q4 onward. Since every principal-diagnosis label is one of several thousand ICD-10 codes, many codes will have 1-5 items in a 3-year bin. This is very likely but unverified.
standing: Edin, Junge, Havtorn, Borgholt, Maistro, Ruotsalo, Maaløe, SIGIR 2023 (arXiv 2304.10909, PDF opened): reproduced ICD coding models and defined the MIMIC-IV ICD-9 and ICD-10 splits (Table 1 numbers quoted above). This is the standard benchmark split; codes seen fewer than 10 times are dropped.

Motzfeldt, Edin, Christensen, Hardmeier, Maaløe, Rogers, EMNLP Findings 2025, arXiv 2509.05378 (abstract and HTML opened): Code Like Humans, a multi-agent coder over the full ICD-10 list, evaluated mainly on MDACE (MIMIC-III).

Yock (arXiv lists Eng), Cao, Chen, Mao, Jiang, EMNLP 2026 main, arXiv 2609.13806 (abstract and HTML opened): neural, workflow and agentic coders compared on rarity-stratified MIMIC-IV discharge summaries.
Liu and Nguyen, arXiv 2605.17755, May 2026 (abstract opened): training on ICD-9 and ICD-10 data together improves a label-wise attention model on rare ICD-10 codes. No LLMs.
Wang, Li, Chen, Luo, Ding, arXiv 2606.13940, June 2026 (abstract opened): prompting vs SFT vs GRPO for generative ICD coding against discriminative baselines. The abstract does not name the dataset.
prior_like_ours: Yock et al., EMNLP 2026 (arXiv 2609.13806, HTML opened): 150 test notes sampled 50 per stratum by the minimum training frequency of their codes (0-100, 101-1,000, >1,000), plus a 153-note multi-step subset. Rare-code micro-F1 is 0.227 for PLM-ICD against 0.560 for the CodeSeeker workflow with Opus 4.6, so the rare-to-LLM / frequent-to-classifier split is published here. Section 4 (read in full earlier, notes/citation-check-2026-11-06.md) gives PLM-ICD candidates to the agent as a tool, with mixed results. No per-document choice between systems. The HTML says outright that it does not use a natural distribution, because uniform sampling is dominated by common codes. Its false-positive analysis covers the multi-step subset only, not rare codes.

Motzfeldt et al., EMNLP Findings 2025 (arXiv 2509.05378, HTML opened): the agent is best on rare codes and PLM-ICD keeps the lead on frequent ones (abstract). Their main table shows the same macro-F1 (0.02) for both, so the rare advantage is not given as a per-stratum table in the main results. No routing or combination is tried; the paper only notes the strengths are complementary and points to human-in-the-loop tools. Evaluated on the MDACE test split, probably at natural prevalence (not stated). The controlled experiments use sampled hard-negative candidate sets.

preprints.org 202512.2138 (the scout's 'PLM-ICD candidates plus an LLM accept/reject filter on 19,801 MIMIC-IV summaries'): the page returned 403 when I fetched it, so it is unverified. If accurate, it is a classifier-then-LLM filter cascade, the closest thing to a combination, but not a per-document choice between coders.

Wang et al., arXiv 2606.13940 (abstract opened): the abstract names full-taxonomy recall as the bottleneck. The scout's claim that it proposes classifier recall plus LLM verification as future work is not in the abstract; the full text was not read.
checked.open_ground: Claim 2 (LLMs beat the encoder on codes with 1-5 training items, the encoder leads on frequent codes) is already published on this data by Motzfeldt 2025 and Yock 2026, so it would only replicate. Claim 1 (a frozen selector that keeps one coder's answer per item, judged by the codes the coders propose, against a cascade, a frequency rule and a majority vote, on a later period) was not found in any MIMIC paper I opened. Yock gives classifier candidates to the agent as a tool, and the 403-blocked preprint is reportedly a candidates-then-LLM filter, so the closest work is cascades, not selection. Claim 3 (natural-proportion evaluation and the false-alarm cost of rare-code answers) also looks open: Yock deliberately avoids natural sampling and has no rare-code false-positive analysis. But it would have to be redone for multi-label, or by reducing to the principal diagnosis, which reviewers may see as a non-standard task. The commercial-LLM arm may not be allowed under the DUA.
risks: The DUA blocks sending notes to the Claude API unless zero retention, no training use and no human review are verified (PhysioNet post, 2025-09-24). The Opus arm might have to be dropped, or run only via a zero-data-retention contract.

No yearly temporal split: dates are shifted per patient, and only anchor_year_group (3-year bins: 2008-10, 2011-13, 2014-16, 2017-19, 2020-22) gives real time. Each patient has one group, so an individual admission's real year is only approximate. ICD-10 starts in late 2015, so an ICD-10 train/test by period is roughly 2014-16 vs 2017-19, which is coarse and partly ICD-9.
The native task is multi-label (median 14 codes). Cutting to the principal diagnosis is not the benchmark everyone reports, and the low-priority ordering is unreliable (MIMIC docs).
The rare-vs-frequent split is already published here (Motzfeldt 2025, Yock 2026), so claim 2 adds nothing new on this dataset.

Labels are billing codes: there is no audit or agreement figure for MIMIC-IV. The expert re-annotation (MDACE) is 354 MIMIC-III charts, far too small for a natural-proportion rare-code test. Known under-coding means a 'false' rare answer may sometimes be right.

Discharge summaries are long (median about 1,500 words, Edin Table 1), so zero-shot plus 10-example prompts over a several-thousand-code list cost a lot of GPU time on the open models and may not fit the context window.
Single hospital (BIDMC). Results are about one coding department.
scout_errors: arXiv 2605.17755 (Liu and Nguyen, opened abstract) does not state that codes seen fewer than 10 times are 69.6% of MIMIC-IV codes. The abstract mentions only '18K rare ICD codes'. The figure may be in the body, but it is unverified and should not be cited from the snippet.
MDACE is a MIMIC-III subset (302 inpatient plus 52 profee charts), not a re-annotated subset of MIMIC-IV, which the scout's record implies by putting it 'with MIMIC-IV-Note'.

The scout says Wang et al. 2606.13940 suggests classifier recall plus LLM verification as future work. The abstract does not say this; it names full-taxonomy recall as the bottleneck. The full text was not read.

Yock 2026's strata (0-100, 101-1,000, >1,000) and rare micro-F1 (0.227 vs 0.560) are correct, but the 0.560 comes from the CodeSeeker workflow system with Opus 4.6, not a free-form 'Opus 4.6 agent' (free-form agent: 0.354).
checked.text: Discharge summaries: in Edin's MIMIC-IV ICD-10 split the median is 1,492 words (IQR 1,147-1,931). That is several pages, longer than our criterion of a sentence to a page. English, with structured sections (history, hospital course, discharge diagnoses). Deidentified, with every PHI item replaced by three underscores (MIMIC-IV-Note page). The discharge-diagnosis section often states the diagnosis in words, so the code's meaning frequently appears in the text, which makes it easier than MAUDE.
checked.time_split: Coarse only. Per-patient date shift into 2100-2200, plus anchor_year_group in 3-year bins from 2008 to 2022 (MIMIC-IV page, opened). ICD-10 starts in Oct 2015. A feasible split is ICD-10 admissions from patients in group 2014-2016 for training and 2017-2019 for test. Whether MIMIC-IV-Note covers 2020-2022 was not checked.
checked.effort: Credentialing (CITI course plus a reference) takes about 1-2 weeks. Downloads after approval: MIMIC-IV-Note discharge.csv.gz is about 1 GB and the hosp tables a few hundred MB (from memory, unverified). Cleaning to principal-diagnosis ICD-10 items with an approximate year: 1-2 days. Items: about 120k ICD-10 admissions in total, so roughly 30-60k for encoder training per period bin. LLM coding of a natural test bin with long notes on local ~30B models would take days of GPU time. Claude only under zero data retention.
unverified: How many principal-diagnosis ICD-10 codes have 1-5 items per 3-year bin (needs diagnoses_icd plus admissions, behind credentialing)
The 69.6% share of codes with fewer than 10 occurrences (scout snippet of 2605.17755)
The preprints.org 202512.2138 hybrid PLM-ICD plus LLM filter (page returned 403)
Whether MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries extend past 2019
File sizes of diagnoses_icd.csv.gz and discharge.csv.gz
Whether the Anthropic API can be set up with verified zero data retention for this user

checked.name: Mozilla Bugzilla (bugzilla.mozilla.org): bug report text to Product::Component
checked.one_line: The scout's counts are right and the tail is real: about 210 codes with 1-5 defects a year, even after dropping admin buckets. The labels are the weak point. They are routing labels: the reporter picks the first, triagers correct some, and Mozilla's own BugBug model moves others (13% of 2024 defects). Nobody has audited them, the text often names the answer, there is no bulk dump and no clear licence. I found no paper that compares LLMs with fine-tuned models by component frequency on this data.
checked.access:
Checked live on 2026-11-11 with curl, no login and no key.
- Both the REST count API and report.cgi CSV answer. report.cgi needs action=wrap and bug_type=defect. Without action=wrap it returns its HTML index page; without bug_type=defect it counts all 64,340 bugs filed in 2024.
- REST also returns summaries and comments without login. I read 200 summaries and the comments of three bugs.
- There is no bulk dump. About 37k defects a year, with first comments and change histories, would have to be paged through REST.
- Security bugs are hidden.
- Licence: I found none for Bugzilla content. The Mozilla services terms page I opened covers Mozilla-account services and does not mention Bugzilla. It licenses user content to Mozilla only, and its footer names no specific Creative Commons licence.
- I found no data-use agreement, no credentialing and no clause on LLM APIs.
Treat the terms as unclear, not as permissive.
checked.who_labels:
The reporter picks the first product and component. Others correct it afterwards.
- The Firefox triage policy page (opened) says managers name a triage owner for each component. New bugs should be triaged within a week, and *::General bugs routed to a specific component within a week. Anyone triaging may move S3/S4 bugs. Firefox::General bugs go through BugBug and are moved automatically when its confidence clears a threshold.
- The BugBot component rule (opened: github mozilla/bugbot, bugbot/rules/component.py and configs/rules.json) does more than that policy page says. It also covers recent bugs in other General components (moves within the same product or to Firefox), Untriaged and Foxfooding bugs, and Fenix subcomponents. The current thresholds are 0.35 overall, 0.8 for General and 0.6 for Fenix.
- I confirmed the bot is BugBug. Three bugs moved by release-mgmt-account-bot carry the bot comment saying that the Bugbug bot is moving the bug.
- Live counts for defects filed in 2024: 11,314 of 37,097 (30.5%) had their component changed and 7,679 their product changed. 4,744 (12.8%) had a component change by the bot, so about 1 in 8 labels is partly a model's output. In the FIXED subset: 2,371 of 11,021 changed, 685 (6.2%) bot-moved.
- I found no agreement study, audit, or expert re-coding of the final components.
The labels are corrected routing assignments, not independent codes. The FIXED subset is better, because a developer actually fixed the bug in that component, but it is still unaudited.
checked.label_space:
Product::Component pairs, one per bug, flat list with a two-level hierarchy (product, then component).
- Defects filed in 2024 fall in 633 pairs, those filed in 2025 in 630.
- The list is not stable over years. Of the 630 pairs used in 2025, 71 (463 bugs) had no 2024 defect. Only 148 of the 218 rare 2024 pairs appear again in 2025.
- Products are reorganized over time (for example Core Graveyard, and the Fenix moves).
- report.cgi counts by the current component, not the component at filing.
- Some products are not software components at all: Invalid Bugs, Web Compatibility site reports, bugzilla.mozilla.org, Data Platform and Tools.
checked.tail_shape:
I checked this myself from report.cgi CSV tables of product by component, filtered with bug_type=defect. All of the scout's figures reproduce exactly.

Defects per year:
- 2024: 37,097
- 2025: 35,636
- FIXED and filed in 2024: 11,021
- All bug types filed in 2024: 64,340

Pairs binned by yearly count (1-5 / 6-20 / 21-89 / 90+):

|---|---|---|---|

checked.text:
Summary plus first comment, in English, from a line to a page. Many FIXED defects are developer- or fuzzer-filed crash reports with assertion messages and source paths (for example /dom/webgpu/...) that point straight at the component.

Crude leakage check: in 68 of 200 FIXED 2024 summaries, a non-trivial word of the component name appears in the summary itself. Leakage is real.

There are many templated crash and intermittent-failure reports, and duplicates are closed as DUPLICATE.
checked.time_split: Creation timestamps are available, so 2024 train / 2025 dev / 2026 test is possible. Code churn between years is about 11% of pairs, so the test set has unseen codes.
standing: Dipongkor and Moran, ASE 2023, arXiv 2310.06913. I opened the HTML. They fine-tune transformer encoders (DeBERTa best) for component and developer assignment on Eclipse JDT, Eclipse Platform, Mozilla Core (105 components) and Mozilla SeaMonkey (33). Split: chronological, 11 folds. No per-frequency analysis, no LLM prompting.

Lajko, Nagy and Vidacs, ICSOFT 2026 (SciTePress), doi 10.5220/0015235300004088. I opened the abstract page. Eclipse only, developer assignment. TF-IDF+XGBoost reaches 76.5% top-1, ahead of fine-tuned E5 (72.5%) and LLM RAG (36.8%). No frequency analysis, no routing.

Dipongkor, An Ensemble Method for Bug Triaging using Large Language Models, ICSE Companion 2024, doi 10.1145/3639478.3641228. Title and venue from Crossref only; ACM returned 403 and there is no abstract.

Patil, Tao and Jadon, GitBugs, arXiv 2504.09651 (2025). I opened the abstract. Nine projects including Firefox; built for duplicate detection, triage and temporal analysis. The abstract does not say whether components are included.

Mozilla BugBug (Mozilla Hacks 2019). I opened the post. It is a production XGBoost component classifier trained on title, first comment and flags. It was limited to components with at least 1% of the largest component's bugs, at 60% confidence, with above 80% precision on bugs from Dec 2018 to Mar 2019.

Also seen as titles only via Crossref: RABTR Retrieval-Augmented Bug Triage With Reasoning (IEEE Access 2026, doi 10.1109/access.2026.3733430); Exploiting Component Information with a Context-Based Language Model for Effective Bug Triage (SSRN 5338906); A Comparative Study of Bug Triage ... from Canonical to Large Language Models (ICAICE 2024, doi 10.1109/icaice63571.2024.10864116). Their datasets and tasks are unverified.
prior_like_ours: I found none that compares a prompted LLM with a fine-tuned encoder by component frequency on Mozilla, picks between them per bug, or tests at natural prevalence.

Closest: Lajko et al. ICSOFT 2026 compare classical, fine-tuned and LLM-RAG triage, but on Eclipse developer assignment, with no frequency breakdown or routing. Dipongkor ICSE-C 2024 ensembles LLMs for triage (content unverified). RABTR 2026 is retrieval-augmented triage (content unverified, could overlap with our retrieval coder).
BugBug itself already routes Mozilla bugs: it acts only above a confidence threshold, a production confidence cascade on exactly this label.
risks: Labels are routing decisions, not audited codes. 13% of 2024 defects were placed by BugBug, which makes them circular if a model is then evaluated against them.
Strong leakage: source paths and component words appear in the text.
No explicit licence for reuse or for sending text to a commercial LLM API. No bulk dump, so the data must be scraped via REST.
The code list churns year to year: 71 new pairs in 2025, and 70 of 218 rare 2024 pairs vanish.
The rare bin holds only about 460 items a year, so per-bin estimates are noisy.
Reviewers in maintenance and reliability may see software triage as a different task.

The literature search was cut short: the WebSearch budget for this turn was exhausted on the first query, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar refused (rate limit) and the arXiv API returned empty. Only Crossref (about 10 queries) worked, so 2025-2026 LLM triage papers on arXiv may be missed.
