The 60% threshold is from 2019. The current BugBot config uses 0.35 overall, 0.8 for General and 0.6 for Fenix.
Not an error: the bot account is indeed BugBug, which I confirmed from bot comments.
report.cgi needs action=wrap and bug_type (not type) to give the defect-only CSV. The scout's numbers are nevertheless correct.
GitBugs listing no component field is not shown on its abstract page; that claim is unverified rather than confirmed.
unverified: The component at filing versus the final component, per bin.
The 2026 year-to-date tail.
Contents of RABTR 2026, the SSRN component paper, ICAICE 2024 and ICSE-C 2024.
Whether GitBugs includes components and under which licence.
arXiv 2508.21156 and 2610.34127, which I did not open.
The DeepTriage line on Mozilla, which I did not open.
checked.effort: No download needed for counts. Text needs about 37k bugs a year via REST, at 1,200 bugs per page or so, plus a history call per bug for the bot filter, about 37k calls a year. That is a day or two of polite paging and 2-3 days of cleaning (drop admin buckets, bot-moved bugs, crash templates). Encoder training would use about 30k items a year (about 10k for FIXED only). LLM coding of a 2026 test set at natural proportions would be about 30k items.

checked.name: US Customs rulings (CBP CROSS) labelled with HTSUS tariff codes
checked.one_line: Large, dated, labelled by government specialists, and the ground is open. But the specialist who picks the code also writes the text and states the code in it. Rulings are few per year and spread over thousands of codes, many rulings carry several codes, there is no official bulk export, and the code list changes every year.
checked.access:
CBP's endpoint rulings.cbp.gov/api/stat/lastupdate (opened 2026-11-11) reports 222,344 searchable rulings. The most recent ruling is dated 2026-10-30.

The CROSS search API refuses scripted calls (security parameters missing), and I did not try to get around it. The CROSS home page states no terms and offers no bulk download. There should be no barrier to LLM APIs because this is US government work, but CBP does not say so; I inferred it.

On Hugging Face:
- The ATLAS original (flexifyai/...) cannot be reached.
- A public mirror, Dayanand314Krishna/cross_rulings_hts_dataset_for_tariffs, is tagged apache-2.0 and has 18,254/200/200 rows (about 24 MB). Each row is an LLM-written question plus the code and LLM-written reasoning. It has no date.
- A third-party scrape, orlandowhite/hts-cross-rulings, has 80,844 rows (about 323 MB) and no card or licence. Its fields include ruling_id, date, hts_code, description, reasoning and original_ruling_text. I read only its first rows.
checked.who_labels:
A CBP specialist (the National Commodity Specialist Division for New York rulings, or Headquarters) issues a binding ruling after an importer asks for one. The ATLAS paper and a sampled original letter confirm this.

The labeller also writes the text. The letter describes the product and states the code; the sampled letter contains a line naming the tariff number. So the label is independent of the importer, but not of the text.

I found no agreement or audit figure for CROSS rulings. Rulings can be modified or revoked later, which is a kind of correction, but I have not counted how often. The 95% expert accuracy belongs to HSCodeComp (632 e-commerce items), a different set. arXiv 2605.14857 reports a manual audit suggesting that some HSCodeComp gold labels break the HS rules.
checked.label_space: There are thousands of 10-digit HTSUS codes. ATLAS reports 2,992 distinct codes in 18,731 rulings. The hierarchy runs chapter, heading, 6-digit HS, then 8 and 10 digits. Rulings can carry several codes: both mirror examples list two. The 10-digit statistical suffixes are revised every year, and the 6-digit HS level changes every five years. The next revision (HS 2027) is from memory and unverified.
checked.tail_shape:
Not verified per year. The totals give roughly 6,000 rulings a year (222,344 over about 37 years), an average only, not a measured yearly count. With 2,992 codes in 18.7k rulings in ATLAS, a single year would have nearly every code in the 1-5 bin and very few with 21 or more, so the head the encoder needs is thin.

The HF filter and rows APIs on the 80,844-row mirror failed (authentication timeouts), so I have no yearly counts. Measuring them needs either the orlandowhite cross_rulings.json (about 292 MB) or the filtered file (about 32 MB), or the datasets-server once it recovers.
standing: ATLAS: Yuvraj and Devarakonda (Flexify.AI), arXiv 2509.18400 (2025). Opened the HTML. 18,731 rulings, 2,992 codes, random 18,254/200/200 split. Inputs and reasoning were rewritten by GPT-4o-mini. Compares a fine-tuned Llama-3.3-70B (40% at 10 digits, 57.5% at 6 digits) with GPT-5-Thinking (25%, 55.5%) and others. No encoder baseline, no analysis by frequency.

HSCodeComp: Lan, Yang et al., ACL 2026 long paper 937 (opened the anthology page) and arXiv 2510.19631 (abstract). 632 e-commerce products labelled by tariff experts. Best agent 46.8%, experts 95%. Does not use CROSS.
Zhang et al., arXiv 2605.14857 (2026). Abstract only. A deterministic agentic workflow on HSCodeComp with Qwen3.6. No fine-tuned encoder.
Nguyen et al., arXiv 2606.16987 (RTD 2026). Abstract only. A consensus multi-agent LLM run on 3,300 private expert-labelled records, not CROSS. No encoder, no routing.

Hari et al., NLLP 2026 paper 49, 'Right Code, Wrong Reasons'. Abstract only. HS-BENCH, 1,390 descriptions paired with legal authorities. Tests whether frontier models give the right reasons. No classifier.
prior_like_ours: None found. None of ATLAS or the three papers that cite it which I opened (2605.14857, 2606.16987, NLLP 2026.49) compares a fine-tuned encoder with an LLM by code frequency, routes between them, or tests at natural prevalence. Search was limited: the web-search budget was used up before this check began, OpenAlex hit its daily limit after one citation listing, and Semantic Scholar returned 429. Only the papers citing ATLAS and HSCodeComp were traced, so older BERT-on-customs work (Korea, China) is unchecked.
checked.open_ground:
All three claims would be new on CROSS: the selector, prompted LLMs beating the encoder on codes with 1-5 items, and the test at natural proportions.

Two things weaken this. First, a natural year is almost all tail, so the encoder-leads-on-frequent-codes half of claim 2 may not show. Second, the rare-code false-positive arithmetic changes, because rarity here is the normal state, not 1 in 1,198.
risks: The labeller writes the text and states the code. Leakage must be stripped, and the style remains.
Multi-code rulings must be reduced to a single label.
No official bulk export. Using a third-party scrape with no licence, or scraping CBP, is a provenance problem for reviewers.
Yearly HTS revisions break the train-2024 / test-2026 code list. Codes would need mapping or truncation to 6 digits.
About 6,000 a year is far smaller than MAUDE, and the head is too thin for the encoder.
Not a failure or maintenance domain. That is now allowed, but it changes the paper's framing.
scout_errors: ATLAS inputs are not raw ruling text: GPT-4o-mini wrote the product descriptions and reasoning (the scout missed this).
The licence is not stated in the ATLAS paper. The scout's 'MIT per the paper' is not confirmed; the HF mirror says apache-2.0.
The ~220k count is now confirmed by CBP's own API (222,344), not only by snippets.
A larger dated mirror (80,844 rows) exists, which the scout missed.
'26 tariff experts' for HSCodeComp is not confirmed; the pages opened say only 'experts'.
unverified: Rulings per year and the code-frequency bins within a year
Share of rulings with more than one code
Rate of ruling revocation or modification
Terms of use of CROSS
Older BERT work on customs HS codes
checked.text: Letters run from a paragraph to a page, in English. They contain the code and the legal reasoning, and both must be removed.
checked.time_split: Rulings are dated, with daily additions into 2026, so a year split is possible. Code revisions complicate it.
checked.effort: Scrape or use the unlicensed mirror (about 0.3 GB). Cleaning (stripping codes, single-labelling, mapping across HTS versions) would take about 1-2 weeks. Roughly 6,000 items a year.

checked.name: US patents with CPC/IPC codes (USPTO grants and applications: HUPD, USPTO-70k, PatentsView / USPTO bulk data)
checked.one_line: Labels are better than MAUDE's (a USPTO primary examiner reviews the codes at issue) and the corpus is huge and well known. But the label is natively multi-label, there is no real 1-5 item tail at the subclass level most papers use, and the encoder-vs-LLM-by-frequency comparison plus uncertainty routing has already been done (Emer et al. 2026), where a long-tail-trained encoder beats the LLMs, rare codes included.
checked.access: HUPD dataset card (https://huggingface.co/datasets/HUPD/hupd, opened): 125 GB; covers applications filed January 2004 to December 2018; the licence tag says cc-by-sa-4.0 but the text says CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The scout was right that these disagree. NonCommercial is the binding text, and research LLM use looks compatible with it, but no terms on LLM APIs are stated. The HF dataset viewer refuses HUPD because it runs a loading script, so no server-side statistics exist (checked with datasets-server /info and /size). HUPD abstract (arXiv 2207.04043, abstract only; the PDF was over 10 MB and not read): over 4.5 million applications as originally filed. USPTO-70k: 70,250 patents (Pujari et al. 2021, as described in Emer et al., opened). The old PatentsView download page now 301-redirects to data.uspto.gov/support/transition-guide/patentsview, which loaded empty for me (a JavaScript page), so I could not confirm current bulk-table names, sizes or terms. That USPTO bulk data is public-domain US government data comes from memory and is unverified. No credentialing or DUA was seen for HUPD.
checked.who_labels: MPEP 905 (https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s905.html, opened) settles this for granted patents. Under 905.03(b), when an application is passed to issue, each primary examiner must personally review its classification and sign the Issue Classification form. Under 905.03(a), each patent family gets exactly one 'first' CPC symbol, defined as the inventive symbol that best represents the invention as a whole. Every other symbol, including all 'additional' ones, is marked 'later'. At least one symbol must be C* (covering what is claimed). So the main code on a grant is set or checked by an office examiner, not by the filer. That passes criterion b on provenance, far better than MAUDE. MPEP 903 (opened) and the USPTO classification-division page (opened) do not say who does the pre-examination classification. Contractors are plausible but unverified. The USPTO page mentions a Classification Quality division that 'develops quality assurance metrics' but publishes no figures. I opened no agreement or audit figure. Emer et al. only say in passing that expert examiners disagree, citing Veefkind 2012, Robinson-Garcia 2024 and Rainville 2025, none of which I opened. One SSRN paper (10.2139/ssrn.6430017, 'expert consensus calibration' for ambiguous patent classification) may carry agreement figures, but SSRN returned 403, so I saw only the title (via Crossref). HUPD's card says annotations come from 'patent applicants or the USPTO'. HUPD holds applications as filed, so its main_cpc_label may be pre-grant classification rather than the examiner-reviewed issue classification (unverified).
checked.label_space: Hierarchy: section, class, subclass, main group, subgroup. Jiang et al. (ACL Findings 2026, opened) count 8 sections, 117 classes and 500 IPC subclasses in their HUPD 2011-2017 subset. CPC totals (about 650+ subclasses, thousands of main groups, about 250k symbols) are from memory; the CPC 'about' page I opened gives no counts. Every patent carries several symbols: in USPTO-70k (per Emer) a training patent averages 1.98 subclasses and a test patent 2.32. The task reduces to one code per item through the single 'first' symbol (MPEP 905.03(a)) or HUPD's main_cpc_label. The CPC scheme is revised several times a year, and PatentsView 'current' tables reclassify old patents to the current scheme. Codes are therefore unstable over time unless one uses classification at issue (memory, unverified).
checked.tail_shape: At subclass level there is no 1-5 tail, even across many years. In the USPTO-70k training set (50,250 patents, 2006-2017; Emer et al. appendix, opened), the most frequent subclass is G06F with 6,272 patents. The rarest are C06C, A44D, B28C and C10C with 9 each, and C12L with 4. That is over 12 years on a 70k subsample. A full natural year of US grants (several hundred thousand; memory, unverified) would put almost every subclass well above 5. The tail our project needs would appear only at main-group or subgroup level. There, CPC's thousands of main groups make many 1-5-item codes in a year likely, but I could not verify this without data. To verify, one would fetch the PatentsView/USPTO CPC-at-issue or g_cpc_current table: one TSV per patent-symbol, a zip I recall as several hundred MB to over 1 GB (unverified, far above the 2 MB limit). Alternatively, one would compute counts from HUPD's per-year JSON files, 125 GB in total. Item counts per year are also unverified this session.
standing: Suzgun et al., HUPD, arXiv 2207.04043 (abstract opened): over 4.5M USPTO applications 2004-2018; tasks include patentability decision and multi-class subject-area classification. Its venue (NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks, I believe) was not verified this session.

Emer, Lippi, Mina, Vandin, arXiv 2601.23200 v1 30 Jan 2026, v2 5 Aug 2026, no venue listed (abstract and full HTML opened): USPTO-70k, multi-label CPC subclass, four encoders against open LLMs, plus a hybrid router. Details under prior_like_ours.

Jiang, Sun, Goetz, 'Reasoning for Hierarchical Text Classification: The Case of Patents', arXiv 2510.07167, ACL 2026 Findings per the arXiv comments (abstract and HTML opened): built PCD-BD from HUPD accepted applications 2011-2017 (22,500 train, 2,500 test, plus 2,845 EPO 2024 OOD), main-IPC subclass (500 labels), 45/5 per subclass balanced split; encoders vs GPT-5/DeepSeek-V3 zero-shot vs RL-trained Qwen/Llama.

Yoo, Zhang, Cao, 'Self-Filtered Distillation with LLMs-generated Trust Indicators for Reliable Patent Classification', arXiv 2510.05431 v4 May 2026, no venue (abstract opened): USPTO-2M, LLM rationales distilled into student models with trust weights.
Yoshikawa and Krestel, World Patent Information 2025, doi 10.1016/j.wpi.2025.102353 (title and authors via Crossref only; no abstract seen).
Xiong et al., 'Scalable multi-label patent classification via iterative LLM-assisted active learning', World Patent Information 2025, doi 10.1016/j.wpi.2025.102380 (Crossref title only).
Arxiv search also returned 2611.09194 (LLM consensus plus topic modelling for patent innovation, Nov 2026) and 2608.23420 (bias in green patent classification) as titles only, not opened.
prior_like_ours: Emer et al. 2026 (arXiv 2601.23200 v2, full HTML read in two parts). Data: USPTO-70k, title+abstract, all CPC subclass labels (multi-label, up to 7 predicted), chronological split 50,250 train 2006-2017 / 10,000 val 2018 / 10,000 test 2019. Encoder vs LLM: base BERT-for-Patents macro-F1 0.208, Qwen3.5-9B zero-shot 0.164, few-shot 0.320, LoRA 0.379, long-tail-trained BERT-for-Patents (oversampling plus asymmetric loss) 0.410 (micro 0.592 to 0.616). No per-frequency-bin table: frequency enters only through Spearman correlations of per-subclass F1 with training count (0.239 encoder, 0.287 LoRA Qwen, 0.247 hybrid) and a rare-label F1 on 10,000 EPO patents for the bottom 20% of subclasses by frequency (adapted encoder 0.180, few-shot Qwen 0.045, LoRA Qwen 0.105, hybrid 0.193). Routing: the encoder's most uncertain 2/5/10/20% go to LoRA Qwen, which picks among encoder- or retrieval-proposed candidates. At 5% the full set moves from 0.616/0.410 to 0.614/0.412 (micro/macro). The routed subset rises clearly (micro 0.298 to 0.378 at 5%; significant at 2/5/10% with Wilcoxon and Bonferroni, not at 20%). Not done: a per-item selector over answer features such as the proposed code's training count, zero-shot vs retrieval-prompted LLM as separate coders, single-label first-symbol coding, a natural-prevalence rare-code precision analysis, or test on a later year beyond one.

Jiang, Sun, Goetz (ACL 2026 Findings, arXiv 2510.07167, HTML read): encoders vs zero-shot GPT-5/DeepSeek-V3 vs RL-reasoning Qwen/Llama on 500 main-IPC subclasses. The in-domain split is balanced by construction (45 train / 5 test per subclass), so there is no frequency analysis and no natural prevalence. Hybrids and ensembles are explicitly excluded. GPT-5 zero-shot matches or beats encoders on the EPO OOD set (accuracy 56.1 vs 49.6 for BERT-for-Patent).

Yoo, Zhang, Cao (arXiv 2510.05431, abstract only): combines LLM and fine-tuned models by distilling LLM rationales with trust scores on USPTO-2M; reports up to 38.7% relative macro-F1 gain. No routing or selection between coders seen, no frequency-binned comparison seen in the abstract.
checked.open_ground: Claim 2, as an observation (LLMs beat the encoder on codes with few training items), is not new here. Emer et al. already show few-shot LLMs beating a standard encoder on macro-F1. They also show that a long-tail-trained encoder overturns this, beating LLMs on the bottom-20% rare subclasses as well. A reviewer would ask us to beat that. Claim 1 (a frozen per-item selector over simple answer features, picking among encoder, zero-shot LLM and retrieval LLM, tested on a later year) would still be new on patents. The nearest thing is Emer's uncertainty-threshold router, and it barely moves full-set scores. Claim 3 (natural-prevalence rare-code precision and a review queue) would be new, but only meaningful at CPC main-group level, where the tail is unverified and nobody I found has published frequency-binned LLM-vs-encoder results. So open ground exists mainly at main-group 'first symbol' level, single-label, with selection and natural-prevalence analysis.
risks: The tail fails at subclass level: the rarest USPTO-70k subclass has 4 to 9 patents even over 12 years of a 70k sample, and a full year of grants would leave almost no 1-5 codes. Moving to main groups changes the task to a several-thousand-way choice, which strains a zero-shot prompt that must list the codes.

Native multi-label: reducing to the single 'first' symbol is defensible (MPEP 905.03(a)), but many 'errors' will be other valid symbols of the same patent. Reviewers may object to single-label scoring.

Prior work: Emer et al. 2026 already ran encoder vs LLM with frequency correlation, uncertainty routing and a temporal split on USPTO CPC, and found a long-tail-trained encoder wins overall and on rare labels. Our claim 2 would need that encoder as a baseline.
CPC is revised often, and 'current' tables reclassify old patents. A train-2024 / test-2026 split must use classification at issue or map scheme versions.

HUPD is CC BY-NC-SA (with a mismatched tag), applications only, ends in 2018, and its label may be pre-grant rather than examiner-reviewed. Recent years (2024-2026) would need USPTO bulk data, whose current access path I could not load.
No published inter-examiner agreement figure was opened, so label reliability rests on the procedure (primary-examiner review at issue), not on a measured audit.

Patents leave the owner's field-report and maintenance framing entirely. Abstracts are written by applicants' attorneys, and code words (technology terms) often appear in the text, which makes the task easier for the encoder.

My search was cut short: the session-wide WebSearch budget was exhausted before my first search, and OpenAlex, arXiv and Semantic Scholar repeatedly returned HTTP 429. Coverage of 2025-2026 patent-LLM work is therefore incomplete.
scout_errors: The scout presents USPTO-70k as 'Emer et al.', but Emer cites it as Pujari et al. 2021. The split itself is correct (50,250 / 10,000 / 10,000).

'LLMs relatively better on rare ones' holds only against the base encoder. With the long-tail-trained encoder (macro 0.410 vs LoRA Qwen 0.379), the encoder also wins rare labels: on the bottom-20% EPO subclasses, adapted encoder F1 0.180 vs few-shot Qwen 0.045 and LoRA Qwen 0.105. The v2 abstract leads with the encoder outperforming the LLM.

'At main-group level there is a real tail' is asserted, but nothing published supports it in what I opened. At subclass level the scout's hedge is right and even stronger: the rarest USPTO-70k subclass still has 4 to 9 training patents.

That USPTO examiners assign CPC was marked as memory. It is now partly confirmed: MPEP 905.03(b) requires primary-examiner review of the classification at issue. Who does the pre-examination classification stays unverified, and HUPD (applications) may carry the pre-grant label.

The routed LLM in Emer's hybrid picks only among encoder- or retrieval-proposed candidates, a detail the scout's record omits. The LLM list (Phi-3, Mistral-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-12B) was not confirmed in the parts I read; the abstract names only Qwen3.5-9B as best.
checked.text: Inputs in the papers are title+abstract (Emer, roughly a paragraph) or claims (Jiang), in English, written by applicants or attorneys. Full texts run to many pages. Technology words that name the class often appear in the text. Duplication is likely across continuations and family members (unverified).
checked.time_split: Strong: patents carry filing, publication and grant dates. USPTO-70k already uses 2006-2017 / 2018 / 2019, and HUPD covers filings 2004-2018. A 2024/2025/2026 split needs USPTO bulk grant data, which I could not load. Scheme revisions between years must be handled.
checked.effort: Download: HUPD is 125 GB. USPTO/PatentsView CPC and abstract tables are probably hundreds of MB to a few GB (unverified). Cleaning: about 2-4 days to pick the first CPC symbol at issue, map scheme versions and deduplicate families. Items: hundreds of thousands of grants a year for encoder training (memory, unverified). LLM coding at main-group level needs a few thousand candidate codes per prompt, or a retrieval shortlist, which makes a zero-shot coder costly.
unverified: Number of US grants and applications per year, and the per-code yearly count distribution at main-group level (needs the CPC bulk table).
Total CPC counts (subclasses, main groups, symbols): from memory only.
Who performs pre-examination CPC classification (examiners vs contractors), and whether HUPD's main_cpc_label is pre-grant or at-issue.
Any published inter-examiner or audit agreement figure for CPC (cited by Emer: Veefkind 2012, Robinson-Garcia 2024, Rainville 2025; not opened). SSRN 6430017 returned 403.
Terms of USPTO bulk data (public domain) and the current PatentsView/data.uspto.gov access path and file sizes.
HUPD venue (believed NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks).
Abstracts and content of the two World Patent Information 2025 papers (titles only via Crossref).

Whether any 2025-2026 paper does frequency-binned LLM vs encoder at CPC main-group level. Queries tried: arXiv API abs:patent+classification+'large language' / patent+CPC+LLM / patent+classification+'long-tail' / HUPD / patent+classification+'few-shot' / patent+'main group' (empty); Semantic Scholar 'patent classification large language models fine-tuned comparison', 'CPC patent classification long tail rare subclasses'; Crossref 'patent classification large language model CPC', 'patent classification zero-shot LLM IPC'. Several more failed on HTTP 429, and WebSearch was unavailable (session budget used up).

checked.name: USPTO patents with CPC labels (USPTO-70k benchmark; HUPD; PatentsView)
checked.one_line: The labels are trustworthy (the patent office assigns them, and the examiner reviews them at issue), the data are large, dated and well known, but Emer et al. 2026 already did encoder vs prompted/LoRA LLM with a temporal split plus encoder-to-LLM routing on exactly this benchmark. The labels are multi-label, the HUPD licence is unclear, and the main-group tail I could not verify.
checked.access: Opened the HUPD Hugging Face card (huggingface.co/datasets/HUPD/hupd). It lists 125 GB of utility applications filed from January 2004 to December 2018, with 34 fields including main_cpc_label, main_ipcr_label, cpc_labels, decision and filing_date. The licence is inconsistent: the metadata tag says cc-by-sa-4.0, while the Licensing section says CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. A NonCommercial term does not obviously block research use with a local LLM or an API, but it should be checked. The HF datasets-server reports viewer, statistics and search as all false, because the loader runs Python code (I checked with the is-valid and info endpoints), so no label statistics are available without downloading. USPTO-70k (Emer et al.) is 70,250 title+abstract items, but I did not open a hosting URL for it. I did not open the raw USPTO bulk data or the PatentsView terms. Public-domain status of USPTO data is from memory only.
checked.who_labels: The patent office assigns the labels, not the applicant, and the label is not filer-chosen as in MAUDE or SDR. MPEP 905 (opened: uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s905.html) says that when an application is passed to issue, each primary examiner must personally review the application's "classification picture" on the Issue Classification form. MPEP 903 (opened) says applications are classified at least 9 weeks before publication but does not say who does it. The pre-grant classifier (USPTO staff or contractors) is not named in either section, and no QC programme or agreement figure appears in either. Emer et al. v2 (opened) call the labels "examiner-assigned classifications" and cite Burke and Reitzig (2007) for non-negligible examiner disagreement; I did not open that source and have no figure from it. The HUPD card says only that annotations were produced by applicants or the USPTO. For HUPD applications (pre-grant text), main_cpc_label may come from pre-grant classification rather than from the examiner's review at issue; this is unverified.
checked.label_space: CPC is hierarchical: section, class, subclass, main group, subgroup. Emer et al. use 4-character subclasses and allow up to 7 predictions per patent. Their training set (opened) has a mean of 1.98 and a median of 2 subclasses per patent, and a maximum of 18. So the task is multi-label, but it can be reduced to one code through the main or first CPC (HUPD main_cpc_label; MPEP 905 defines one 'first' symbol per family that best represents the invention). The total number of subclasses (about 650) and main groups (thousands) is from memory only. CPC is revised several times a year, with reclassification, so codes are not perfectly stable over years; this is from memory and unverified.
checked.tail_shape: Verified only for the USPTO-70k training set (50,250 patents, 2006-2017, a sample, not a natural year). The most frequent subclass, G06F, has 6,272 items. The least frequent, C12L, has 4, and C06C, A44D, B28C and C10C have 9 each. The authors say the rarest subclasses have fewer than ten training instances (Emer v2, Table 8, opened). How many subclasses fall in the 1-5 bin is not given. In a natural year (the USPTO grants on the order of 300k+ utility patents a year; from memory, unverified), most subclasses would have far more than 5 items, so a 1-5 tail at subclass level is unlikely. A tail like ours would need the main-group level (main_cpc_label truncated to the group), which is unverified. Verifying it would need either the HUPD per-year metadata (the full repo is 125 GB; the per-year feather/metadata file is likely hundreds of MB, size unverified) or a USPTO/PatentsView CPC-current table (a bulk TSV of several GB, unverified) or the PatentsView API (needs a key; not tried).
standing: Emer, Lippi, Mina, Vandin, arXiv 2601.23200 (v1 30 Jan 2026, v2 5 Aug 2026, not peer-reviewed). Opened the abstract page and the full v2 HTML in two parts. USPTO-70k, temporal split, 4 BERT-family encoders vs 5 open LLMs, LoRA, EPO external validation. https://arxiv.org/html/2601.23200

Suzgun et al., HUPD, arXiv 2207.04043. Opened the abstract only. 4.5M+ applications 2004-2018; tasks include acceptance prediction and multi-class subject-area classification. The page names no venue (a NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks publication is from memory, unverified).
USPTO-70k (Pujari et al. 2021) is named by the scout as an established benchmark. Not opened, unverified.
CPC classification has a long literature (PatentBERT, BERT-for-Patents, etc.). This is from memory; none of it was opened in this check.
prior_like_ours: Emer et al. 2026 (arXiv 2601.23200 v2, opened in full). On USPTO-70k (train 2006-2017, val 2018, test 2019) they compare encoders with zero-shot, zero-shot+RAG, few-shot and few-shot+RAG open LLMs and a LoRA Qwen3.5-9B. Off-the-shelf, the LLM has the higher macro-F1. An encoder retrained for the long tail (macro-F1 0.410, up from 0.208) beats the best LLM. Their hybrid routes the most encoder-uncertain 2/5/10/20% to the LoRA LLM. Routed-subset micro-F1 goes 0.210->0.338 at 2%, 0.298->0.378 at 5%, 0.377->0.418 at 10% and 0.448->0.451 at 20% (the last not significant). The full set at 5% is 0.614 micro / 0.412 macro, essentially unchanged. On EPO, the bottom-20%-frequency rare-F1 is 0.1801 for the adapted encoder and 0.1930 for the 5% hybrid. What they did NOT do: a learned per-item selector over several coders (theirs is an uncertainty threshold, i.e. a confidence cascade), single-label coding, a fine-grained label space with 1-5-item codes, a frequency-bin table of encoder vs LLM (only aggregate micro and macro, plus an EPO rare bin), or any precision-at-natural-prevalence analysis of rare-label answers.
The project's own notes (lit-check-2026-08-18, citation-check-2026-11-06) already list Emer as the closest methodological precedent and say routing is not new; this check confirms that.

No other 2023-2026 work on HUPD or USPTO-70k comparing LLMs and fine-tuned models by label frequency was found, but the search was cut short (see risks): the web-search budget for this turn was exhausted on my first query, so the required eight distinct queries were NOT run.
checked.open_ground: Claim 1 (a learned per-item selector over three coders, fitted and frozen, that beats a confidence cascade) would still be new relative to Emer, whose method is a confidence cascade. But the headline story (LLM for the tail, encoder for the head, route between them, temporal split) is now published on this exact benchmark. Claim 2 (LLM beats encoder on 1-5-item codes at every training size) would be new only at main-group level; at subclass level Emer's long-tail encoder already reverses the LLM advantage. Claim 3 (natural-proportion rare precision, review queue) has not been done on patents as far as I could check, but needs a full natural year, i.e. HUPD- or PatentsView-scale data, not USPTO-70k.
risks: The ground is largely taken by Emer et al. 2026 on the same benchmark with the same temporal-split and routing idea.
The labels are multi-label; reducing to main CPC changes the task from what Emer and others report.
The HUPD licence conflicts (CC-BY-SA tag vs CC BY-NC-SA text), and there is no dataset-server statistics access, so the tail can only be measured after a multi-GB download.

At subclass level a natural year probably has few or no 1-5-item codes; the tail exists only at main-group or subgroup level, which is unverified and makes for a very large code list (thousands) to put in a zero-shot prompt.
Patent abstracts are written to be classifiable, and the code words often appear in the text, so the task may be easier and less like field reports.
The CPC scheme is revised over time, so the code list drifts between years.
Examiner disagreement exists (cited by Emer via Burke and Reitzig 2007), but I found no figure.

The search was incomplete: the WebSearch budget was exhausted at the first query, and per the harness instruction I did not work around it with scholarly APIs. Further prior-work searching needs a follow-up.
scout_errors: The scout said the v1 abstract claims LLMs do relatively better on rare subclasses. The current (v2) abstract, which I opened, leads with the best encoder beating the best LLM and does not mention rare labels or the temporal split; I did not open v1 text separately, so the v1 claim is unverified rather than wrong.
The scout's numbers (70,250 / 50,250 / 10,000 / 10,000 split; G06F 6,272; C12L 4; median 2; routed 5% 0.298->0.378; EPO 0.1930 vs 0.1801) were all confirmed in v2.

'Who labels' is now partly verified: MPEP 905 requires the primary examiner to review the classification at issue. It is not entirely unknown as the scout said, but the pre-grant classifier is still unnamed.
checked.text: Patent title+abstract (USPTO-70k) or full application sections (HUPD: abstract, claims, background, summary, description), in English, from one paragraph to many pages. The applicant writes the text and the office assigns the label. Technical vocabulary overlaps strongly with the CPC titles. Boilerplate and duplication (continuations, family members) exist (from memory, unverified).
checked.time_split: Yes. USPTO-70k is already split 2006-2017 / 2018 / 2019 (verified), and HUPD has filing dates for 2004-2018 (verified on the card). For a 2024/2025/2026 design, HUPD stops at 2018; newer years would need USPTO bulk or PatentsView (unverified).
checked.effort: USPTO-70k: small (70k abstracts), but it is a sample and not natural proportions. HUPD: 125 GB in total, though one year of metadata plus abstracts is far smaller (size unverified). Cleaning is about 2-4 days (CPC normalisation and version mapping). Encoder training on one natural year at main-group level is feasible. LLM coding of one test year (~300k+) is costly, and a zero-shot prompt with thousands of main groups is long.

not_checked.name: VAERS (Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System), MedDRA Preferred Terms
not_checked.weakest_point: Multi-label by design. Each report carries several PTs, and there is no principal-term field, so reducing to one code is artificial. Reporters are often patients or providers, and the text is partly copied by coders. The domain is vaccine-specific and heavily skewed toward COVID years.
not_checked.who_labels: The guide says that 'All reports are coded and entered to the VAERS database' by VAERS (MedDRA since 17 January 2007). Coders are VAERS program staff or contractors, not the reporter. I found no published QC or agreement figure.

not_checked.name: NIOSH/CDC NEISS-Work OIICS event-code competition set (HF mayerantoine/injury-narrative-coding)
not_checked.weakest_point: There is no long tail at the released granularity, and the test labels are withheld.
not_checked.who_labels: NIOSH coders, per the competition description; details not opened.

not_checked.name: MSHA Accident/Injury/Illness file (Part 50, Form 7000-1)
not_checked.weakest_point: Labels are probably operator-chosen (criterion b fails much like MAUDE), and the code lists may be too short for a real tail.
not_checked.who_labels: Mine operators and contractors file Form 7000-1 (NIOSH paper). The definition file does not say whether MSHA staff assign the codes; several fields carry '?' for invalid codes. No quality-control or agreement figure was found. Treat as filer-labelled unless shown otherwise.

not_checked.name: ATSB National Aviation Occurrence Database
not_checked.weakest_point: Nothing about labels, taxonomy size or access could be opened. The dataset is small per year and the classification papers use short label sets (flight phase).
not_checked.who_labels: Probably ATSB staff coding notifications under the ATSB taxonomy (from memory; the ATSB site timed out twice, so unverified).

not_checked.name: NVD CVE descriptions -> CWE (NIST-analyst subset, plus CNA and CISA-ADP labels)
not_checked.weakest_point: The labels that are third-party (NIST or CISA) are sparse in 2024-2026 and limited to roughly 130-200 View-1003 classes. The labels that cover the long tail are mostly CNA labels, i.e. written by the same party that wrote the text, which is MAUDE's problem again. The topic is also crowded with LLM work.
not_checked.who_labels: Two sources sit side by side in the NVD record. The CNA, often the vendor that wrote the description, supplies a CWE (the 'Secondary' entry). NIST analysts may add their own ('Primary', source nvd@nist.gov). CISA Vulnrichment (CC0) adds a CWE chosen by CISA analysts for some higher-risk CVEs that lack one, and drops it if the CNA later supplies one. My NVD API samples: on 2024-06-03, 113 CVEs, NIST CWE on 38 and CNA CWE on 106; of the 35 with both, 19 were identical and 16 differed. On 2025-09-02, 144 CVEs, NIST CWE on only 19, and all 19 differed from the CNA set. NVD publishes CVMAP reports comparing each CNA's CWE with NIST's, which amounts to an audit, but the pages are rendered by JavaScript and I could not read the summary figures. Mosievskiy calls the NVD labels noisy, with CWE-20 used as a catch-all.

not_checked.name: CBP CROSS customs rulings -> HTS tariff code (ATLAS benchmark)
not_checked.weakest_point: Too few rulings a year for 'tens of thousands per year' (unverified, probably a few thousand). Leakage of the code and reasoning into the ruling text. The ATLAS input is a GPT-4o-mini rewrite of the ruling, not the original text. Bulk access is awkward.
not_checked.who_labels: CBP National Import Specialists, legal experts who are not the importer. The importer asks for a ruling and describes the product; CBP writes the ruling and assigns the code. Third-party expert labels, legally binding. Caveat: the ruling text states the code and its reasoning, so the input has to be cut to the product description.

not_checked.name: SemEval-2025 Task 5 LLMs4Subjects (TIBKAT records with GND subject headings)
not_checked.weakest_point: Multi-label, with no natural single code per record. The overview already reports that LLM advantages over traditional subject-indexing methods are debatable, and over 700 participants have worked this ground (a very crowded field). Per-year volume and dating are unverified.
not_checked.who_labels: Subject librarians at TIB (German National Library of Science and Technology), using the GND authority file. The task overview adds a qualitative evaluation by subject specialists. No published inter-indexer agreement figure was found for this set.

not_checked.name: Library catalogue classification (LC call number / DDC) from Library of Congress MARC records
not_checked.weakest_point: No 2024-2026 data in the free dump (latest release 2016), so a train-2024/test-2026 design is impossible. For most records the text is short, often only a title, and the subject headings leak the label. Prior LLM work (Dobreski & Hastings, LRTS 2025; LLM4DDC 2025) finds LLMs weak at fine levels.
not_checked.who_labels: LC professional catalogers (a third party to the author). LC's own 2024 ML pilot found no model reached its 95% threshold for subject classification (blog, snippet only).

not_checked.name: US congressional bills: CRS legislative subject terms / Policy Agendas Project subtopics
not_checked.weakest_point: Fails the long-tail criterion for single label. The only long-tailed label is multi-label, and the recent Policy Agendas codes may be machine-assigned.
not_checked.who_labels: (a, b) Congressional Research Service / LC legislative indexers. (c) Trained student coders aiming at about 90% major-topic agreement, though later versions moved to automated coding (snippet).

not_checked.name: EU EBTI binding tariff information (CN 8-digit)
not_checked.weakest_point: Bulk access is not established, and the texts are multilingual.
not_checked.who_labels: Customs authority officers of the issuing member state; legally binding.

not_checked.name: Library cataloguing: DDC / subject coding (e.g. Swedish union catalogue, LLMs4Subjects)
not_checked.weakest_point: Text is often only a title or short abstract. Unverified sizes and access. LLM4DDC already compares fine-tuned RoBERTa with prompted LLMs.

not_checked.name: MultiEURLEX / EURLEX57K (EuroVoc-indexed EU legislation)
not_checked.weakest_point: Multi-label, with several descriptors per document, and only a few thousand documents a year, so it fails 'tens of thousands per year'. Single-code reduction is unnatural.
not_checked.who_labels: Indexers at the Publications Office of the EU (dataset card). No agreement figure was seen.

not_checked.name: CAIL2018 (Chinese criminal judgments: charge and law-article labels)
not_checked.weakest_point: Not English, and label quality is not clearly better than the English options. I found no case dates, so a year-to-year split is uncertain. The legal-judgment-prediction field is crowded with LLM studies (unverified).
not_checked.who_labels: The court, through the judgment itself, so the label is a judicial decision. The fact text is also written by the court.

wildcard: Comparative Agendas Project (policy topic codes): only about 220 subtopics, the hand-coded national datasets are small per year so there is no deep natural tail, and LLM-versus-fine-tuned work already exists (Sebők et al. 2025, arXiv 2509.10199, major topics; I saw this only as a search snippet).

wildcard: Occupation coding (ISCO/SOC/KldB/HISCO): the text is usually a few words; the large coded survey sets are restricted; the public sets are historical (OccCANINE, HISCO) or silver-labelled (Gnehm & Clematide, ACL Findings 2025, CH-ISCO with 670 classes; snippet only).

wildcard: MADE (ACL 2026, MAUDE multi-label): already known to the owner. I opened the ACL Anthology PDF. It confirms fine-tuning versus few-shot with more than 20 models, a temporal split, and that large reasoning models do better on rare labels. It is the same MAUDE filer-label problem.

wildcard: ATLAS dataset as released: its inputs are rewritten by GPT-4o-mini and its test split is random and only 200 rulings. Usable only if CROSS is re-scraped from the raw rulings, which is why CROSS is listed as a candidate instead.
wildcard: NEISS-Work / NIOSH OIICS event coding (the CDC text-classification competition data): too few codes (two-digit event codes, about 48) for a tail. Not opened; from memory.
wildcard: OSHA Severe Injury Reports: already judged in the 2026-10-23 search (labels possibly made by the BLS autocoder).

wildcard: Library of Congress MARC records (LCC/LCSH): cataloguers assign the labels, but the usable text is mostly titles, under a sentence. Library of Congress (LoC) tests reported LLMs matching only 26% of cataloguer subject headings on about 23k ebooks (snippet only). Kept off the list because it fails criterion a.
wildcard: PubMed MeSH (BioASQ): multi-label. I recall that NLM moved to automated indexing for most citations in 2022, which would remove the human labels, but I could not verify this.
wildcard: arXiv categories, Stack Overflow tags, e-commerce product categories, CFPB complaint issues, Companies House SIC: the author or filer chooses the label, which fails criterion b.

wildcard: SEC EDGAR SIC codes (assigned by SEC staff): the label belongs to the company, not to each filing, and is stable across years, so there is no meaningful item-level temporal test. Not opened.
wildcard: FDA 510(k) product codes (reviewer-assigned): only a few thousand clearances a year. Not opened (search budget ran out).

wildcard: Generic LLM-versus-classifier surveys (Vajjala & Shimangaud 2025, arXiv 2502.11830; Bucher & Martini 2024; EMNLP Findings 2025 'Do BERT-like models still perform better'): mostly fewer than 50 classes, so no long-tail datasets to borrow. Seen only as snippets.

prior.title: Choosing per item between a fine-tuned classifier and an LLM

report.answer: Choosing per item between a fine-tuned classifier and a prompted LLM is now a crowded idea, but nearly every version I found makes that choice from the encoder's confidence. L2D-Clinical (LREC ClinicalNLP 2026) feeds BERT entropy, margin and text features into a logistic deferral model. CMBS (JBCS 2026, arXiv 2408.09629) uses a calibrated RoBERTa confidence threshold. Emer et al. 2026 (arXiv 2601.23200 v2) pass the 2-20% most uncertain patents to a LoRA Qwen that picks among the encoder's candidates. Zaera 2025 and AdaptiveLog 2025 use classifier uncertainty, and TRACER 2026 uses an acceptor over top-1, top-2, margin and entropy. Abedini & Heydarnoori 2025 instead send an item to GPT-4o when two fine-tuned models disagree. Other designs fuse rather than choose: LabelFusion 2025 runs an MLP over the RoBERTa embedding plus the LLM's label vector. Filter-then-rerank and SuperICL are already in the draft. None of the papers I read uses the training frequency of the proposed label as a selection input, and none compares three coders' answers side by side; the acceptors and deferral models take only confidence, margin, entropy or text features. Results by label-frequency bin are rare: Emer reports one rare-label F1 (bottom 20% of training frequency) and correlations with frequency, and L2D-Clinical, CMBS, TRACER, LabelFusion and Abedini report no per-frequency results. Only Emer tests on a later time period (train 2006-2017, test 2019, plus an external EPO 2019-2022 set). There, the uncertainty-routed hybrid is level with the encoder overall (Macro-F1 0.412 vs 0.410) and slightly ahead on rare labels on EPO (0.193 vs 0.180). In clinical ICD coding the rare/common split is reported (Motzfeldt 2025; Yock/Eng, now EMNLP 2026 main). The only tested combination I found there (Eng) gives an LLM agent the classifier's candidates as a tool, with mixed results. A Dec 2025 preprint (PLM-ICD candidates filtered by an LLM, seen only as a search snippet) and the arXiv 2606.13940 abstract offer no per-report selector either. One caution for the draft: its Related Work says the training support of each answer "has no counterpart" in dynamic classifier selection. That is risky, because classical methods already judge a classifier by the class it outputs: Local Class Accuracy (Woods et al. 1997) and confusion-matrix or behaviour-knowledge-space combination (Xu, Krzyzak & Suen 1992; Huang & Suen 1995). I could not open text that confirms these definitions, so they are listed as unverified. My web-search budget ran out after about 20 web queries (plus 12 arXiv API queries, 5 OpenAlex queries and citation chasing on three papers), so product categorization, occupation coding and answer-aware routers were searched less than the rest.

closest.citation: Emer et al., Large Language Models, Encoder Architectures and Hybrid Approaches for Patent Classification, arXiv 2601.23200 v2 (2026-08-05; v1 title 'Large Language Models for Patent Classification: Strengths, Trade-offs, and the Long Tail Effect')
closest.what_they_did: Multi-label CPC subclass classification. Fine-tuned encoders, including a long-tail-adapted BERT-for-Patents with asymmetric loss and oversampling, are compared with few-shot, RAG and LoRA Qwen3.5-9B. The hybrid ranks patents by encoder uncertainty (1 minus max probability) and sends the top 2/5/10/20% to the LoRA LLM, which picks among encoder-proposed or retrieved subclasses. Temporal split: USPTO train 2006-2017, validation 2018, test 2019, plus an external EPO 2019-2022 set without retraining. Rare F1 is computed on subclasses in the bottom 20% of training frequency (EPO only). Training frequency correlates with per-subclass F1 at rho about 0.24-0.29.
closest.overlap: Covers the general claim that a per-item hybrid of an encoder and an LLM helps on a long-tailed code list, the time-split evaluation, and a rare-label breakdown. The draft already cites it (emer2026patent).
closest.difference: Routes by one model's confidence only, not by the training support of the proposed code. Two models, not three. Overall the hybrid is level with the encoder (0.412 vs 0.410 Macro-F1); on EPO rare labels it is 0.193 vs 0.180. It has no 1-5 or 21+ bins and does not compare frequency routing with confidence routing. Note that v2's lead message is that the best encoder beats the best LLM.

closest.citation: L2D-Clinical: Learning to Defer for Adaptive Model Selection in Clinical Text Classification, arXiv 2604.13285 (ClinicalNLP workshop at LREC 2026)
closest.what_they_did: A logistic regression estimates whether BERT is wrong from BERT confidence, entropy and margin plus text features (length, keyword flags), and defers to GPT-5-nano few-shot above a threshold. Tasks: ADE detection (2 classes) and MIMIC-IV treatment outcome (3 classes). ADE F1 0.928 vs BioBERT 0.911 with 7% deferred. MIMIC 0.980 vs ClinicalBERT 0.887 and LLM 0.967.
closest.overlap: The same form as our selector: a per-item logistic model choosing between a fine-tuned encoder and an LLM, fitted on labelled data. It takes away any claim that a learned per-item encoder/LLM choice is new.
closest.difference: 2-3 classes, no long tail, no per-frequency results, random splits, no time test. Features do not include the predicted label or its training count. One model per decision (is BERT wrong?), not one model per coder comparing answers.

closest.citation: de Andrade et al., Call My Big Sibling (CMBS), J. Brazilian Computer Society 2026; earlier arXiv 2408.09629 'A Strategy to Combine 1stGen Transformers and Open LLMs for Automatic Text Classification'
closest.what_they_did: A calibrated logistic regression on the RoBERTa CLS embedding gives a confidence. Below a tuned threshold (95% or 99%) the document goes to a zero- or few-shot open LLM. The arXiv version tests 11 binary sentiment datasets; the journal version (seen only in a search snippet) reports 13 datasets. Routed fractions are mostly 2-31%. Beats RoBERTa on 7 of 11 datasets and ties on 4.
closest.overlap: Confidence-cascade encoder-to-LLM text classification, which is our baseline (confidence cascade) as a published method.
closest.difference: Binary classes, no long tail, cross-validation, no time test, confidence only.

closest.citation: TRACER: Trace-Based Adaptive Cost-Efficient Routing for LLM Classification, arXiv 2604.14531 (2026)
closest.what_they_did: Trains a cheap surrogate on LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.6) outputs. A logistic acceptor over the surrogate's top-1, top-2, margin and normalised entropy decides whether to keep the surrogate or defer to the LLM, with a parity gate and periodic refits. Banking77 (77 classes) and CLINC150 (150). At alpha 0.95, Banking77 coverage is 83.2% with teacher agreement 0.959.
closest.overlap: A learned acceptor between a classifier and an LLM on tasks with many classes, and a flywheel that refits over batches.
closest.difference: The target is agreement with the LLM, not gold. Confidence features only. No frequency bins (only six example labels shown). Batches are not shown to be chronological; no real later-period test.

closest.citation: Abedini & Heydarnoori, Hybrid LLM Routing for Efficient App Feedback Classification, arXiv 2507.08250 v2 (2025)
closest.what_they_did: Two fine-tuned models classify app reviews. If they agree the label is kept, otherwise GPT-4o decides. Three coarse classes. Keeps 98.4-100.4% of zero-shot GPT-4o F1 with 67.8% fewer requests.
closest.overlap: Uses agreement among answers as the routing signal, which is one of our 14 selector inputs, and is close to our majority-vote baseline.
closest.difference: 3 classes, no tail, no frequency analysis, no time split; the goal is cost.

closest.citation: LabelFusion, arXiv 2512.10793 v2 (2025)
closest.what_they_did: An MLP over the concatenated RoBERTa CLS embedding and the LLM's per-label 0/1 vector, on Reuters-21578 with 10 labels. The LLM alone beats the fusion until about 60-80% of training data. The fusion wins at full data (F1 96.0 vs RoBERTa 94.6 and GPT-5-nano 93.4).
closest.overlap: Stacking a fine-tuned encoder with LLM outputs, and the finding that the LLM wins with little data.
closest.difference: Learned fusion, not selection. 10 classes, macro only, no per-frequency results, ModApte split (not temporal).

closest.citation: Yock, Cao, Chen, Mao, Jiang, Understanding the Limits of Agentic ICD Coding, EMNLP 2026 main pp. 36028-36037 (arXiv 2609.13806)
closest.what_they_did: A rarity-stratified MIMIC-IV ICD-10 evaluation of neural, workflow and agentic coders, with a 0.43 micro-F1 rare-common gap for the neural classifiers; 'No single system dominates across all conditions'. Section 4 (per the project's earlier reading) gives the classifier's candidates to an agent as a tool, with mixed results.
closest.overlap: The rare/common split (our claim 2) and the motivation for combining. Already in the draft.
closest.difference: No per-report selector over answers, and no later-period test.

closest.citation: Zaera, Popa, Sekulic, Rosso, Efficient Out-of-Scope Detection in Dialogue Systems via Uncertainty-Driven LLM Routing, arXiv 2507.01541 (2025)
closest.what_they_did: Uncertainty on a deployed in-scope intent classifier's output sends high-uncertainty queries to a fine-tuned LLM for the final decision. Reports state-of-the-art results on out-of-scope benchmarks.
closest.overlap: An encoder-to-LLM confidence cascade in production.
closest.difference: Out-of-scope detection, not a long-tailed code list. The abstract gives no frequency analysis.

closest.citation: Nie, Ding, Hu, Jermaine, Chaudhuri, Online Cascade Learning for Efficient Inference over Streams, ICML 2024 (arXiv 2402.04513)
closest.what_they_did: A cascade from logistic regression up to an LLM, with a deferral policy learned online by imitation learning. Small models update on the LLM's demonstrations. The abstract reports up to 90% cost reduction and robustness to input shift.
closest.overlap: Deferral between cheap classifiers and an LLM, assessed over a stream with shift.
closest.difference: The selector is updated online rather than frozen. Confidence and cost driven; no label-frequency signal or per-frequency results in the abstract.

closest.citation: Cortes, Mao, Mohri, Zhong, Optimized Deferral for Imbalanced Settings (MILD), arXiv 2604.27723 (ICML 2026)
closest.what_they_did: Two-stage learning to defer among existing predictors (including LLM routing), with margin-based cost-sensitive losses for imbalance among experts.
closest.overlap: Theory for learning which existing predictor to trust per input, the formal family our selector belongs to.
closest.difference: The imbalance is over experts, not label frequency. No text-coding application with a long-tailed code list.

closest.citation: Zhang, Huang et al., Do BERT-Like Bidirectional Models Still Perform Better on Text Classification in the Era of LLMs? arXiv 2505.18215 (Findings of EMNLP 2025 per a snippet)
closest.what_they_did: Compares BERT-like models and LLMs on six datasets and proposes TaMAS, which picks the model family per task (pattern-driven tasks go to BERT, knowledge-heavy tasks to LLMs).
closest.overlap: Choosing the coder by task, which is the 'choose once per dataset' practice the draft argues against.
closest.difference: Task-level, not per item, with no long-tail analysis.

taken: Per-item choice between a fine-tuned text encoder and a prompted or fine-tuned LLM, including a learned logistic deferral model (L2D-Clinical 2026; CMBS 2024/2026; Zaera 2025; AdaptiveLog 2025; TRACER 2026; Emer 2026). Our selector cannot be called the first per-item encoder/LLM chooser.

A confidence cascade from encoder to LLM for text classification, including on a long-tailed code list with a time split (Emer 2026, patents, 2019 test year). Our confidence-cascade baseline is a published method, not a straw man, and it should be cited as such (CMBS, Emer, L2D-Clinical).
Routing on agreement or disagreement between models' answers (Abedini & Heydarnoori 2025: the LLM decides only when two fine-tuned models disagree). Agreement as a selector input is not new.
Fusing encoder features with LLM label outputs by a learned meta-model (LabelFusion 2025; classical stacking).
The rare-to-LLM, common-to-encoder split, and its link to training frequency (Motzfeldt 2025; Yock/Eng EMNLP 2026; Emer 2026, rho 0.24-0.29 between training frequency and per-subclass F1).

The idea of judging a classifier's answer by the class it outputs (Local Class Accuracy in dynamic classifier selection; confusion-matrix combination). See unverified: definitions not confirmed from full text. The draft's sentence that training support 'has no counterpart' in dynamic selection should be softened to 'is a class-level reliability estimate computed from training counts rather than from a validation set'.
open: Using the training count of the code each coder proposes as the main selection signal. I found no paper among the encoder/LLM routing, deferral, cascade and stacking work (about 20 web queries, 12 arXiv API queries, 5 OpenAlex queries, Semantic Scholar citation lists of SuperICL (248 citing works) and FrugalGPT (98), plus Emer (3)) whose router inputs include the training frequency of the predicted label. All read acceptors use confidence, margin, entropy, text features, or agreement.

Choosing among three coders' answers at once (encoder, zero-shot LLM, retrieval LLM) with one model per coder estimating each answer's correctness. The published systems are two-model cascades or binary deferrals.

A selector frozen on one year and tested on a later year, reported by training-frequency bin (1-5, 6-20, 21+), with the frequency-signal selector compared with a confidence cascade on the same data. Emer 2026 has a time split and a single bottom-20% rare F1 but routes on confidence; no one compares the two signals.

Encoder/LLM selection on safety or failure reports (MAUDE device problem, FAA SDR) with several hundred codes. No selector paper in that domain was found. The MADE benchmark (MAUDE, ACL 2026) compares models but does not select per report (from project notes, not re-read here).

Natural-proportion evaluation of a per-item encoder/LLM hybrid where the rare-code base rate is about 1 in 1,000, with false rare answers counted per year. No selector or cascade paper reports this. The closest is Jiang et al. 2026 (selective prediction on the rare-disease tail), which shows confidence gates fail there, but it does not combine an encoder and an LLM.

Searched less: e-commerce product categorization, occupation coding (ISCO/SOC) and MedDRA hybrids (one web query each, nothing with per-frequency routing found), and answer-conditioned routers in general LLM routing (search budget exhausted).
ideas: Constrained LLM correction (Emer 2026; filter-then-rerank): for uncertain reports, let the LLM pick only among the encoder's top-k codes plus retrieved codes, instead of the whole 471-code list. This could cut false rare answers on ordinary reports, which come from the LLM naming rare codes freely. Needs the encoder top-k (already computed) and one more LLM pass on a subset (open models on GPU with the owner's approval, or a small Opus run).

Learned deferral with uncertainty and text features (L2D-Clinical): add encoder entropy and top-2 margin and simple text features (length, boilerplate flag) to the selector if not already among the 14 inputs. Shows whether training support beats these features in the same model. CPU only.
Top-2 margin as the gate rather than top score (Jiang et al. 2026, rare-disease tail). Cheap check on the encoder softmax. CPU.

Classifier output in the prompt (SuperICL; credit-default study arXiv 2608.30086, where adding the classifier's probability raised the LLM's AUC from 0.72 to 0.78): give the LLM the encoder's top code and confidence. Needs one LLM pass.

Online or periodic refitting of the selector (TRACER flywheel; Nie et al. ICML 2024 online cascade): refit monthly on newly coded reports and compare with the frozen 2024 selector on 2026. This addresses the year-to-year drift in the notes. CPU.

A behaviour-knowledge-space or confusion-matrix combination baseline (classical: look up the most likely true code for each tuple of three answers, or weight each coder by its precision on the code it names, estimated on 2024). This directly tests whether training support adds anything over a per-code precision table, which is the reviewer question the 'no counterpart' sentence invites. CPU.
Imbalance-aware deferral loss (MILD, Cortes et al. 2026) as a principled replacement for one logistic model per coder. CPU, moderate implementation effort.

unverified: Local Class Accuracy (Woods et al. 1997) judges a classifier by its local accuracy on neighbours of the class it outputs. A search snippet describes LCA as choosing the classifier with highest accuracy 'in relation to a specific class label'. The Woods abstract (OpenAlex) only says 'local accuracy in small regions of feature space' and does not confirm the class conditioning.

Xu, Krzyzak & Suen 1992 (IEEE TSMC, doi 10.1109/21.155943) combine classifiers through each classifier's confusion matrix, and Huang & Suen 1995 propose the Behaviour-Knowledge Space that maps the tuple of classifier answers to a class. From memory; the 1992 abstract I opened mentions combination at different levels of output information but not the confusion matrix; Huang & Suen not opened.

'Label space compression and prompt alignment for collaborative inference with small and large language models' (2026) and 'A Cost-Aware Approach for Collaborating LLMs and SLMs' (2025) appear among SuperICL's citing works; not opened, so whether they use label-level signals is unknown.
Zhang et al. 2505.18215 reported as Findings of EMNLP 2025 and an average 2.3% TaMAS gain (snippet/third-party summary only).
Classical long-tail expert ensembles (RIDE, SADE test-time aggregation of head- and tail-specialised experts) as an analogue of frequency-aware selection: from memory, not opened in this pass.

checks.detail: I read the arXiv abstract page. It exists. v2 is dated 2026-08-05 and is titled 'Large Language Models, Encoder Architectures and Hybrid Approaches for Patent Classification'. The hybrid sends the patents with the highest encoder uncertainty to the LLM, and the best encoder beats the best LLM; both points are confirmed. The abstract does not mention the temporal split (train 2006-2017, test 2019, EPO 2019-2022), the rare-label F1 (0.193 vs 0.180) or rho 0.24-0.29, so I did not re-check them. The report says it read the full text. Already cited in the draft as emer2026patent.

I read the abstract only. It exists, by Kondadadi and Ortega, April 2026. The deferral from BERT to an LLM uses 'uncertainty signals and text characteristics'. ADE F1 0.928 vs BioBERT 0.911 with 7% deferred, and MIMIC-IV 0.980 vs ClinicalBERT 0.887 and GPT-5-nano 0.967, are confirmed; the abstract adds that 16.8% are deferred on MIMIC-IV. The abstract does not confirm the logistic-regression form, the exact features, the class counts or the LREC ClinicalNLP venue.

checks.item: CMBS / de Andrade et al. arXiv 2408.09629
checks.detail: I read the arXiv abstract. It exists (Aug 2024) and confirms confidence-based routing from first-generation transformers to open LLMs on 11 sentiment datasets. The arXiv page lists no journal reference, so the J. Brazilian Computer Society 2026 version is still unverified. I did not re-check the threshold values or the 7-of-11 result.

I read the abstract. It exists (Adam Rida, April 2026). It trains surrogates on LLM traces with a parity gate and reports 83-100% coverage on the 77-class benchmark with a Sonnet 4.6 teacher; on the 150-class benchmark the surrogate replaces the teacher entirely. The abstract does not state the acceptor features (top-1, top-2, margin, entropy), so they are not re-checked. Its target is agreement with the LLM, not gold labels, which is consistent with the report.

I read the abstract. It exists. Simple cases go to fine-tuned models and ambiguous cases to an LLM, keeping 98.4-100.4% of zero-shot LLM accuracy with 67.8% fewer requests; this is confirmed. The abstract does not say that 'ambiguous' means two fine-tuned models disagree, so that detail rests on the first agent's full-text reading.

I read the abstract. It exists. It concerns financial news, and fuses the LLM output with RoBERTa embeddings through an MLP on a 10-class Reuters subset, reaching 96.0 macro F1 against RoBERTa 94.6. Two small differences from the report: the abstract gives the stand-alone LLM 93.9 F1 (the report says 93.4), and says the LLM leads until about 80% of training data (the report says 60-80%).

checks.item: Yock et al., EMNLP 2026 main pp. 36028-36037 (arXiv 2609.13806)
checks.detail: I read the ACL Anthology abstract. Title, authors, pages and the rarity-stratified MIMIC-IV evaluation are confirmed, and the conclusion that no single system wins everywhere is confirmed. The abstract does not mention a classifier-candidates tool or the 0.43 gap, so I did not re-check those. Note that the draft's bib currently calls this 'Eng et al.', but 'Yock' is the family name the Anthology lists.
I read the abstract. Uncertainty on a deployed intent classifier sends uncertain queries to a fine-tuned LLM for out-of-scope detection, as the report says.

I read the abstract. It is an online cascade from logistic regression up to an LLM with a deferral policy learned by imitation, reporting up to 90% cost reduction and robustness to shift, as the report says.

checks.item: Cortes, Mao, Mohri, Zhong, MILD arXiv 2604.27723
checks.detail: I read the abstract. The comments list ICML 2026. The imbalance it handles is among experts (deferral tends to favour the majority expert), not label frequency, as the report says. It tests on image classification and LLM routing.
I read the abstract. TaMAS chooses BERT-like models or LLMs per task, not per item; confirmed. The arXiv page has no journal reference, so the Findings of EMNLP 2025 venue is still unverified.

checks.item: Classical class-conditional selection (LCA, BKS, confusion matrix)
checks.detail: Local Class Accuracy is now confirmed from the DESlib documentation (https://deslib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/modules/dcs/lca.html, read). Each base classifier's competence is its local accuracy on neighbours that belong to the class that classifier predicted. Source: Woods, Kegelmeyer & Bowyer, IEEE TPAMI 19(4) 405-410, 1997, doi 10.1109/34.588027; title confirmed via Crossref. The titles of Huang & Suen 1995 (BKS, doi 10.1109/34.368145) and Xu, Krzyzak & Suen 1992 (doi 10.1109/21.155943) are confirmed via Crossref, but I did not read how they define their methods. The draft's sentence in paper/manuscript.tex line 131, that the training support of each answer 'has no counterpart' in dynamic selection, is therefore contradicted at least by LCA, which judges each classifier by the class it outputs.

missed: I found no closer prior work in this pass, and that result is weak. The shared WebSearch budget for this turn (200 calls) was used up before my first query ran. The arXiv API returned empty bodies, and OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429. A Crossref bibliographic query returned nothing relevant. So I could not run new queries on the open items (frequency-aware routing in relation extraction, entity typing or linking, XMC, product categorisation, occupation coding, recommendation). Only direct fetches of known URLs were possible.

ICXML (Zhu & Zamani, arXiv 2311.09649; I read the abstract): zero-shot extreme multi-label classification that generates candidate labels in context and then reranks them. It is a neighbour of the filter-then-rerank family, not an answer-level selector, and nothing in the abstract routes by label frequency.

Woods, Kegelmeyer & Bowyer 1997, LCA (doi 10.1109/34.588027): confirmed through the DESlib documentation as class-conditional competence, meaning each classifier is judged by its accuracy on the class it predicted. This is the closest prior form to 'judge each coder by the code it proposes'. It uses local accuracy on neighbours, not training counts, and predates LLMs.
taken_after_check: Choosing per item between a fine-tuned encoder and an LLM, including through a learned deferral model: L2D-Clinical 2026, CMBS 2024, Zaera 2025, Emer 2026, TRACER 2026, Nie et al. ICML 2024 (online cascade).

A confidence cascade from encoder to LLM, including on a long-tailed label set with an LLM correction step (Emer 2026, patents). The draft's confidence-cascade baseline is a published method and should be cited as one.

Routing on how ambiguous an item is, or whether models disagree, with a cheap fine-tuned tier and an LLM tier (Abedini & Heydarnoori 2025; the disagreement rule rests on the first agent's full-text reading).
Learned fusion of encoder embeddings with LLM label outputs (LabelFusion 2025), and the finding that an LLM leads when training data are small.
The finding that LLMs do better on rare codes and classifiers on common ones, by rarity stratum (Motzfeldt 2025; Yock et al. EMNLP 2026; Emer 2026).

Judging a base classifier by the class it outputs (Local Class Accuracy, Woods et al. 1997, confirmed via DESlib). The draft's sentence that training support 'has no counterpart' in dynamic selection should be softened. Training support is a class-level reliability estimate taken from training counts rather than from local validation neighbours.
Learning-to-defer theory for imbalance among experts (MILD, ICML 2026).
open_after_check: Using the training count of each proposed code as the main selection signal between an encoder and LLM coders. I found no counterexample, but this pass could not run new searches, so the item rests on the first agent's search of about 20 web, 12 arXiv and 5 OpenAlex queries plus citation chasing. That search under-covered relation extraction and entity typing (SLM-LLM collaboration on long-tail relations), XMC with LLM rerankers, product and occupation coding, and recommendation (LLMs for long-tail items). The closest classical analogue is class-conditional local accuracy (LCA).

One model per coder estimating whether each of three answers (encoder, zero-shot LLM, retrieval LLM) is correct, then keeping one. The published systems I saw are two-tier cascades, binary deferral or fusion.

A selector frozen on one year and tested on a later year by training-frequency bin, compared head to head with a confidence cascade. Emer has a time split and routes by confidence; nobody I saw compares the two signals.
Encoder/LLM per-report selection on MAUDE or FAA SDR codes.
Natural-proportion evaluation of an encoder/LLM hybrid with a rare-code base rate near 1 in 1,000, counting false rare answers per year.
