prior.title: LLM classifiers at natural prevalence: false rare predictions

report.answer: Many papers show in general terms that precision falls as prevalence falls, and some show it for LLMs. None that I found measures what a zero-shot or retrieval-prompted LLM does across hundreds of codes when each rare code turns up about once in 1,000 reports. Norén, Meldau & Ellenius (arXiv 2510.04341, full text read) give the Bayes argument for pharmacovigilance with a worked example: 99.95% specificity gives only 55% precision at low prevalence, and 98% specificity would give 3%. They recommend projecting precision to the real prevalence from sensitivity and specificity, and reviewing errors case by case. Srivastav et al. (EMNLP-F 2026) show LLM-judge precision collapsing between 50% and 5% prevalence and say auditing fails unless false-positive rates are almost zero. Neither tests a fix. The closest work on prompt fixes is Zhang, Hangya & Fraser (COLING 2025, full text read). Putting the label distribution into a zero-shot prompt reduces over-prediction in some models. In others it does nothing, overshoots, or hurts (GPT-3.5 flipped into over-predicting hate speech). They tested 3-class tasks with prevalences of a few percent or more, never 1 in 1,000. On clinical coding, an LLM writing codes itself has very low precision, and using it as a verifier over a trained model's candidates cuts false positives a lot (Akkhawatthanakun et al., Informatics 2026, abstract only). Recall was not reported. There is a new precedent for claim 2 that is not in the draft. Martin, Feng & Peng (arXiv 2605.21845, NVDRS suicide narratives, full text read) find that LLMs beat a fine-tuned RoBERTa on low-prevalence circumstances, and they propose LLMs for rare labels and the fine-tuned model for common ones, chosen per circumstance. Their test sets are balanced 100/100, so they never meet the false-positive problem. Eng et al. (EMNLP 2026, full text read) also sample by stratum (50/50/50 notes). The read-first list is in substance technology-assisted review (priority screening with a recall target and stopping rules: Wang et al. ECIR 2024, plus the stopping-rule literature). That field already treats ranking for human reading as the normal endpoint, so the list is a known kind of method rather than a new one, and it is also a respectable framing. I found no paper showing any fix (verifier, definitions, abstention, frequency hints, conformal sets, prior correction) that makes per-report rare-label answers mostly right at 1 in 1,000. That absence fits the project's own negative result rather than contradicting it.

closest.citation: Norén GN, Meldau E-L, Ellenius J. Critical appraisal of artificial intelligence for rare-event recognition: principles and pharmacovigilance case studies. arXiv 2510.04341 (Oct 2025)
closest.what_they_did: A framework paper from the Uppsala Monitoring Centre for judging AI on rare events. It covers test-set design (enrichment with positive controls), prevalence-aware metrics, cost-sensitive targets, structured case-level examination (SCLE: reviewing stratified samples of false positives, false negatives and true positives), and a checklist. Three case studies: rule-based retrieval of pregnancy reports, duplicate detection, and name redaction with a fine-tuned BERT. Worked Bayes example: 99.95% specificity gave 55% precision, and 98% would give 3%. Recommends computing precision at the assumed real prevalence from sensitivity and specificity. Notes that specificity near 1 needs very many negative controls to estimate.
closest.overlap: Covers the base-rate arithmetic behind claim 3 and the exploration finding that false rare answers come from the base rate. Also covers the idea that enriched or balanced test sets overstate precision. Our 'only correct if the false-naming rate drops 40-266x' is the same logic.
closest.difference: No LLM classifier over a large code list, no multi-coder selector, and no measured false-naming rate per class across hundreds of codes. The 'LLM' case is a fine-tuned BERT tagging tokens. No fix is shown to work.

closest.citation: Zhang Y, Hangya V, Fraser A. LLM Sensitivity Challenges in Abusive Language Detection: Instruction-Tuned vs. Human Feedback. COLING 2025, pp. 2765-2780
closest.what_they_did: Measures zero-shot over- and under-prediction bias (ratio of predicted to gold label frequency) for Flan-T5, OPT-IML, LLaMA-2-Chat and GPT-3.5 on abusive-language datasets. Adds the label distribution to the prompt, as numbers or as words ('X occurs more frequently than Y'). Also tests made-up distributions and a feedback prompt.
closest.overlap: The same idea as our frequency-hint prompt (V2). Their finding matches ours: hints move the output distribution bluntly. They help LLaMA-2-Chat; they do nothing for Flan-T5 and OPT-IML; for GPT-3.5 they overshoot. Even the true test distribution did not fix GPT-3.5 on the 3-class task.
closest.difference: Two or three classes at prevalences of several percent or more. Nothing near 1 in 1,000, no hundreds of codes, no per-class precision for very rare classes.

closest.citation: Martin G, Feng XZ, Peng Y. Comparing LLM and Fine-Tuned Model Performance on NVDRS Circumstance Extraction with Varying Prompt Complexity. arXiv 2605.21845 (May 2026)
closest.what_they_did: 25 low-prevalence circumstances from 191,696 suicide narratives. GPT-5.2, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Llama-3-70B against a fine-tuned RoBERTa. LLMs win clearly where training positives are few (e.g. Abuse or Neglect: RoBERTa F1 .131, GPT-5.2 about .88-.89). A hybrid that picks the prompt type per circumstance reaches macro-F1 .893 against RoBERTa's .800. The authors argue for LLMs on rare circumstances and fine-tuned models on common ones.
closest.overlap: A direct precedent for claim 2 (LLMs beat a fine-tuned encoder on rare labels; split the work by frequency). It is not in the draft's references, and it weakens novelty for the rare-to-LLM split in a third domain. Its routing is per circumstance, not per report.
closest.difference: Test sets are balanced (100 positive, 100 negative per circumstance). No precision and no natural prevalence, so the false-positive collapse we see never appears. Binary per-circumstance tasks, not one code from hundreds. No per-report selector.

closest.citation: Eng CY (Yock), Cao Y, Chen Y, Mao K, Jiang H. Understanding the Limits of Agentic ICD Coding. EMNLP 2026 main, pp. 36028-36037
closest.what_they_did: Compares PLM-ICD, workflow LLM coders and agentic LLM coders on 150 MIMIC-IV notes, sampled 50 per rarity stratum (training frequency 0-100, 101-1,000, >1,000). Results: PLM-ICD micro-F1 .227 on rare codes and .656 on common; CodeSeeker with Claude Opus 4.6 reaches .560 on rare. Per-bin precision is in an appendix. False positives are binned by the predicted code's frequency.
closest.overlap: The same rare-to-LLM, frequent-to-trained-model split (claim 2, already cited in the draft). Binning false positives by the predicted code's training frequency is close to our rare-answer precision.
closest.difference: Stratified sampling of notes, not natural prevalence. They note that uniform sampling hides rare-code performance and chose stratification for that reason, so the 1-in-1,000 precision problem is never measured. No selector. Their 0.43 gap is a rare-versus-common difference, not a routing rule.

closest.citation: Akkhawatthanakun et al. Integrating Agentic Artificial Intelligence to Automate ICD-10 Medical Coding. Informatics 2026, 13(3):39, doi:10.3390/informatics13030039 (preprint 10.20944/preprints202512.2138)
closest.what_they_did: 19,801 MIMIC-IV summaries. PLM-ICD alone gives 55.8% precision with 15 suggestions. Four LLMs generating codes themselves reach only 1.5-34.6% precision. LLMs auditing PLM-ICD's 15 candidates keep 2-8 codes; for example Llama-3.2-3B goes from 1.5% precision as a generator to 55.1% as a verifier and removes 73% of false positives.
closest.overlap: Evidence that LLMs over-name codes when they generate freely, and that an LLM auditing a trained model's candidates is a known fix for precision.
closest.difference: Recall and F1 not reported, and nothing by code rarity, so we cannot tell whether the verifier also throws away the rare finds. That is exactly our problem: our 'drop if the encoder disagrees' lost 129 of Opus's 154 correct rare answers. Multi-label ICD, not one code per report.

closest.citation: Srivastav D, Pape D, Schönherr L. Unknown Unknowns: Do Hidden Intentions in LLMs Evade Detection? arXiv 2601.18552 (EMNLP Findings 2026)
closest.what_they_did: Stress-tests LLM judges and classifiers that detect hidden intentions in LLM outputs, at varying prevalence. GPT-4.1 precision .82 at 50% prevalence collapses at 5%. Precision-versus-miss-rate curves are given at 0.1%, 1% and 10% prevalence. Concludes that detection does not work unless false-positive rates are tiny, and that larger models and reasoning models do not close the gap.
closest.overlap: An independent 2026 statement that LLM classifiers' false positives swamp low-prevalence detection, and that scaling does not fix it. Matches our finding that Opus is better than Qwen and Gemma but still about 2% precise on rare codes.
closest.difference: Binary detection of a safety property, not one code from hundreds. Mitigations are discussed but not tested.

closest.citation: Nawrath et al. Validating Large Language Models for Title-Abstract Screening in Low-Prevalence Systematic Reviews: An Environmental Science Case Study. Information 2026, 17(5):501
closest.what_they_did: Five LLMs (GPT-4.1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash, DeepSeek V3, Mistral Large) screen 500 records with 8 inclusions (1.6%). Sensitivity and specificity trade off, e.g. Gemini sensitivity 1.00 with specificity .858, and DeepSeek specificity .980 with sensitivity .375. Kappa looks poor at low prevalence while other agreement indices do not.
closest.overlap: An LLM classifier evaluated at natural low prevalence, with a human reviewer kept in the loop. The same conclusion as our 'review queue'.
closest.difference: 1.6% prevalence, 8 positives, binary task. No large label set, no rare-code false-naming analysis, no fix.

closest.citation: Wang S, Scells H, Zhuang S, Potthast M, Koopman B, Zuccon G. Zero-shot Generative Large Language Models for Systematic Review Screening Automation. ECIR 2024, LNCS 14608:403-420; arXiv 2401.06320
closest.what_they_did: Eight zero-shot LLMs score documents by the yes/no token-probability difference. A threshold calibrated to a target recall (0.95 or 1.0) decides inclusion, and an ensemble saves screening work against prior methods on five collections.
closest.overlap: Our read-first list (200 of 552 rare reports in about 7,000 reads) is the same kind of method: technology-assisted review, a ranked list read against a recall target. The idea of a ranked LLM list for human screening is taken.
closest.difference: Needs token probabilities. Binary relevance, not finding which of hundreds of rare codes applies within a coding stream. No multi-coder signals. Prevalence is a few percent, not 0.1%.

closest.citation: Collot S et al. Balanced Accuracy: The Right Metric for Evaluating LLM Judges -- Explained through Youden's J statistic. arXiv 2512.08121 (EACL 2026 Industry)
closest.what_they_did: Argues that accuracy, precision, F1 and macro-F1 all depend on prevalence, so judge rankings change with the class mix of the golden set. Recommends balanced accuracy (macro-recall) and Youden's J.
closest.overlap: Supports our point that a macro-F1 gain on a later year and per-report precision at natural proportions answer different questions.
closest.difference: No rare classes, no long tail. It argues for a metric that does not depend on prevalence, which is the opposite of what a deployment at 1 in 1,000 needs (precision at the real prevalence).

closest.citation: Linder F, Leeper T, Haimovich D, Tax N, Perini L, Vojnovic M. Multicalibration for Unbiased Model-Based Prevalence Estimation (v1 title: Unbiased Prevalence Estimation with Multicalibrated LLMs). arXiv 2604.21549 (2026)
closest.what_they_did: Shows that correcting counts from known error rates fails under covariate shift. Proves that multicalibration (calibration conditional on features) is enough for unbiased prevalence estimates. Applications: American Community Survey employment, and classifying political texts with an LLM.
closest.overlap: Directly relevant to our failed count correction (Rogan-Gladen, BBSE, EM collapsed because false-naming rates shifted from 2025 to 2026, e.g. Gemma 136 to 219 per 10k). It names the cause, unstable error rates across populations, and offers a fix.
closest.difference: Common classes, not 1 in 1,000. Needs calibration data covering the dimensions that shift (for us manufacturer and product, which are empty in the 2025 and 2026 pools). Not tested on label-list classification.

closest.citation: Ding T, Fermanian J-B, Salmon J. Conformal Prediction for Long-Tailed Classification. arXiv 2507.06867 (v3 Feb 2026; ICLR 2026 poster listing)
closest.what_they_did: Proposes a prevalence-adjusted softmax score and an interpolation between marginal and class-conditional conformal thresholds. The aim is to keep rare classes in prediction sets while keeping sets small. Tested on Pl@ntNet-300K (1,081 classes) and iNaturalist-2018 (8,142).
closest.overlap: Conformal sets for long-tailed labels: the fix the angle asked about. It could put a coverage guarantee on an encoder candidate set that an LLM then chooses from.
closest.difference: Image classifiers with softmax outputs. Aims at coverage (recall), not precision of single answers. No LLMs and no 1-in-1,000 per-report precision.

taken: That precision of any classifier collapses at low prevalence (Bayes), and that balanced or enriched test sets overstate it: Norén et al. 2025 (pharmacovigilance, worked 55% to 3% example), Srivastav et al. 2026 (LLM judges), and Axelsson 2000 already in the notes. Our base-rate diagnosis is standard arithmetic, not a finding.
That LLMs carry their own label priors and over- or under-predict classes zero-shot: Zhao 2021, Fei 2023, Jiang 2023, Reif & Schwartz 2024 (already known), plus Zhang, Hangya & Fraser COLING 2025.

That telling the LLM the label frequencies in the prompt steers predictions bluntly and inconsistently (works for some models, overshoots or hurts for others): Zhang et al. COLING 2025. Our V2 frequency-prompt result repeats this.

That LLMs generating codes from a large list over-code with low precision, and that using an LLM to verify a trained model's candidates restores precision: Akkhawatthanakun et al. 2026 (1.5% to 55.1%), and the LLM-codex line (GPT-4 over-predicts ICD codes; seen only in search snippets).

That prompted LLMs beat fine-tuned encoders on rare labels and fine-tuned models win on common ones, with the work split by frequency: Motzfeldt 2025 and Eng 2026 (already cited), and now also Martin, Feng & Peng 2026 on NVDRS (RoBERTa vs GPT-5.2, Gemini, Llama, with a per-label hybrid). Claim 2 has a third published precedent outside clinical coding, absent from the draft.

Ranking items for human reading against a recall target, i.e. the read-first list: this is technology-assisted review or priority screening (Wang et al. ECIR 2024; stopping-rule literature, Yang et al. 2021; Stop-method evaluation 2025 in PMC). We cannot claim the ranked-queue idea as new, only its use for rare codes inside a coding stream.
That macro-F1 and accuracy depend on prevalence and that metric choice changes conclusions: Collot et al. 2025/2026; Opitz TACL 2024 (seen as a snippet).

That correcting counts from fixed error rates fails when error rates shift across populations: Linder et al. 2026 (multicalibration). Our failed Rogan-Gladen, BBSE and EM attempt is an instance of a known failure.
open: A measured false-naming rate per code for zero-shot and retrieval-prompted LLMs across a list of several hundred codes, on a natural stream where rare codes are about 1 in 1,000 (we have 1 in 45 to 1 in 100 ordinary reports given some rare code, and precision 0.9-2.3%). Searched for this with about 22 web queries, 6 arXiv API queries and 5 OpenAlex queries (terms: low prevalence, base rate, label prior, over-predict, rare class precision, label shift, quantification, pharmacovigilance, rare disease PPV, incident reports, content moderation, systematic-review screening, conformal long tail, abstention), plus citation chasing from Eng 2026 and Srivastav 2026. Every LLM study found used balanced (Martin 2026), stratified (Eng 2026), reduced (MADE) or few-class low-prevalence (Nawrath 2026, 1.6%) test sets.

Any demonstrated fix that makes per-report rare-label answers mostly correct at 1 in 1,000 while keeping the finds. None found for verifiers (recall not reported), frequency prompts (tested only at a few percent), abstention (no long-tail test found), or conformal sets (they target coverage, not precision). Our negative result looks unreported rather than contradicted.

A per-report selector across encoder and LLM coders, judged both on macro-F1 and at natural proportions: the neighbours route per label (Martin 2026), or route by cost and difficulty without a long tail (RouteLLM etc., already read).

Technology-assisted-review-style evaluation (reads needed to reach a fixed recall of rare-code reports, with a stopping rule) for rare-code discovery inside a multi-class coding stream, using several coders' disagreement as the ranking signal. TAR work found is binary relevance with token probabilities. Medium confidence that this is unpublished; I did not search the TAR literature exhaustively.

Measuring how false-naming rates and the encoder's accuracy drift from one year to the next on a large code list, and what that drift does to count correction. Linder 2026 gives the theory but nobody has tested it for rare codes.
ideas: Report precision at the real prevalence, computed from per-code specificity and sensitivity via Bayes (Norén 2025), together with structured case-level examination: a stratified sample of false and true rare answers read by people. Needs: CPU, and the 1.5-2 h of human reading already proposed in the notes.

Use technology-assisted-review stopping rules (target-recall stopping, e.g. Yang et al. heuristic rules, or the counting-process plus classifier rule in arXiv 2312.03171) on the read-first list. The owner's 'automation' objection could then be answered as 'stop reading once X% recall is reached, with known confidence'. Needs: CPU only, using saved answers and 2025 to set the rule.

LLM as auditor over the encoder's top-k (Akkhawatthanakun 2026), as opposed to the binary 'drop if the encoder disagrees' veto we tried. Give the LLM the encoder's top 10-15 codes plus the LLM's own rare code and ask it to accept or reject. Measure what it does to rare recall, not just precision. Needs: Opus agent or API on a few hundred reports (within the remaining credit), or GPU for Qwen and Gemma.

Tell the model the distribution is balanced, or use a feedback prompt ('you named X too often in a sample'), the variants Zhang et al. found steadier than giving the true distribution. Needs: Opus agent re-ask on the 233-report prompt set.

Multicalibration-style count correction: fit false-naming rates conditional on features (text cluster, boilerplate, device family) rather than one rate per code, on 2024-2025, and apply to 2026 (Linder 2026). Needs: CPU; limited because manufacturer and product fields are empty in the 2025 and 2026 pools.

Conformal prediction sets on the encoder with the prevalence-adjusted score (Ding et al. 2025), so the LLM chooses only within a set that keeps rare codes with a stated coverage. This targets the 333 of 552 rare reports no coder reaches only if the encoder's set contains them. Needs: encoder softmax over 2025 for calibration (GPU 1-3 h if the scores were not saved).
Report balanced accuracy and macro-recall next to macro-F1 (Collot 2025) to separate gains from treating classes evenly from gains in precision. Needs: CPU only.

checks.detail: Opened the abstract page and the full PDF (text extracted). The worked example is in the text: 99.95% specificity gave only 55% precision because positives were rare, and by Bayes 98% specificity would give 3%. The redaction case uses a fine-tuned BERT with a classification layer, not a generative LLM, as the report says. The abstract mentions constrained generative LLMs in general terms only. URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04341 (the HTML version returns 404; the PDF works).

Opened the ACL Anthology page and the full PDF. Putting the label distribution in the prompt reduces bias for LLaMA-2-Chat. It is ineffective for Flan-T5 and OPT-IML. For GPT-3.5 on HateXplain it overshoots into over-predicting hate speech, and the test-set distribution did not fix this; a feedback prompt worked better. The tasks have 2-3 classes. https://aclanthology.org/2025.coling-main.188.pdf

Opened the full HTML. Each circumstance has a test set of 200 narratives (100 positive, 100 negative). Abuse or Neglect F1: RoBERTa .131, GPT-5.2 .882 (simple prompt) and .894 (complex). Hybrid macro-F1 .893 against RoBERTa .800. The tables show F1 only, although the methods section says precision was computed. The conclusion recommends LLMs for rare circumstances and fine-tuned models for common ones. One addition: the paper is accepted at IEEE ICHI 2026, so cite it as ICHI 2026, not only arXiv. It is a real precedent for claim 2 and is missing from the draft.

The paper says scaling and reasoning models do not close the gap (e.g. GPT-5.4 lowers FPR but raises FNR). Mitigations are discussed but not tested.

Opened the Crossref abstract only. 500 records with 8 inclusions (1.6%) and five LLMs. Gemini: sensitivity 1.00, specificity .858. DeepSeek V3: specificity .980, sensitivity .375. Kappa is low while PABAK and AC1 are high. https://api.crossref.org/works/10.3390/info17050501

Opened the abstract only. It confirms eight zero-shot LLMs, five collections, calibration to a preset recall threshold, and an ensemble. I did not confirm from the source that scoring uses the yes/no token-probability difference.

Opened the abstract page. Published at EACL 2026 Industry Track, pp. 927-936. It argues that accuracy, precision and F1 depend on class imbalance, and recommends Youden's J and balanced accuracy for choosing a judge. It has no long-tail content, as the report says.

Opened the abstract page. Correcting counts from fixed error rates is biased under covariate shift, and multicalibration fixes this. Applications are ACS employment and LLM classification of political texts. The authors stress that calibration data must cover the dimensions that shift.

Opened the abstract page. It proposes a prevalence-adjusted softmax score aimed at macro-coverage, plus an interpolation between marginal and class-conditional conformal thresholds. Datasets are Pl@ntNet-300K (1,081 classes) and iNaturalist-2018 (8,142). I did not check the ICLR 2026 listing.

Now opened (abstract): Yang, Batra, Stremmel & Halperin, 'Surpassing GPT-4 Medical Coding with a Two-Stage Approach', ML4H 2023 extended abstract. The abstract says GPT-4 predicts too many ICD codes (high recall, low precision). An LSTM verifier on the LLM's evidence proposals fixes this, and the authors claim state-of-the-art results on rare codes on MIMIC. This moves from unverified to confirmed at abstract level.

checks.detail: Opened the abstract. DocEng 2021. Quant and QuantCI stopping rules reach target recall in technology-assisted review at lower review cost.

missed: Yang Z, Batra SS, Stremmel J, Halperin E. Surpassing GPT-4 Medical Coding with a Two-Stage Approach (LLM-codex), ML4H 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.13735 (abstract read). The first agent saw it only as a snippet. It is a stronger precedent than Akkhawatthanakun for 'an LLM over-names codes, and a trained verifier restores precision', and it claims gains on rare codes. Its test is MIMIC multi-label, and it does not use a natural 1-in-1,000 single-code stream.

Boyle JS et al. Automated clinical coding using off-the-shelf large language models, NeurIPS 2023 DGM4H workshop, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06552 (abstract read). Zero-shot LLM ICD coding by sparse search of the code tree. It is not closer, because the abstract reports neither rare-code precision nor natural-prevalence results; I list it only so it is not looked up again.
Martin, Feng & Peng should be cited as IEEE ICHI 2026, not only as the arXiv preprint (shown on the arXiv page).
taken_after_check: Precision of any classifier collapses at low prevalence by Bayes, and balanced or enriched test sets overstate it: Norén et al. 2025 (worked example, 99.95% specificity -> 55% precision, 98% -> 3%; text verified), Srivastav et al. EMNLP-F 2026 (LLM judges; scaling does not close the gap), Axelsson 2000. The project's base-rate diagnosis is standard arithmetic.
LLMs bring their own label priors and over- or under-predict zero-shot: Zhao 2021, Fei 2023, Jiang 2023, Reif & Schwartz 2024, and Zhang, Hangya & Fraser COLING 2025 (verified).

Putting label frequencies in the prompt steers predictions bluntly and inconsistently: it helps LLaMA-2-Chat, does nothing for Flan-T5 and OPT-IML, and overshoots for GPT-3.5 even with the true test distribution (Zhang et al. 2025, full text verified). The project's V2 frequency prompt repeats this.

LLMs that generate codes from a large list over-code with low precision, and a verifier (an LLM over a trained model's candidates, or a trained verifier over the LLM's proposals) restores precision: LLM-codex, Yang et al. ML4H 2023 (now verified); Akkhawatthanakun et al. 2026 (1.5% -> 55.1%; recall not reported).

Prompted LLMs beat fine-tuned encoders on rare labels and fine-tuned models win on common ones, with the work split by label frequency: Motzfeldt 2025, Eng et al. EMNLP 2026 (verified; stratified 50/50/50), and Martin, Feng & Peng IEEE ICHI 2026 (verified; NVDRS, balanced 100/100, per-circumstance hybrid). Claim 2 has a third precedent that the draft does not cite.

Ranking items for human reading against a recall target, with stopping rules, is technology-assisted review: Wang et al. ECIR 2024; Yang, Lewis & Frieder DocEng 2021 (verified). The ranked read-first list belongs to this known family of methods.
Accuracy, precision, F1 and macro-F1 depend on prevalence, so the choice of metric changes conclusions: Collot et al. EACL 2026 Industry (verified).

Correcting counts from fixed error rates fails when the error rates shift across populations: Linder et al. 2026 (verified). The project's failed Rogan-Gladen, BBSE and EM correction is an instance of this known failure.
Conformal sets for long-tailed labels that keep rare classes in the set (aimed at coverage, not single-answer precision): Ding et al. 2025/2026 (verified).
open_after_check: A measured per-code false-naming rate for zero-shot and retrieval-prompted LLMs over a list of several hundred codes, on a natural stream where rare codes occur about 1 in 1,000. None of the verified sources does this: Martin uses balanced sets, Eng stratified ones, Nawrath has 1.6% prevalence and 2 classes, Srivastav is binary. My own attempt to break this item (occupation coding, injury-narrative OIICS autocoding, MedDRA coding, learning-to-defer) could not run, because the shared web-search budget was used up. Treat this item as open at medium confidence only.

A demonstrated fix that makes per-report rare-label answers mostly right at 1 in 1,000 while keeping the finds. The verifiers (LLM-codex, Akkhawatthanakun) report precision but not rare recall at natural prevalence. Frequency prompts were tested only at a few percent. Conformal sets target coverage. No counter-example found, but neighbouring fields were not searched (see above).

A per-report selector across an encoder and LLM coders, judged both on macro-F1 and at natural proportions. Martin routes per label, not per report. The learning-to-defer and multi-expert deferral literature was NOT checked and is the most likely place for a counter-example; search it before claiming this.

TAR-style evaluation (reads needed to reach a fixed recall, with a stopping rule) for finding rare-code reports inside a multi-class coding stream, ranked by disagreement among several coders. The TAR work verified here is binary relevance. Rare-category detection (active learning for discovering rare classes) and audit sampling were not checked and may hold close prior work.

How false-naming rates and encoder accuracy drift from year to year over a large code list, and what that drift does to count correction. Linder 2026 gives the theory for common classes; I found no test on rare codes.

prior.title: Finding rare-category items with a ranked list instead of labels

report.answer: The ranked read-first list belongs to technology-assisted review (TAR, used in e-discovery and systematic-review screening), and that field has owned it since about 2014. Its standard measures are recall reached for a given amount of reading (the gain curve), work saved over sampling (WSS@95, WSS@r), success rate (the share of topics that reach a target recall) and statistically valid stopping rules (Lewis, Yang, Cormack and Grossman, Callaghan, Stevenson). So our "200 of 552 found in about 7,000 reads against about 240,000 at random" is, in their terms, recall against effort, and the method cannot be claimed as new. Putting LLM proposals together with a trained ranker is also published. Bron et al. (IAL@ECML-PKDD 2024) restrict continuous active learning to the documents the LLM includes, then reopen the full pool. At equal reading effort, misses fell from 16 to 6 of 183, and WSS@95 rose from about 71% to about 81% over AutoTAR, at 3.8% prevalence. Wang et al. (ECIR 2024) set a zero-shot LLM's threshold to reach a target recall and beat a fine-tuned BioBERT on WSS. LGAR (ACL Findings 2025) ranks with an LLM's graded scores followed by a dense re-ranker. Statistical offices (the UK Office for National Statistics, the Norwegian census) run the same split as automatic coding above a confidence threshold plus a manual share. Both report that rare codes and small classes do worst, and at the ONS per-class thresholds fell short of their accuracy target. On cutting the human share to near zero, the literature says the same as our notes. "Available Guardrails" (arXiv 2609.22048) shows that units with little calibration evidence cannot be certified at a target precision at all. A conformal-triage audit (arXiv 2605.20956) shows that a lower review rate under prevalence shift can hide positives released unreviewed. Clustered conformal prediction (Ding et al. 2023) helps only by pooling rare classes, so the guarantee then covers the group, not each code. I found nothing that runs TAR across hundreds of rare codes at once (multi-category, about 1 in 1,198, where the reader must also name the code), on safety or failure reports, with a ranking frozen on the year before and checked on later years. I also found no regulator (FDA, EMA, FAA) that publishes a per-report ranking of this kind; the one pharmacovigilance triage model I read (Lareb) works at 36.5% prevalence. That combination is the open ground, but it is a narrow application claim. A methods claim would need TAR's own baselines and measures.

closest.citation: Bron MP, Greijn B, Messina Coimbra B, van de Schoot R, Bagheri A. Combining Large Language Model Classifications and Active Learning for Improved Technology-Assisted Review. IAL@ECML-PKDD 2024, CEUR-WS Vol-3770, pp. 77-95
closest.what_they_did: An LLM judges each screening criterion on 4,836 records with 183 relevant (3.8% prevalence). Phase 1 runs AutoTAR active learning only over the LLM-included records until 25 irrelevant ones in a row. Phase 2 reopens the whole pool, with a classifier that learns when to accept the LLM's judgement. Over 30 simulation runs at the LLM's own effort (1,295 reads), misses fell from 16 to 6 and WSS@95 was 80.5% against 71.4% for AutoTAR.
closest.overlap: Closest in method. Ranking with a trained model plus LLM proposals, and measuring recall against reading effort, are both already published here. Our 2.3-2.5x saving from adding LLMs to the encoder ranking is the same kind of result.
closest.difference: One binary topic at 3.8% prevalence, against hundreds of codes at about 0.08% in total. It uses human feedback (active learning) during review, where our ranking is frozen on the previous year. One dataset, a workshop paper, no time split, no safety reports.

closest.citation: Wang S, Scells H, Zhuang S, Potthast M, Koopman B, Zuccon G. Zero-shot Generative Large Language Models for Systematic Review Screening Automation. ECIR 2024. arXiv 2401.06320
closest.what_they_did: Eight zero-shot LLMs on the CLEF TAR 2017/2018/2019 and Seed collections. A score is made from the yes/no token probabilities and the threshold is set to a target recall, using other topics or seed studies. Measures: recall, WSS, and success rate at recall 0.95. Llama2-7b-ins beat a fine-tuned BioBERT on WSS (for example 0.56 against 0.26 uncalibrated on CLEF-2017). An ensemble of models did best.
closest.overlap: Already published: a zero-shot LLM beating a fine-tuned encoder on reading saved at low prevalence, and setting a threshold for a target recall instead of reading labels off the model.
closest.difference: Binary relevance per topic, not choosing among hundreds of codes. It needs token probabilities, which we do not use. No natural-proportion stream of reports, no frozen fit on a previous year.

closest.citation: Yang E, Lewis DD, Frieder O. Heuristic Stopping Rules for Technology-Assisted Review. DocEng 2021 (arXiv 2106.09871); Lewis DD, Yang E, Frieder O. Certifying One-Phase Technology-Assisted Reviews. CIKM 2021 (arXiv 2108.12746); Lewis DD et al. The Delayed Countdown Method for Validating Review-Oriented AI Workflows in eDiscovery (arXiv 2610.31311, 2026)
closest.what_they_did: Stopping rules (Quant, QuantCI, and sample-based quantile rules) that reach a recall target with statistical validity. Overshooting the target is shown to be a major source of excess cost, and paying for more sampling usually lowers total cost. The 2026 paper gives valid frequentist confidence intervals for effectiveness under any stopping rule.
closest.overlap: These define how a read-first list is judged in TAR: recall at a stopping point, with a certificate. Our list has no stopping rule and no recall certificate.
closest.difference: Single topic, with active learning. They do not cover many rare categories at once or LLM proposals. I read the abstracts only, so how cost behaves at very low prevalence is not checked.

closest.citation: Priye P, Wang Y, Ling H, Chaykowsky M. Available Guardrails: Certifying Selective Prediction across ML Systems. arXiv 2609.22048 (Sep 2026)
closest.what_they_did: Certifies precision at a target level for each reporting unit (a label, tool or subgroup) of a selective predictor. Units with little calibration data may be unable to certify at all. The paper calls this 'availability', computed by exact-binomial inversion, and plans how units are grouped and how the error budget is spent. On 60 model effects, splitting the planning and selection data gave +0.060 mean coverage over support balancing.
closest.overlap: Directly confirms our finding that rare codes cannot be auto-accepted with guaranteed precision, as a general statement about certifying selective prediction.
closest.difference: Intent routing, tool calling and moderation, not field reports. Rare units in a moderate-prevalence setting, not 1 in 1,198. No LLM-versus-encoder routing.

closest.citation: ONS Data Science Campus. Automated coding of Standard Industrial and Occupational Classifications (SIC/SOC)
closest.what_they_did: Logistic regression on TF-IDF features. A record is coded automatically when its top probability clears a threshold (0.6 overall for a 95% accuracy target); the rest go to human coders. Census SOC: 0.73 match rate, 0.95 accuracy on matched records. Per-class thresholds missed their 97.5% target (81-90% reached). Smaller classes had lower recall, and new occupations are expected to fall below the threshold and go to manual coding.
closest.overlap: The standard human-in-the-loop coding design, with an automatic share and a manual share. It already shows that rare or small classes are where per-class thresholds fail.
closest.difference: No LLMs, no ranked queue for rare classes, no evaluation over time. Prevalence is not extreme.

closest.citation: Norwegian 1950 census occupation-code review: More efficient manual review of automatically transcribed tabular data. arXiv 2306.16126
closest.what_they_did: After a model transcribed 2.3M codes at about 97% accuracy, the 3% it was least confident about (90,000) went to human review. Reviewers corrected 62.8% of these and agreed with the model on 31.9%. Two reviewers agreed on 86.4% of 9,000 doubly reviewed codes. The model favoured frequent codes and made more errors on rare ones.
closest.overlap: Confidence-based review share in official statistics. It confirms that rare codes are where automatic coding fails, and it measures agreement between human reviewers, which we lack.
closest.difference: Handwriting transcription, not text coding. Review is ordered by low confidence, not by likelihood of a rare code. No LLMs.

closest.citation: Rathje/LGAR: LLM-Guided Abstract Ranker, ACL Findings 2025, arXiv 2505.24757 (authors not recorded from the page)
closest.what_they_did: Zero-shot ranking for abstract screening: an LLM gives graded relevance scores, then a dense re-ranker orders the records. On 57 systematic reviews it beats QA-based ranking by 5-10 points of mean average precision (mAP). It notes that most LLM screening work classifies instead of ranking.
closest.overlap: Ranking with LLM scores instead of hard labels is published and is moving toward the standard in screening.
closest.difference: No trained supervised ranker, one topic at a time, no rare-code multi-class setting, no time split.

closest.citation: Jiang S, Malkomes G, Converse G, Shofner A, Moseley B, Garnett R. Efficient Nonmyopic Active Search. ICML 2017; Nguyen Q, Garnett R. Nonmyopic Multiclass Active Search with Diminishing Returns for Diverse Discovery. arXiv 2202.03593
closest.what_they_did: Active search: find as many members of a rare class as possible under a labelling budget. The multiclass version rewards diversity through diminishing returns, so further finds from an already well-found class count for less. Proven hardness results, and nonmyopic policies that beat baselines, for example in drug discovery.
closest.overlap: The exact objective of our read-first list (cumulative rare finds per read), stated formally. The multiclass version targets a risk our list has: being dominated by a few rare codes.
closest.difference: No text, no LLM, Bayesian models updated with labels during the search. Our list is static.

closest.citation: Marchant NG, Rubinstein BIP. Needle in a Haystack: Label-Efficient Evaluation under Extreme Class Imbalance. KDD 2021. arXiv 2006.06963
closest.what_they_did: Adaptive importance sampling to choose which items to label when estimating a performance measure, with consistency and a central limit theorem. Built for imbalance of about 1 in a million. Lower error than prior methods on a fixed label budget.
closest.overlap: None of our claims. It addresses our measurement weakness: one uniform-sample report stands for about 164 reports, so per-report false rare answers have wide intervals.
closest.difference: An evaluation method, not a coding method.

closest.citation: Li C et al. A Deployment Audit of Release-Side Risk in Conformal Triage under Prevalence Shift. arXiv 2605.20956 (2026)
closest.what_they_did: Audits three-way conformal triage (release, urgent flag, defer to a human) after prevalence shifts, on a lung-cancer cohort. Prevalence-corrected pooled conformal lowers review by releasing more patients, some of whom are event-positive. A class-wise check shows the pilot had too few event labels to support a low-review rule.
closest.overlap: Matches our conclusion that a near-zero human share is not supportable for rare positives, and that a lower review rate can hide missed positives. Our 2025-to-2026 shift is a prevalence shift of this kind.
closest.difference: A clinical binary event, not multi-class coding. No LLMs.

closest.citation: Lieber T et al. Natural language processing for automated triage and prioritization of individual case safety reports for case-by-case assessment. Front Drug Saf Regul 2023;3:1120135
closest.what_they_did: At the Netherlands pharmacovigilance centre (Lareb), ranks incoming adverse-drug-reaction reports by the probability that they need in-depth assessment. Bagged decision trees on structured fields plus bag-of-words text features. AUC 0.921 on 49,928 reports, 36.5% of which needed full assessment. The text features added little.
closest.overlap: An existing example of a regulator-side ranked reading list for safety reports.
closest.difference: Binary, at 36.5% prevalence, no rare codes, no LLMs. It reports no reading saved.

closest.citation: Han B, Mathrani A, Susnjak T. Evaluating Prompting Strategies and LLMs in Systematic Literature Review Screening. arXiv 2510.16091 (2025); TiAb Review Plugin arXiv 2604.08602 (2026)
closest.what_they_did: 2510.16091: six LLMs and five prompt types for screening. Zero-shot maximises recall, chain-of-thought with few-shot examples balances precision and recall, and a staged design escalates only borderline cases to a stronger model. 2604.08602: an LLM screener on five datasets at 0.5-2.0% prevalence reached 94-100% recall, 2-15% precision and 46-89% WSS@95.
closest.overlap: Confirms that at about 1% prevalence even good LLM screeners have low precision, the same base-rate arithmetic as our false rare answers.
closest.difference: Binary topics, prevalence at least 0.5%, no fine-tuned ranker, no multi-code task.

taken: A ranked read-first list, judged by recall against reading effort, work saved over random sampling (WSS@r) and the number of reads needed to reach a target recall. This is the core of TAR and e-discovery (since about 2014) and of systematic-review screening.

Combining LLM judgements with a trained ranker or active learning to cut reading at equal recall (Bron et al. 2024: WSS@95 80.5 against 71.4). Our 'adding LLMs to the encoder ranking cuts reads 2.3-2.5x' is a result of the same kind.
A zero-shot LLM beating a fine-tuned encoder (BioBERT) on reading saved at low prevalence, with the threshold set to a target recall (Wang et al. ECIR 2024).
Ranking with LLM scores instead of hard LLM labels (LGAR, ACL Findings 2025).
Low precision of LLM screeners at prevalence near 1% (2-15% at 0.5-2%), and the general base-rate explanation for it.
Automatic coding above a confidence threshold with the rest sent to human coders, and the observation that rare or small codes are where it fails (ONS SIC/SOC; Norwegian census).

That precision cannot be certified for units or classes with few calibration examples (Available Guardrails 2026, exact-binomial 'availability'). So a near-zero human share with guaranteed precision on rare codes is a known impossibility, not our discovery.
That under a prevalence shift a lower review rate can hide positives released unreviewed (conformal triage audit, 2026).
The formal objective 'find as many rare-class members as possible per label', including a multiclass version that rewards finding diverse classes (active search, Garnett group).
open: TAR/active search over hundreds of rare codes at once, where the reader must also name the code, at about 1 in 1,198 combined prevalence. I found only single-topic binary TAR and the image or drug-discovery multiclass active search. Queries tried: multi-category or multi-label TAR, 'rare category' plus LLM, propose-then-rerank for incident triage. Moderately hard look: about 25 web searches, arXiv API, OpenAlex.
A ranking fitted on one year and frozen, then tested on later years of a live report stream. TAR work simulates within one collection, with active learning on that same collection.

Applying TAR measures (recall against effort, WSS) to safety or failure reports (MAUDE, FAA SDR, ASRS) or to regulator triage of device reports. I found no FDA, EMA or FAA publication of a per-report ranked review list, and no MAUDE paper that ranks reports for review (searches on CDRH MDR triage, EudraVigilance ICSR triage, ASRS LLM triage). The one triage paper read (Lareb) is at 36.5% prevalence.

Encoder probability of the LLM-proposed code used as the ranking signal (LLM proposes, encoder scores). I did not find it under that name. Bron's acceptance classifier on the LLM's reasoning is the nearest. This is a small difference, not a contribution on its own.

How much reading a statistically certified stopping rule (for example QuantCI or certified one-phase TAR) needs when positives are 1 in 1,198 and spread over many codes. I found no measurement at that prevalence.
ideas: Report the list in TAR's terms: gain curves, WSS@r, and reads to reach recall r, against TAR baselines (AutoTAR or continuous active learning with logistic regression from the TARexp framework, and an LLM-only ranking). Needs CPU and the saved scores. Without these baselines, referees from information retrieval will see the list as a weak TAR system.

Continuous active learning on top of the frozen ranking: re-rank after each batch of human reads, using the labels just read. TAR shows this beats a static ranking. It can be simulated on the stored 2026 answers (CPU), but only on reports that have been coded, so it is limited to the uniform sample plus the full set of rare reports.

Certified stopping: add a Quant or QuantCI stopping rule (Yang, Lewis and Frieder 2021) or Lewis's Delayed Countdown so the list comes with a recall estimate and confidence interval. This answers 'when can people stop reading'. Needs CPU plus a random check sample of the unread reports.

Diversity-aware ranking (multiclass active search with diminishing returns, Nguyen and Garnett) so the list does not fill up with a few rare codes, such as the two pump and battery stock phrases. Needs CPU and a per-code value function.

Grouped certification for automatic acceptance: use clustered conformal prediction (Ding et al. 2023) or Available-Guardrails-style grouping, pooling rare codes into groups (for example by level-1 IMDRF code) and auto-accepting only where a group can be certified at the target precision. Expect few or no groups to certify at 1 in 1,198. That result would itself be the honest answer to 'can automation replace people'. Needs labelled calibration data and CPU.

Label-efficient evaluation under extreme imbalance (importance sampling as in Marchant and Rubinstein 2021, or low-shot validation as in Poms et al.) for the per-report false-rare counts, instead of a uniform sample in which each report weighs about 164. Needs a new labelling or LLM-coding budget drawn by importance weights (GPU or API time).

Prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al. 2023) to estimate rare-code counts per year with valid intervals from LLM outputs plus a small labelled sample. This is a different tool from the BBSE or prior-shift count corrections already tried. It gives an automation route that targets counts instead of individual reports. Needs CPU and the existing labelled sample.

My own arithmetic, not from a source: auto-accepting a rare code with 95% confidence that its precision is at least 90%, when all accepted examples are correct, needs at least 29 checked examples (0.9^29 < 0.05). Most of our 1-5-report codes cannot supply this one code at a time.

checks.item: Bron et al., IAL@ECML-PKDD 2024, CEUR Vol-3770 paper8
checks.detail: Full text opened (https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3770/paper8.pdf, extracted locally). 4,836 records with 183 included (3.78%). Runs were stopped at 1,295 reads, which is the LLM's own include count. Misses fell from 16 to 6 (recall 96.68% against 96.52% for AutoTAR). Mean WSS@95 was 80.53% against 71.41%. All figures match the report.

checks.item: Wang, Scells et al., ECIR 2024, arXiv 2401.06320
checks.detail: Full text opened (arxiv.org/html/2401.06320v2). It covers CLEF TAR 2017/18/19 plus the Seed collection, and measures recall, WSS and success rate. BioBERT is a supervised baseline. On CLEF-2017 the uncalibrated WSS is 0.56 against 0.26, as the report says. But at that point Llama2-7b-ins had lower recall (0.87 against 0.95) and a much lower success rate (0.26 against 0.74). A fairer comparison is the calibrated one at 0.95: WSS 0.44 against 0.34 at equal recall (0.92). The report's 'beat BioBERT on WSS' leaves out the recall cost. The paper calls Bio-SIEVE its fine-tuned comparison, not BioBERT.

checks.item: Yang/Lewis/Frieder stopping rules (2106.09871), certified one-phase TAR (2108.12746), Delayed Countdown (2610.31311)
checks.detail: I opened the abstracts of 2108.12746 and 2610.31311 (Lewis, Emory, Gray, Noel, Pickens, Yang; submitted 22 Oct 2026). Both match the report. 2106.09871 was seen only as an arXiv listing entry.

Abstract page opened. Authors Priye, Wang, Ling, Chaykowsky, 18 Sep 2026. It certifies precision per unit by exact-binomial inversion, with 'availability' as the bottleneck. Planning/selection split gave +0.060 mean coverage, in 59 of 60 model effects. Matches the report.

checks.item: ONS Data Science Campus SIC/SOC autocoding page
checks.detail: Page opened. Global threshold 0.6, census SOC match 0.73, matched accuracy 0.95. The per-class threshold aimed at 0.975 reached only 90/86/81% matched accuracy on CIS/ASHE/DLHE. These hold. I could not confirm 'smaller classes had lower recall' or 'new occupations expected to fall below threshold' from what I fetched. The page recommends more training data for under-represented classes and says confidence works worse on datasets under 900 samples.

Abstract opened. Pedersen et al.: 2.3M codes at 97% accuracy, 90,000 (3%) reviewed, 62.8% changed, 31.9% agreed, 86.43% agreement on 9,000 doubly reviewed, more errors on the rarest codes. Matches the report.

Abstract opened. The content is right: 57 reviews, LLM graded scorer plus dense re-ranker, +5-10 points mAP over QA-based ranking. The citation is wrong: the authors are Jaumann, Wiedholz and Friedrich, not 'Rathje'.

checks.item: Nguyen & Garnett, Nonmyopic Multiclass Active Search, arXiv 2202.03593 (and Jiang et al. ICML 2017)
checks.detail: I opened the 2202.03593 abstract and the content matches. arXiv lists no peer-reviewed venue, so cite it as a preprint. Jiang et al. ICML 2017 was not opened.
Abstract opened. Adaptive importance sampling for evaluation at about 1 positive in a million or more, with consistency and a CLT. Matches the report.

Abstract opened. Li C, Liu, Zhang ... Philip Yu, v2 Aug 2026, lung-cancer cohort. Lower review comes from releasing event-positive patients, and the classwise check shows too few event labels. Matches the report.

checks.item: Lieber et al., Lareb ICSR triage, Front Drug Saf Regul 2023
checks.detail: Full text opened (PMC12443081). Bagged decision trees, 49,928 reports, 36.5% labelled 'case', AUC 0.921. NLP features contributed little, and no workload saving is reported. Matches the report.

checks.item: Han et al. arXiv 2510.16091; TiAb Review Plugin arXiv 2604.08602
checks.detail: Both abstracts opened. 2510.16091: six LLMs, five prompt types, zero-shot maximises recall, CoT-few-shot balances precision and recall, staged escalation. 2604.08602 (Kataoka et al.): five datasets at 0.5-2.0% prevalence, recall 94-100%, precision 2-15%, WSS@95 46.3-89.3%. Matches the report.

Its existence was confirmed only as a Crossref record ('Class-Conditional Conformal Prediction with Many Classes', NeurIPS 2023, 10.52202/075280-2817). The paper was not opened. It gives coverage guarantees for prediction sets, not precision guarantees for auto-accepting a label, so it fits our problem less directly than the report suggests.

missed: Yang E, Lewis DD, Frieder O. On Minimizing Cost in Legal Document Review Workflows. DocEng 2021, arXiv 2106.09866. Full text read. It analyses one-phase TAR against two-phase TAR (train first, then review in ranked order), which is the TAR name for our frozen ranker, and shows that category prevalence changes which workflow and stopping point is cheapest. It also shows the field's blind spot: of RCV1-v2's 804,414 documents and 658 categories, the 'too rare' bin (<500 positives, about 0.06%; 270 categories) was left out of the experiments. That is direct support that our prevalence is unstudied in TAR, and it is the right baseline frame (two-phase TAR).

Thomas J et al. Machine learning reduced workload with minimal risk of missing studies: Cochrane RCT Classifier. J Clin Epidemiol 2021;133:140-151, PMID 33171275, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8168828/. Abstract and full text read. A classifier trained on 280,620 records had its threshold fixed on a separate calibration set for 99% recall (precision 0.08). It was then deployed unchanged on Cochrane's live record stream, where it spared manual checks of 185,039 of 449,480 records in 2018, and older records were missed more often. This is published prior art for 'fit once, freeze, apply to a later stream with a recall-targeted threshold' (binary, about 3% prevalence).

Botsis T, Nguyen MD, Woo EJ, Markatou M, Ball R (FDA CBER). Text mining for VAERS: medical text classification using informative feature selection. JAMIA 2011;18:631-8, PMID 21709163. Abstract read. Classifies VAERS narratives for anaphylaxis (237 positives of 6,034) explicitly to cut medical-officer review workload. This is a regulator's own staff publishing workload-reducing text triage of safety reports, so 'no regulator publication' needs softening.

Ciccarelli L, Mahaux O et al. Optimising Pharmacovigilance Efficiency with MLIT (Machine Learning for Intelligent Triage). Drug Saf 2026, doi 10.1007/s40264-026-01696-0, PMID 42573921. Abstract read. Industry (GSK) triage of statistical safety alerts with XGBoost, run as two four-month prospective validations over 20+ products. 92% of alerts closed in line with the top prediction and 98% within the top 3, and reviewers reported 24% less triage time. Shows prospective (forward-in-time) triage evaluation with time saved in pharmacovigilance.

Li L, Yin J, Wang Z, Xu J. AI-Assisted Risk Prioritization of Surgical Stapler Adverse-Event Reports for Post-Market Surveillance. Int J Med Device Inform 2026;1(2):6, doi 10.66128/IJMDI202602.1, https://perennial.pub/journal/ijmdi/1/2/6. Article page read. 52,250 MAUDE reports for development with external validation on 5,593 Jiangsu reports, using LR, RF and XGBoost on structured fields, IMDRF code indicators and narrative-derived variables. It reports AUC and AP only, with no reading or workload measures. So a MAUDE report-prioritisation paper does exist, but it is binary (seriousness), single device, and not measured as recall against reads.

Yang E, Lewis DD, Frieder O. TAR on Social Media: A Framework for Online Content Moderation. DESIRES 2021, arXiv 2108.12752. Abstract read. Moves TAR workflows and cost models to moderation queues, cutting cost by about 20-55% on two datasets. It is precedent for taking TAR outside literature and legal review into a stream of reports, which weakens 'applying TAR to a new report stream' as novelty.

Pelleg D, Moore A. Active Learning for Anomaly and Rare-Category Detection (NIPS 2004); He J, Carbonell J. Nearest-Neighbor-Based Active Learning for Rare Category Detection (NIPS 2007). Seen only as OpenAlex metadata listings, not opened. This is the classic literature whose goal is to surface examples of many rare classes with few labels, which is closer to our multi-code setting than single-topic TAR. Its aim is the first example of each class, not recall of all items.

Coleman C et al. Similarity Search for Efficient Active Learning and Search of Rare Concepts (SEALS), arXiv 2007.00077. Abstract read. Active search for rare concepts at web scale, with candidates restricted to nearest neighbours of labelled examples. Images only.

arXiv 2609.01833 (Sep 2026). Candidate Generation and Definition-Guided Verification for Sentence-Level Depression Symptom Recognition. Abstract read. A fine-tuned encoder proposes one candidate category and a fine-tuned LM verifies it against a definition. This is the reverse of our 'LLM proposes, encoder scores' order, and the authors say rare categories stay weak. It is the nearest published propose-then-verify split I found.

SSRN 7321995 (2026). 'Leakage-Controlled Seriousness Triage of Spontaneous Adverse-Event Reports: ... Temporal Validation Framework'. Title only (Crossref listing; SSRN returned 403). Possibly a temporally validated report triage paper; unverified.
taken_after_check: A ranked read-first list judged by recall against reading effort, WSS@r and reads to reach a target recall. This is the core of TAR, e-discovery and systematic-review screening, with Cormack/Grossman CAL papers listed in OpenAlex (SIGIR 2014, 2016).

Two-phase TAR: train a ranker once, then review in ranked order without further learning, with cost analysed as a function of category prevalence (Yang, Lewis, Frieder DocEng 2021). Our frozen ranker is an instance of this.

Fixing a recall-targeted threshold on calibration data and then running the frozen classifier on a later live stream with large workload savings (Cochrane RCT Classifier, Thomas et al. 2021; 99% recall target, about 41% of 2018 records spared). Binary, about 3% prevalence.
Combining LLM judgements with a trained or active-learning ranker to cut reading at equal recall (Bron et al. 2024: misses 16 to 6, WSS@95 80.5 against 71.4 at 3.8% prevalence).

A zero-shot LLM reaching more work saved than a supervised BioBERT once both are calibrated to the same recall (Wang et al. ECIR 2024; calibrated 0.95: WSS 0.44 against 0.34 at recall 0.92 on CLEF-2017). Uncalibrated, the LLM's higher WSS came with lower recall.
Ranking with graded LLM scores instead of hard LLM labels (LGAR, Jaumann, Wiedholz and Friedrich, ACL Findings 2025).
Low precision of LLM screeners at prevalence near 1% (TiAb plugin: precision 2-15% at 0.5-2%), and the base-rate explanation for it.

Automatic coding above a confidence threshold with a manual share, where per-class thresholds fall short of accuracy targets (ONS SIC/SOC) and rare codes are where automatic coding errs (Norwegian census).

Certifying precision fails for units with too little calibration data (Available Guardrails 2026), and a lower review rate under prevalence shift can hide released positives (conformal triage audit 2026).

Workload-reducing text triage of safety reports, at regulators and in industry pharmacovigilance: FDA CBER on VAERS (Botsis 2011), Lareb ICSR ranking (2023), GSK MLIT with prospective validation and 24% triage time saved (2026). Also a MAUDE prioritisation model, stapler seriousness (Li L et al. 2026), though it reports AUC only.
TAR applied outside literature and legal review, to a stream of user reports (content moderation, Yang et al. 2021).

The formal objective of finding as many rare-class items per label as possible, including a multiclass version that rewards diversity (active search, Garnett group). Also classic rare-category detection (Pelleg and Moore 2004, He and Carbonell 2007; metadata only).
open_after_check: Recall against reads for hundreds of rare codes pooled at about 1 in 1,198, where the reader must also name the code. Still not found. The strongest evidence that this is a gap is that the main TAR cost study dropped RCV1 categories with fewer than 500 positives in 804k (about 0.06%) from its experiments. Rare-category detection is the nearest multi-class literature, but it aims to find the first example of each class, not high recall, and uses no text LLMs.

Freezing a ranker on one calendar year and measuring recall against reads on later years of the same report stream. The general move is taken (Cochrane's frozen threshold on a live stream; prospective validation of MLIT). Only the multi-code, very-low-prevalence, year-on-year version on safety or failure reports remains open. That is an application claim, not a method claim.

TAR-style measures (gain curve, WSS, reads to recall r) on MAUDE or FAA SDR. Report triage at regulators exists (VAERS 2011, Lareb, MLIT), and a MAUDE prioritisation paper exists (stapler, 2026), but none reports reading effort, and none covers device-problem codes or SDR. Narrow but still open.

An LLM proposing the code and the fine-tuned encoder's probability for that code ordering the queue. Not found. The nearest is the reverse order: an encoder proposes and an LM verifies (arXiv 2609.01833). A small design difference, not a contribution on its own.

How much reading a statistically certified stopping rule needs at about 1 in 1,198 spread over many codes. Not found, and TAR experiments explicitly avoid such rare categories. This could be a measurable contribution if run with QuantCI or Delayed Countdown baselines.
check.net: The report is accurate on substance. Every 'closest' source exists and says roughly what the report claims. Two corrections: LGAR's authors are Jaumann, Wiedholz and Friedrich, not 'Rathje'. Wang et al.'s uncalibrated 'beat BioBERT on WSS' came with lower recall (0.87 against 0.95); the fair comparison is calibrated (WSS 0.44 against 0.34 at recall 0.92). ONS small-class details are only partly confirmed, and Nguyen and Garnett is a preprint. The 'open' list is too generous on two items. (a) 'Frozen on a previous period, then applied to a later stream' is published: the Cochrane RCT Classifier (threshold fixed for 99% recall, deployed unchanged, about 41% of 2018 records spared) and two-phase TAR (Yang, Lewis and Frieder 2021). (b) 'No regulator publishes report triage' is wrong: FDA CBER on VAERS (Botsis 2011), Lareb, and GSK's prospectively validated MLIT (2026) exist, and a MAUDE stapler-report prioritisation paper (2026) exists, though none measures reading effort. What survives as open is narrow: multi-code recall against reads at about 0.08% pooled prevalence, which TAR studies leave out on purpose (RCV1 categories under 500 positives were dropped), on device and aviation reports, frozen year to year, with certified stopping. That is an application and measurement contribution, publishable only if framed in TAR terms with two-phase TAR, CAL and LLM-only baselines. Search effort: about 25 WebFetch and API calls. The WebSearch budget for this turn was already used up when I started (200 calls shared across agents), so I could not run new web searches. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were also rate-limited. The attack on 'open' therefore relied on arXiv API (about 15 queries), PubMed E-utilities (about 11), Crossref (5) and direct page fetches. A follow-up run with search budget should try: multi-label or multi-issue e-discovery review, rare-category detection with LLMs (2024-26), FAERS/VAERS LLM triage (2025-26), and content-moderation queues for rare violation types. prior.title: What reliability and safety journals publish on text coding with LLMs

report.answer: Reliability and safety journals published plenty in 2024-2026 on LLM classification of incident, accident and maintenance text. Almost all of it is one of three kinds: a zero- or few-shot comparison of off-the-shelf LLMs on one dataset of a few hundred to a few thousand reports with 4-40 classes (Aljasmi 2026 Safety Science; Smetana 2026 EAAI; Yang 2025 J Loss Prev; Bharati 2026 arXiv), a fine-tuned versus prompted comparison (Wang 2026 JAMIA, where fine-tuned BERT beat the decoder LLMs; Shin 2026 Safety Science), or a pipeline with a downstream risk model or knowledge graph (RESS ship-collision, crane and aviation papers; Xian 2025 Part O). I found no paper in RESS, ESWA, EAAI, CAIE, Safety Science, J Loss Prev, AEI, Computers in Industry, IEEE TR, Part O or PHM venues that codes MAUDE device-problem codes, codes SDR PartCondition, or picks per report between a fine-tuned encoder and a prompted LLM by the training support of the proposed code. I also found no paper there that studies hundreds of codes at natural proportions over a frozen future year. So nobody has published the core selector-plus-long-tail result in these venues. But several pieces of the story are already taken. Sending only uncertain codes to a person is decades old: Marucci-Wellman 2017 sent the least confident 30% of injury narratives to people, and the BLS autocoder assigns a code only above a confidence threshold. Dela Peña 2026 already codes FAA SDR JASC codes with a classifier, retrieval and a conformal 'review-required' abstention rule. Al Hajri 2026 (ADIPEC) runs a production ISO 14224 work-order coder with retrieval, three-run LLM consensus and human override. Sirago 2026 shows that LLM errors are correlated across models, that majority voting does not help and that no model beats the reporter, which matches our finding that LLM agreement does not rescue the rare labels. Bharati 2026 treats official database codes as an agreement reference, not truth, and shows a keyword rule matching the best frontier LLM on macro-F1. On venues: Safety Science, EAAI, AEI, JAMIA, Part O, IEEE TR and Transactions of the Institute of Aviation all publish evaluation-only or simple-pipeline papers. Prior project notes say RESS papers usually add a downstream reliability or risk model. Caveats: the shared web-search budget ran out partway through, and several close Elsevier abstracts (Ding EAAI 2026, Hou EAAI 2026, Chhetri AEI 2026, the RESS ship-collision hybrid) could not be read, so a scoop inside those four cannot be fully ruled out.

closest.citation: Dela Peña A, Clariza J, Aballiar-Vista MA (2026). Evidence-Grounded Decision Support for Aircraft Line Maintenance Using Conformal Prediction and Retrieval-Augmented NLP from Technical Log Records. Transactions of the Institute of Aviation.
closest.what_they_did: FAA SDRS, 4,430 deduplicated events 2021-2023, heavily imbalanced JASC codes as labels (filer-chosen). Chronological 70/10/20 train/calibration/test split plus a station hold-out. TF-IDF + linear SVM triage (top-1 0.509, top-3 0.683), TF-IDF retrieval of precedents, split-conformal prediction with a review-required abstention rule (coverage 0.919 at a 90% target). Performance falls under station shift.
closest.overlap: Covers 'SDR coding with temporal split' and 'route uncertain reports to human review' for SDR. Already listed in project note section 17 as an SDR ML use; the conformal-abstention detail is new here.
closest.difference: JASC component codes, not PartCondition; no LLM; no rare-code analysis; small scale; no encoder-vs-LLM selection.

closest.citation: Al Hajri SB, Al Araimi AS, Mohammed S (2026). Reliability AI: A Production LLM System for Converting Maintenance Data into ISO 14224-Compliant Reliability Information. ADIPEC 2026, SPE-236015-MS.
closest.what_they_did: Production deployment: hierarchical RAG over labelled work orders plus a three-run LLM consensus that scores candidate failure codes (vote agreement, confidence, consensus). Human override-and-approval workflow writes corrections back into the vector store without retraining. Blind evaluation on 300 historical work orders gives about 70% (the figure is cut off in the abstract).
closest.overlap: Takes 'LLM + retrieved labelled examples for failure-code assignment, with a human review loop' as a deployed pattern. Overlaps our kNN-prompted coder and our review-queue conclusion.
closest.difference: Private oil-and-gas data, ISO 14224 codes, no fine-tuned encoder, no rare/frequent split, no temporal frozen test, tiny evaluation.

closest.citation: Sirago G, Sabato S, Sebastiani N, Zotti F, Dell'Erba A, Ferorelli D (2026). Large Language Models as Raters of Hospital Incident Reports: A Blinded Multi-Model Evaluation of Severity Under-Grading and Shared Errors. Jt Comm J Qual Patient Saf.
closest.what_they_did: Five commercial LLMs classify 824 hospital incident reports against an expert-adjudicated reference and the original reporter. Event type kappa 0.82-0.84; severity weighted kappa 0.39-0.47. Errors are correlated (model-model kappa above model-reference), majority voting does not help, no model surpasses the reporter, and confidence is weakly informative. Test-retest and prompt variants are included.
closest.overlap: Already shows our finding that LLM agreement/voting does not fix errors and that confidence is weakly informative. It also has the expert-adjudicated reference our labels lack.
closest.difference: Few categories, no fine-tuned model, no long tail, no selector, hospital incidents not devices.

closest.citation: Bharati S, K C Khatri R, Bharati S (2026). Benchmarking Frontier Large Language Models Against Official Crash Database Coding Using Police Crash Narratives. arXiv 2607.29064.
closest.what_they_did: 4,194 Arkansas fatal crashes; six frontier LLMs, one zero-shot prompt, six coded attributes; agreement, macro-F1, kappa, coverage and selective agreement against always-majority, always-Unknown and keyword-rule baselines. The always-majority baseline beat the LLMs on raw agreement, and the keyword rule matched the best LLM on macro-F1 and kappa. Disagreement is explicitly not read as model error, because the official record can be wrong.
closest.overlap: The framing 'agreement with official/filer coding, not accuracy' (our section 19-20 idea of renaming the metric) and transparent rule baselines (like our 60-character template rule) are already used here.
closest.difference: Few categories per attribute, no fine-tuned model, no long tail, no selection between coders, preprint.

closest.citation: Marucci-Wellman HR, Corns HL, Lehto MR (2017). Classifying injury narratives of large administrative databases for surveillance: a practical approach combining machine learning ensembles and human review. Accident Analysis & Prevention 98:359-371. Plus the BLS SOII autocoder page.
closest.what_they_did: Marucci-Wellman: compared filtering by prediction strength with filtering by algorithm agreement to choose which narratives go to manual coding; sending the bottom 30% to people gave high final accuracy (search snippet only). BLS: the autocoder assigns SOC/OIICS codes only above a confidence threshold; about 85% of codes were autocoded in 2019, about 92% in 2021-22 and about 81% in 2023 after the OIICS v3.02 migration; logistic regression, then a CNN/LSTM, then a transformer.
closest.overlap: Takes the human-machine split and the review queue as a decades-old operational pattern with hundreds of codes, and code-revision shocks hurting the autocoder (our 2026-08-17 code revision).
closest.difference: Pre-LLM; no rare-code analysis at natural proportions; no fine-tuned-vs-prompted choice.

closest.citation: Wang Y, Bowditch L, Molloy C, Yu Y, Hibbert P, Magrabi F (2026). Fine-tuning and evaluating large language models for patient safety tasks: classification of contributing factors in incident reports. JAMIA 33(8):1494-1503.
closest.what_they_did: 300 expert-labelled investigation reports (1,338 contributing factors, 12 categories over 6 system levels). Fine-tuned BERT (micro-F1 63.6%) beats LLaMA2, GPT-2 and Phi-2. The authors call for better coverage of rare system levels.
closest.overlap: Another instance of 'fine-tuned encoder wins in aggregate'; it flags rare classes as the weak spot.
closest.difference: Small, expert-labelled, few classes, no prompted frontier LLM, no combination.

closest.citation: Xian M, Wang T, Zhang S, Xu F, Ma Z (2025). A knowledge-informed large language model framework for U.S. nuclear power plant shutdown initiating event classification for probabilistic risk assessment. Proc IMechE Part O 239(6):1257-1264.
closest.what_they_did: Two-stage pipeline on 10,928 events: a binary screen built on 44 text patterns removes more than 97% of non-events, then fine-tuned BERT sorts events into 4 types (95.1% mean accuracy). It names scarce labels, imbalance and noisy labels as the problem.
closest.overlap: Shows that Part O accepts a short, simple screen-then-classify paper (already listed as a precedent in journal-search-2026-10-23).
closest.difference: 4 classes, BERT only, no LLM prompting, no long tail.

closest.citation: Aljasmi A, Ali L, Dixit V, Al Jassmi H (2026). Decoding crash narratives: a comparative evaluation of large language models for accident cause classification. Safety Science 200:107231.
closest.what_they_did: 2,886 Abu Dhabi police crash reports, 37 cause categories, five LLMs zero-shot with single-label output; ChatGPT best (accuracy 0.7308), Mistral second; reports cost, time and unclassified rate. No new method.
closest.overlap: Venue evidence: Safety Science publishes evaluation-only LLM coding studies (already in project venue notes).
closest.difference: No fine-tuned model, no rare-class analysis, private data, small label set.

closest.citation: Verhagen WJC, Scott M (2025). Automating Aircraft Defect Report Code Classification Using Natural Language Processing. Advances in Transdisciplinary Engineering.
closest.what_they_did: Predicts JASC codes from FAA SDRS defect text, comparing a legacy NLP model with an LLM-based method on a subset; notes data imbalance and explainability as open problems.
closest.overlap: Takes 'LLM vs classical model on SDR code assignment' (JASC), already noted in project section 17.
closest.difference: JASC not PartCondition, subset only, no long-tail binning, no selector, no temporal test.

closest.citation: Anwar MS, de Costa M, Mercier D, Hammad I (2026). Automated Classification of Nuclear Power Plant Condition Records Using Large Language Models. IEEE SEGE 2026.
closest.what_they_did: Two-stage few-shot LLM pipeline: stage 1 isolates equipment-reliability events, stage 2 maps them to ISO 14224 failure modes (75% detection, 71% failure-mode accuracy). It favours false positives on purpose so that possible degradation goes to human review.
closest.overlap: Explicitly accepts over-flagging plus human review as a design choice, the same trade-off as our rare-code review queue.
closest.difference: No fine-tuned model, private data, no rare-code base-rate analysis.

closest.citation: Ding Y, Zhu F, Zheng P, Xie M (2026). Hierarchy-aware prompt tuning with bidirectional information propagation for failure data mining. Knowledge-Based Systems 347:116252. Sister paper: Ding Y, Zhu F, Li H, Xie M (2026), A large language model-augmented hierarchical text classification approach for intelligent failure data management, EAAI 115750.
closest.what_they_did: KBS: few-shot hierarchical classification of failure texts by prompt-tuning pre-trained LMs with layer-wise label propagation and uncertainty quantification; offshore wind O&M corpus from 313 turbines plus DBpedia. EAAI sister: abstract unavailable; the title says LLM-augmented hierarchical failure-text classification.
closest.overlap: The closest venue-side 'failure-text classification with LMs under scarce labels' line (PolyU, Min Xie group). It may cover hierarchy and few-shot ideas.
closest.difference: Private wind data; per the KBS abstract, no long-tail binning, no frozen next-year test, no encoder-vs-LLM selection. The EAAI paper's content is unverified.

taken: Routing uncertain automatic codes to human coders by confidence threshold or classifier agreement, for hundreds of codes in administrative narrative data (Marucci-Wellman 2017; BLS SOII autocoder since 2014). Our review queue is not new as an idea.
Conformal or abstention-based 'review-required' output for FAA SDR code assignment with a chronological split (Dela Peña 2026, JASC).
LLM vs classical/legacy NLP for SDR code assignment (Verhagen & Scott 2025, JASC).
Deployed LLM + retrieved-labelled-examples coder for ISO 14224 failure codes with human override that writes corrections back to the retrieval store (Al Hajri 2026 ADIPEC).

LLM errors are correlated across models, majority voting does not help, and confidence is weakly informative on safety reports (Sirago 2026). Our 'LLM agreement does not fix rare labels' finding repeats this direction.
Treating official/filer codes as an agreement reference rather than truth, and benchmarking LLMs against always-majority and keyword-rule baselines that can match them (Bharati 2026).

Fine-tuned encoders beating prompted or decoder LLMs in aggregate on safety-incident classification, with rare classes named as the weak point (Wang 2026 JAMIA; Gondara 2025 and Bucher 2024 already in references).
Over-flagging on purpose so a person reviews possible failures (Anwar 2026); two-stage screen then fine classify (Xian 2025 Part O).

A MAUDE narrative-vs-structured-problem-code comparison for safety signals already exists as a preregistered study (Balcı & Akgüller 2026, OSF, recall detection), so 'narratives carry signal beyond the codes' is not ours alone.
open: Per-report selection between a fine-tuned encoder and prompted LLMs using the training support of the proposed code, frozen and tested on a later year. Not found in any of the target venues. Looked: OpenAlex venue-filtered title/abstract queries over 13 ISSNs (RESS, ESWA, EAAI, CAIE, Safety Science, JLPPI, AEI, Comput Ind, IEEE TR, IJPHM, Part O, PSEP, 2024-2026, about 25 queries), venue-wide title scans for LLM/BERT/text-classification/narrative terms (about 150 titles read), PubMed for MAUDE/incident-report LLM work, arXiv API (8 queries before rate limit), and citation chasing from Stewart 2023 (21 citers), MADE and Li H 2026.

MAUDE device-problem-code assignment with hundreds of leaf codes in any reliability or safety journal: none found. The MAUDE LLM papers in PubMed are single-device tabulations (Sohoni 2026 Urology; Shi & Gong 2025; Kesharwani 2026), not code assignment.
