ideas: Split-conformal or class-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction sets with a review-required abstention rule, as in Dela Peña 2026. It turns the selector into a coverage-guaranteed set-valued coder and gives the review queue a stated error rate. Needs the 2025 dev year as the calibration set; CPU only.

A deployment metric borrowed from BLS and Marucci-Wellman: the share of reports auto-coded at a fixed agreement level (for example 90% or 95%), and the manual-coding share needed to reach it, compared across encoder alone, selector and cascade. This reframes the result as 'automation share at target quality', which answers the owner's 'automation is meant to avoid people' objection with a number. CPU only on existing outputs.

Report model-model agreement against model-reference agreement (Sirago 2026) and add always-majority and keyword/template-rule baselines (Bharati 2026; we already have the 60-character rule) in the main tables. CPU only.

A simulated feedback loop (Al Hajri 2026): stream the 2026 test year month by month, add reviewer-confirmed rare-code reports to the kNN retrieval store, and measure how fast later reports of the same rare code are found. Needs re-running the kNN-prompted coder on the open models (GPU, user approval) or a CPU retrieval-only proxy.

Two-stage screen (Xian 2025; Anwar 2026): a cheap binary 'possible rare-code report' screen trained on the training year before the LLM coder, judged by reads per rare find at natural proportions. CPU for the screen; LLM calls only on screened reports.

A downstream safety-signal test that does not depend on filer codes (Balcı & Akgüller 2026): check whether rare-code finds by the selector or read-first list come before later Class I recalls of the same device. Needs the public FDA recall list (small) and CPU.
Hierarchy-aware scoring or prompting (Ding KBS 2026): score at IMDRF level 1/2/leaf, which the project already listed as item 3 of section 20; this literature supports it as a standard evaluation.

missed: EnergyRoute (Sci Rep 2026, doi:10.1038/s41598-026-49886-1; abstract read via Europe PMC). This is the closest prior work to the selector that either agent found. It routes each case through three tiers: a fine-tuned transformer encoder for confident cases, retrieval-augmented kNN fusion for moderately uncertain ones, and an evidence-grounded LLM for the hardest. The task is 301 severely imbalanced leaf classes (82,316 Korean biotech R&D projects), and it is checked again on Web of Science (142 classes). It reports a significant macro-F1 gain over the fine-tuned encoder while sending 20% of cases to the LLM, and it beats confidence-based cascading. Our three coders (encoder, LLM with retrieved neighbours, LLM) and our comparison against a cascade therefore have a published analogue. Differences: it routes before any LLM answer, using the encoder's logit energy, not using the training support of the code the LLM proposes; it is not failure or safety text; it has no frozen later-year test and no natural-proportion rare-code analysis.

Critical Appraisal of AI for Rare-Event Recognition: Principles and Pharmacovigilance Case Studies (Drug Safety 2026, doi:10.1007/s40264-026-01649-7; abstract read). It sets out prevalence-aware evaluation, warns about optimism from unrealistic class balance and test sets without difficult positive controls, covers integration into human workflows and cost-sensitive targets, and includes LLMs constrained to classify. So the general base-rate argument behind our natural-proportion result is already published as principle. The specific measurement of LLM over-naming of rare codes is not.

Machine Learning to Prioritize High-Severity Patient Safety Events (JMIR Med Inform 2026, doi:10.2196/101393; abstract read). On 101,239 safety reports, ranking models (LLaMA3.1 ranker) beat classification models and the reporter-assigned severity. The ranker retrieves 83.0% of high-severity events in the top 200, against 41.0% under reporter severity. This is published precedent for the ranked read-first list framing in safety reporting, judged by Recall@k and Precision@k.

Classification of health product defect reports by deep learning (Sci Rep 2026, doi:10.1038/s41598-026-43961-3; abstract read). It uses 13,830 expert-labelled defect reports in 21 categories with prospective validation. Per-category accuracy rises with category sample size (r 0.64) and with confidence (r 0.93). This is a published observation that training support predicts accuracy, which is the main input of our selector. It is not LLM work.

Marucci-Wellman 2017 abstract (above): it explicitly aims at filtering 'rare, emerging or ambiguous narratives for manual review' with hundreds of BLS OIICS codes, so a review queue for rare codes is older than the report says.

Comparison of proprietary and fine-tuned LLMs for billing codes from radiology reports (Eur Radiol 2026, doi:10.1007/s00330-026-12445-3; abstract read). On 499,601 reports, a fine-tuned 4B model beat the best frontier LLM on 500 real reports (F1 70.3 vs 58.2), but GPT-5 won on 350 cleaned reports. Whether the fine-tuned model or the frontier LLM wins depends on label and text quality, which is relevant to our filer-label argument.

Automated Classification of Radiation Oncology Safety Events Using LLMs (Pract Radiat Oncol 2026, doi:10.1016/j.prro.2026.08.001; abstract read). GPT-5 classifies failure mode and other dimensions. Agreement between the model and each reviewer (mean kappa 0.31) is about the same as agreement between reviewers (0.42). It proposes asking for human validation when the model is uncertain. This is another case of measuring a model against human-human agreement instead of a single label.

ASA-PS hybrid ML-LLM ensemble (JMIR 2026, doi:10.2196/90724; abstract read). A weighted average of XGBoost and GPT-4o, with an expert-panel ceiling of macro-F1 0.59. It is hybrid ML+LLM classification, but with few classes and structured data.

prior.title: Clinical coding after Motzfeldt 2025 and Eng 2026

report.answer: Clinical coding already reports the split our draft relies on, so it is taken. Motzfeldt et al. (EMNLP-F 2025) read it from macro versus micro F1 on MDACE, with no frequency bins. Yock/Eng et al. (EMNLP 2026) measure it directly with per-bin F1 on 150 MIMIC-IV notes, giving rare/uncommon/common at 0-100/101-1,000/>1,000 training notes. PLM-ICD scores .227/.471/.656 and CodeSeeker with Opus 4.6 scores .560/.483/.607. Combining a fine-tuned coder with an LLM is also not new. Yock tested PLM-ICD as a tool for the agent and the results were mixed. Akkhawatthanakun et al. (Informatics 2026) had an LLM audit PLM-ICD's 15 candidates, which mainly trims false positives. L2D-Clinical (arXiv 2604.13285) trains a logistic deferral model that sends some instances from BERT to an LLM, but only for 2-3 classes. Two 2026 papers list a hybrid PLM-LLM design as future work: Wang et al. (EMNLP-F 2026, arXiv 2606.13940) and Gan et al. (RAG-Coding). None of these picks one answer per note or per code from several coders using features of the proposed codes, such as how many training notes they have. None tests on a later time period: every paper read uses random or Edin-style splits of MIMIC or MDACE. None reports the false-positive burden of LLM rare-code predictions at true prevalence. Yock samples 50 notes per bin, so its rare-bin precision of .317 for Opus is measured at an inflated prevalence, and the paper does not say so. The papers name these open problems: precision ("selection is harder than verification"), label noise and the ceiling it puts on F1, single institutions, and keeping coders in the loop. For label checking, MDACE (Cheng 2023) and MDACE-2025 (Gan et al. 2026) are the expert re-annotation models: MDACE overlaps less than half with the original MIMIC codes, and MDACE-2025 has alpha 0.66 against MDACE. The 1.8-million-patient Danish study confirmed 76-86% of the model's apparent false positives as true under-coding when they were reviewed by hand. That is the strongest published case for "the model is right and the label is wrong", and it is close to our MAUDE situation. I found no public clinical coding dataset that has expert labels, allows commercial APIs, is single-label with hundreds of codes, and has yearly releases. MIMIC/MDACE needs zero-data-retention services under PhysioNet's 2025 guidance, and CodiEsp (CC BY 4.0, coded by professionals) has only 1,000 multi-label cases. The best biomedical-adjacent candidate is NEISS: hundreds of product codes chosen by trained hospital coordinators and checked daily by CPSC, released yearly, with only 100-case LLM studies so far. My web-search budget ran out before I finished the rare-disease false-positive and NEISS checks.

closest.citation: Motzfeldt A, Edin J, et al. Code Like Humans: A Multi-Agent Solution for Medical Coding. Findings of EMNLP 2025, pp. 22612-22627. arXiv 2509.05378
closest.what_they_did: Built a four-agent ICD-10-CM pipeline (extract evidence, navigate the alphabetical index, validate against the tabular list, reconcile) and evaluated it on MDACE, where expert coders verified code evidence. Compared it with PLM-ICD. CLH-large has the higher macro-F1 (0.28 vs 0.25) and PLM-ICD the higher micro-F1 (0.48 vs 0.43). Precision is the main weakness (0.40 final). They also fine-tuned a 1B LLM on MIMIC-III-50.
closest.overlap: Covers our claim 2 in direction only: LLM better on rare codes, fine-tuned model better on frequent ones. The evidence is macro versus micro F1, with no per-frequency bins, no training-size sweep and no later year.
closest.difference: No combination or routing of any kind. No temporal split. No analysis of false positives at real prevalence. Multi-label inpatient notes, not one code per short report. Future work points to keeping coders in the loop, fine-tuning each agent, and self-refinement.

closest.citation: Yock EC (arXiv listing: Eng CY), Cao Y, Chen Y, Mao K, Jiang H. Understanding the Limits of Agentic ICD Coding. EMNLP 2026 main, pp. 36028-36037. arXiv 2609.13806
closest.what_they_did: Evaluated 150 MIMIC-IV discharge notes, 50 per rarity bin, binned by each note's least frequent code in training (0-100 / 101-1,000 / >1,000). Systems: PLM-ICD, the CodeSeeker workflow agent and a free-form nine-tool agent, run on six LLMs including Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.2. Rare/uncommon/common F1: PLM-ICD .227/.471/.656, CodeSeeker-Opus .560/.483/.607. Also a multi-step subset (S/T and V-Y chapters). Giving the agent PLM-ICD as a tool helped GPT-5.2 on rare codes and hurt Opus. Agents verify many candidates and submit under 4%. Correct codes are found earlier than wrong ones, which they suggest but do not test as a precision signal.
closest.overlap: Takes the rare-versus-frequent split, measured by training frequency, with Claude Opus, and says no single system dominates. Takes the first combination step: classifier output given to the LLM.
closest.difference: No choice of answer per note or per code. Rare-bin precision (Opus .317) comes from a stratified sample, not real prevalence. No temporal split. Notes, not short reports. No training-size sweep. No confidence-cascade or vote baselines.

closest.citation: Akkhawatthanakun K, Narupiyakul L, Wongpatikaseree K, Hnoohom N, Termritthikun C, Muneesawang P. Integrating Agentic Artificial Intelligence to Automate ICD-10 Medical Coding. Informatics 2026, 13(3):39. doi:10.3390/informatics13030039 (preprint: preprints.org 202512.2138)
closest.what_they_did: On 19,801 MIMIC-IV summaries, compared PLM-ICD alone (15 codes per case, precision 55.8%), LLM-only generation (precision 1.5-34.6%), and a hybrid in which an LLM audits PLM-ICD's candidates, keeping 2-8 codes. LLMs: Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Phi-4-mini and Sonnet-4.5. Llama-3.2-3B goes from 1.5% precision as a generator to 55.1% as a verifier and cuts false positives by 73%. Evaluation is guided by precision because coders add any missing codes.
closest.overlap: A published hybrid of a fine-tuned coder and an LLM in clinical coding, judged by false positives and coder workload. Its conclusion, the LLM as quality controller rather than generator, is the opposite of using the LLM's long-tail strength.
closest.difference: A filter-then-rerank pattern: the LLM can only remove the classifier's candidates, so it cannot add rare codes the classifier misses. No selection among several coders, no rare-code analysis, no temporal split. Recall and F1 are left to future work.

closest.citation: Kondadadi R, Ortega JE. L2D-Clinical: Learning to Defer for Adaptive Model Selection in Clinical Text Classification. arXiv 2604.13285 (2026)
closest.what_they_did: A logistic-regression deferral model with BERT uncertainty features and hand-made text features predicts when BERT is wrong and sends those instances to GPT-5-nano few-shot. Run on ADE Corpus (2 classes) and MIMIC-IV treatment outcome (3 classes). Baselines: fixed confidence threshold and random deferral. MIMIC F1 rises from 0.887 to 0.980 with 16.8% deferred.
closest.overlap: Closest to our selector in form: a logistic model over simple features picks, per instance, between a fine-tuned encoder and an LLM, compared against a confidence-threshold baseline.
closest.difference: 2-3 classes, so no long tail. Features describe the encoder's uncertainty and the input text, not the proposed answers. One LLM. Random splits with tiny test sets (279 and 500). MIMIC labels are LLM consensus. Not peer-reviewed.

closest.citation: Wang Z, Li W, Chen S, Luo Y, Ding K. Can Post-Training Turn LLMs into Good Medical Coders? An Empirical Study of Generative ICD Coding. Findings of EMNLP 2026. arXiv 2606.13940
closest.what_they_did: SFT, then GRPO, then progressive hint injection for Qwen 1.5B and 4B on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, Top-50 and Full label sets, against PLM-ICD and other classifiers. On the Full set the LLMs stay below PLM-ICD, macro-F1 especially (about 19-20 vs 28.3 on MIMIC-III).
closest.overlap: Matches our LoRA-tuned 4B result: a tuned small LLM does not beat the encoder on the full label set. Names a hybrid PLM-LLM coder as future work.
closest.difference: No per-frequency bins, no hybrid, no temporal split, no analysis of false positives.

closest.citation: Gan Y, Nguyen DD, Lin Y, Zhong P, Vu T, Duong L, Li YF. Enhancing LLM Medical Coding with Structured External Knowledge (RAG-Coding; MDACE-2025). arXiv 2605.27377 (2026)
closest.what_they_did: A training-free agent grounded in a knowledge graph of the ICD tabular list and summarised guidelines. One certified coder re-annotated the MDACE test set (61 encounters) under the 2025 guidelines. Agreement with MDACE: alpha 0.67 for diagnoses, 0.41 for procedures. Against PLM-ICD on MDACE: recall +11, precision -6. On MDACE-2025 the agent wins on micro-F1 (0.56 vs 0.48).
closest.overlap: A model for checking labels: an expert re-codes the test set and the systems are ranked again. The guideline update gives a change of the reference standard rather than of time.
closest.difference: No per-frequency bins (macro and micro only), no combination: PLM-ICD's code set is used only as a post-hoc filter. Tiny re-annotated set, release terms not stated. No later-period notes.

closest.citation: Edin J, Motzfeldt A, Flachs S, Maaloe L (Corti). Symphony for Medical Coding. arXiv 2603.29709 (2026)
closest.what_they_did: An agentic coder that reasons over guidelines. Evaluated on ACI and MDACE plus proprietary US ED/ambulatory sets and an NHS neurology set. Beats PLM-ICD on the restricted code sets. Precision at dataset prevalence ranges from 24.6 to 66.
closest.overlap: Shows that the same group behind Code Like Humans moved to an LLM-only system, not a hybrid.
closest.difference: No frequency analysis, no combination, no temporal test. Company authors.

closest.citation: (Danish population cohort) A medical coding language model trained on clinical narratives from a population-wide cohort of 1.8 million patients. arXiv 2603.00221 (2026)
closest.what_they_did: Trained on 5.8M records from 2006-2016 and evaluated on 270k held-out patients (micro-F1 71.8%). For three secondary-diagnosis codes, manual review confirmed 76-86% of the model's uncoded flags as valid, which the authors read as systematic under-coding.
closest.overlap: Published evidence that many 'false positives' against routine codes are label errors, which a manual review can show. This bears directly on our 97%-false rare answers and the filer-chosen MAUDE label.
closest.difference: Fine-tuned model only, no LLMs, no rare-code routing. The holdout is by patient, not by later year (not verified beyond the abstract).

closest.citation: Cheng H et al. MDACE: MIMIC Documents Annotated with Code Evidence. ACL 2023. arXiv 2307.03859
closest.what_they_did: Professional coders re-annotated a subset of MIMIC-III with code evidence spans.
closest.overlap: The template for checking our labels with experts (double reading with adjudication). Expert codes overlap with the original MIMIC codes by less than half (per the search snippet).
closest.difference: Clinical inpatient data under a DUA. No LLM work in the original.

closest.citation: Nanda G et al. Examining the Efficacy of LLMs for Injury Surveillance (HFES 2025, doi:10.1177/10711813251357913); Chakravarty RR, Ahmad M, Nanda G. Automated Injury Diagnosis Coding Using LLMs (2026, doi:10.1177/10711813261485840)
closest.what_they_did: Prompted LLMs (ChatGPT-3.5, later GPT-5, Llama 4, Mistral 7B) to code 100 NEISS narratives for cause, product and diagnosis, against logistic regression, MLP and LSTM baselines.
closest.overlap: Shows the NEISS product code has been touched by LLM work, but only on 100 cases.
closest.difference: No long-tail binning, no fine-tuned transformer, no selector, no later year. Tiny sample.

taken: That LLMs (agentic or prompted) beat a fine-tuned PLM-ICD-type coder on rare codes while the fine-tuned coder leads on frequent ones. Motzfeldt 2025 shows it via macro vs micro F1; Yock/Eng 2026 shows it per training-frequency bin with Claude Opus, saying no single system dominates.
Measuring rarity by how many training examples the code has (Yock/Eng bins, 0-100 / 101-1,000 / >1,000).

Giving an LLM a fine-tuned classifier's candidates or output. Yock/Eng tested PLM-ICD as a tool and Akkhawatthanakun 2026 had an LLM audit PLM-ICD candidates. Both are published, so 'combining an encoder and an LLM' alone is not a contribution.
A per-instance logistic deferral model choosing between BERT and an LLM, compared against a fixed confidence threshold (L2D-Clinical 2026, few classes only).
A fine-tuned small LLM (LoRA, SFT or RL) not beating the encoder on the full label set (Wang 2026; Motzfeldt's 1B LLM).
Rank aggregation and voting across several LLMs for ICD codes (da Silva Santos 2026, Borda/RRF beat plurality vote).
That LLM coding has a precision problem, overpredicts, and needs human review (Motzfeldt, Yock 'selection is harder than verification', Symphony, Soroush 2024, Yuan 2025 near-miss errors).
Expert re-annotation as the way to check labels (MDACE 2023, MDACE-2025, Kim 2021). Manual review showing that a model's 'false positives' are often under-coding (Danish 1.8M-patient model, 2026).
open: Choosing one answer per report or code among three coders (encoder, zero-shot LLM, retrieval-augmented LLM) with features of the proposed codes, chiefly their training-set count. Not found in clinical coding: closest are L2D-Clinical (encoder-uncertainty features, 2-3 classes) and filter-then-audit hybrids. Searched about 20 web queries plus Semantic Scholar citations of Motzfeldt (20 citing papers checked by title, the relevant ones by abstract) and OpenAlex 2026 'agentic ICD coding' (25 titles). Semantic Scholar returned no citing papers for Yock/Eng, so citation chasing for it is incomplete.

Fitting such a choice rule on one year, freezing it, and testing on a later year. No clinical LLM-coding paper I read uses a temporal split; all use random or Edin-style MIMIC splits. Liu & Nguyen 2026 handle ICD version change by training, not by a later-year test.

Reporting the false-positive load of LLM rare-code answers at true prevalence (1 in ~1,200) and turning it into a review-queue size. Yock's rare-bin precision comes from a stratified sample; no paper corrects for prevalence. Not found after targeted queries on precision at real prevalence and deferral in clinical coding.
A training-size sweep (1k to 656k) of the rare/frequent crossover against several encoders and a LoRA LLM. Not seen in clinical coding.

A single-label coding benchmark with hundreds of codes, expert or trained-coder labels, yearly releases and terms that allow commercial APIs, used with LLM-vs-encoder tail analysis. Clinical options fail on terms (MIMIC needs zero data retention) or size (CodiEsp 1,000 cases, MDACE-2025 61 encounters). NEISS looks open: only 100-case LLM studies found. Not exhaustively checked; my web-search budget ran out.
ideas: Precision signal from the agent's own trace (Yock/Eng: correct codes are discovered earlier in the session than wrong ones). For us: how early or how firmly the LLM names the rare code, or whether it names it in both the zero-shot and the retrieval runs. Needs the LLM outputs we already have plus a rank or order field. Untested even by Yock.
LLM as auditor of the encoder's top-k (Akkhawatthanakun 2026), as a cheap precision-first arm and a baseline reviewers will expect. Needs encoder top-15 candidates and one LLM pass (CPU/API).

Agentic navigation of the code hierarchy (Code Like Humans: analyze, locate in an index, validate against the tabular list, reconcile; or Yock's tool agent with grounding to discovered codes) instead of a flat list of 471 codes. The FDA device-problem code hierarchy could serve as the index. Needs an agent harness and more API calls.

Expert re-annotation of a small test subset in the MDACE-2025 style (one certified reader or two plus an adjudicator, report Krippendorff alpha against the filer label). For MAUDE, aim it at the 'false' rare answers, following the Danish study, which confirmed 76-86% of model-only flags on manual review. Needs human readers and the owner's approval.
Learning-to-defer trained to predict when the encoder is wrong (L2D-Clinical), as a further baseline beside the confidence cascade. Needs only CPU and existing outputs.
Rank aggregation (Borda, reciprocal rank fusion) across coders' ranked lists (da Silva Santos 2026), as a stronger combination baseline than majority vote. Needs ranked outputs.

Synthetic training reports for rare codes to strengthen the encoder tail (Vo et al. 2025, arXiv 2511.14112: modest macro-F1 gain). Needs LLM generation plus encoder retraining on the GPU, which needs the owner's go-ahead.

Multi-version or multi-year pooled training for rare codes (Liu & Nguyen 2026: +27% micro-F1 on rare codes by adding ICD-9 data). The analogue for us is pooling earlier years or earlier code versions.

The preprint text of Akkhawatthanakun et al. (preprints.org returned 403). Only the OpenAlex abstract was read; whether Sonnet-4.5 ran on MIMIC-IV through a zero-retention service is not checked.

checks.item: Motzfeldt et al., Code Like Humans (arXiv 2509.05378, Findings EMNLP 2025)
checks.detail: Read the full text at https://arxiv.org/html/2509.05378. Authors: Motzfeldt, Edin, Christensen, Hardmeier, Maaløe, Rogers. On MDACE with about 1K labels, PLM-ICD scores micro 0.48 and macro 0.25; CLH-large scores 0.43 and 0.28. The reconciler's precision is 0.40 at recall 0.47. There are no frequency bins, no combination with a fine-tuned coder and no temporal split. Future work matches the report: self-refinement, fine-tuning each component, and keeping coders in the loop. The fine-tuned 1B LLM is Llama-3.2-1B with LoRA on 7,500 MIMIC-III-50 examples. With label-wise attention it scores micro 0.71 and macro 0.65, about equal to PLM-ICD. So on MIMIC-III-50 a tuned 1B LLM matches the encoder rather than losing to it, which is more nuanced than the report's 'taken' item.

checks.item: Yock/Eng et al., Understanding the Limits of Agentic ICD Coding (arXiv 2609.13806, EMNLP 2026)
checks.detail: Read the full text at https://arxiv.org/html/2609.13806. Authors: Eng Chong Yock, Cao, Chen, Mao, Jiang (NTU and ASUS). 150 MIMIC-IV notes, 50 per bin, with bins 0-100, 101-1,000 and >1,000 by minimum training frequency. F1 across the bins: PLM-ICD .227/.471/.656, CodeSeeker-Opus 4.6 .560/.483/.607. Rare-bin precision for Opus with full tools is .317. Adding PLM-ICD as a tool hurts Opus on rare codes and helps GPT-5.2. The 'Selection is harder than verification' heading is present. The abstract says no single system dominates. There is no temporal split. The paper concedes the stratified sampling departs from real code frequencies, but it does not correct precision for prevalence. Listed limitations: single institution, label noise, fixed model versions, small multi-step subset. One addition: on multi-step (S/T chapter) codes, CodeSeeker-Opus collapses to about .01 F1 while PLM-ICD stays at .26-.44. The report mentions this subset only in passing.

Read only the abstract, via OpenAlex for doi 10.3390/informatics13030039; MDPI returned 403. Every reported figure matches: 19,801 MIMIC-IV summaries; PLM-ICD gives 15 codes at 55.8% precision; LLM-only precision is 1.5-34.6%; the agentic audit keeps 2-8 codes; Llama-3.2-3B goes from 1.5% to 55.1% and trims false positives by 73%; recall and F1 are left to future work. The LLMs include Sonnet-4.5.

Read the full text at https://arxiv.org/html/2604.13285. Logistic-regression deferral from BioBERT or ClinicalBERT to GPT-5-nano few-shot. Features are confidence, entropy, margin and text features. ADE has 2 classes and MIMIC-IV outcomes 3. MIMIC F1 goes from 0.887 to 0.980 with 16.8% deferred. Test sets are 279 and 500. MIMIC labels come from GPT-5.2 and Claude 4.5 consensus, with a 5% expert spot check. Baselines: fixed threshold at 0.95 (F1 0.971) and random deferral. One correction: GPT-5-nano alone already scores 0.967, so the LLM by itself beats BERT by about 8 points and the deferral adds little over the LLM alone.

checks.item: Wang et al., Can Post-Training Turn LLMs into Good Medical Coders? (arXiv 2606.13940)
checks.detail: Read the full text at https://arxiv.org/html/2606.13940 (Northwestern). Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen3-4B are trained with SFT, GRPO and PHI. Best macro-F1 on MIMIC-III Full is 20.0 against 28.3 for PLM-ICD. There are no frequency bins. The paper names 'Hybrid PLM-LLM coding' as a future direction, with the PLM supplying a high-recall candidate set. That is the filter-then-rerank pattern, not per-report selection. I did not check the venue on the ACL Anthology.

Read the full text at https://arxiv.org/html/2605.27377 (Oracle Health). One certified coder (CCS and CPC) re-annotated the 61-encounter MDACE test set. Agreement is alpha 0.67 for diagnoses, 0.41 for procedures and 0.66 overall. On MDACE, PLM-ICD scores micro 0.53 and RAG-Coding 0.55; on MDACE-2025, 0.48 and 0.56. PLM-ICD's code set serves only as a post-hoc filter. The 'closest' entry is correct. The report's answer text, however, says Gan lists a hybrid PLM-LLM design as future work. I found no such statement: the future work names expanding the annotation, other coding systems and other languages. Release terms for MDACE-2025 are not stated (the arXiv page is CC BY-NC-ND).

checks.item: Edin et al., Symphony for Medical Coding (arXiv 2603.29709)
checks.detail: Read the full text at https://arxiv.org/html/2603.29709. All authors are at Corti. Datasets: ACI, MDACE, and private NEURO, ED and AMB sets. Symphony beats PLM-ICD in the restricted setting (MDACE F1 0.62 vs 0.48 in the table; the prose says 0.58). Full-code diagnosis precision runs from 24.6% (NEURO) to 66.0% (AMB). There is no per-frequency breakdown, no hybrid and no temporal test.

Read only the abstract at https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00221. Authors: Edin, Butt Balaganeshan, Kristensen, Maaløe, Louloudis, Brunak, so it is the Corti/Copenhagen group, which the report left unchecked. Data are from 2006-2016, with 270k held-out patients and micro-F1 71.8%. Manual review confirmed 76-86% of flagged uncoded cases for three codes. The abstract does not describe how the holdout was split.

Read the abstract at https://aclanthology.org/2023.acl-long.416/; the PDF did not parse. Confirmed: built on MIMIC-III, annotated by professional coders, 302 inpatient and 52 profee charts. The claim that expert codes overlap the original MIMIC codes by less than half is not on the abstract page and stays unverified. Related verified fact: Khadka et al. 2026 (see 'missed') estimate a 76.3% undercoding rate in MDACE.

checks.item: Nanda et al. 2025 (HFES) and Chakravarty, Ahmad & Nanda 2026 (NEISS LLM coding)
checks.detail: Read only the OpenAlex abstracts for both DOIs. Nanda 2025: 100 random NEISS cases coded for cause, product and nature of injury, with ChatGPT-3.5 against logistic regression and an MLP. Chakravarty 2026: 100 narratives, single-diagnosis injury coding (diagnosis only, not product), with GPT-5 (P 0.81, R 0.82), Llama 4 and Mistral 7B against LSTM/RNN baselines. So the NEISS product code has been tested with an LLM only by Nanda 2025, on 100 cases.

checks.item: Report's 'open' claim: nobody picks one answer per note or code among several coders using features of the proposed codes
checks.detail: Not refuted, but I could not search for it. The shared web-search budget (200 per turn) was used up before my first query, so I did no new keyword searches. I used WebFetch and OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar citation lookups only. OpenAlex lists 12 citing works of Motzfeldt; I read the abstracts of 7 of them (MedDCR, ICDAGENT, Clinico, Zhou et al. Qwen3.6 system, LTR-ICD, the Khadka audit, the 2026 systematic review). None routes per note or per code between an LLM and a fine-tuned coder. Yock/Eng has 0 citing works in both OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar. The L2D-Clinical citation lookup was rate-limited.

checks.item: Report's 'open' claim: no clinical LLM-coding paper tests on a later time period
checks.detail: Nearly holds, but there is a near-miss. Li et al., Clinico (medRxiv 2026, doi 10.64898/2026.08.31.26361789; full text read): an LLM coding agent against PLM-ICD and a LoRA-tuned Qwen3-32B on real-prevalence stays. The internal split is random, and the external test is another hospital, May-July 2025. 38.1% of the external hospital's unique codes are unseen in training. Micro-precision drops from 89.5% internally to 37.8% externally. This is a site shift, not a frozen-then-later-year test of a selector. The claim stands with that caveat.

checks.item: Report's 'open' claim: nobody reports the false-positive load of LLM rare-code answers at true prevalence
checks.detail: Not refuted. Clinico and Symphony report precision at natural prevalence, but for all codes, not split by code rarity. Akkhawatthanakun reports false-positive reduction, also not by rarity. I found no turning of rare-code precision into a review-queue size.

checks.item: Report's 'open' claim: no public clinical coding dataset with expert labels and commercial-API-friendly terms
checks.detail: Confirmed for CodiEsp's size, but its 'coded by professionals' status needs a caveat: Khadka et al. 2026 found a 29.7% error rate in CodiEsp. On NEISS, the CPSC data page (https://www.cpsc.gov/Research--Statistics/NEISS-Injury-Data, read) shows a Product_3 field, so a case can carry up to three products and NEISS is not strictly single-label. The data are released yearly, around April. Case counts and terms of use are not on that page.

missed: Khadka S, Jiang X, Palade V. LLM-assisted clinical coding audit through an interpretable coding pipeline. Int J Med Inform 2026, doi:10.1016/j.ijmedinf.2026.106605 (preprint medRxiv 2025.08.24.25334321; I read the abstract via Semantic Scholar). It combines LLM evidence extraction and verification with a trained multiclass classifier and uses the pipeline as an audit tool. Three professional coders corrected the MDACE and CodiEsp labels, estimating 76.3% undercoding in MDACE and a 29.7% error rate in CodiEsp. Re-scoring models on the corrected labels improved their results. This is the closest published template for a model-assisted expert label audit, which bears on the plan to check MAUDE's filer labels. It also weakens CodiEsp and MDACE as clean expert gold.

Li Y et al. Adjudicating evolving inpatient diagnoses with a clinical coding agent: a retrospective multicentre study. medRxiv 2026, doi:10.64898/2026.08.31.26361789 (full text read). A training-free LLM agent against PLM-ICD, a LoRA-tuned Qwen3-32B and MedCodER, at natural prevalence, with an external test hospital (May-July 2025). It reports micro-precision 89.5% internally and 37.8% externally, and 38.1% of external unique codes unseen in training. There are no rarity bins and no combination of coders. It is the nearest clinical work to evaluation at real prevalence under shift.

MedDCR (Findings ACL 2026, doi:10.18653/v1/2026.findings-acl.627) and ICDAGENT (ACL 2026, doi:10.18653/v1/2026.acl-long.643), both citing Motzfeldt; abstracts read via OpenAlex. Both are agentic LLM-only coders (learned workflows; a coder agent plus a critic). Neither combines with a fine-tuned coder or routes between coders. They are neighbours to cite, not overlaps.
taken_after_check: LLMs (agentic or prompted) beat a fine-tuned PLM-ICD coder on rare codes while the fine-tuned coder leads on frequent ones. Motzfeldt 2025 shows it via macro vs micro F1 on MDACE; Yock/Eng 2026 shows it per training-frequency bin with Claude Opus 4.6, saying no single system dominates. Yock/Eng also shows the reverse on multi-step codes, where PLM-ICD wins.
Measuring rarity by a code's training-set count (Yock/Eng bins 0-100 / 101-1,000 / >1,000).

Feeding a fine-tuned classifier's candidates to an LLM: as a tool (Yock/Eng, mixed results), as an audit or filter (Akkhawatthanakun 2026), or as an LLM-plus-classifier pipeline (Khadka 2026). 'Combining an encoder and an LLM' is not by itself a contribution.

A per-instance logistic deferral model choosing between a BERT model and an LLM, compared against a fixed confidence threshold (L2D-Clinical 2026; 2-3 classes; the LLM alone already beats BERT there).

A tuned small LLM not beating the encoder on the full label set (Wang 2026: macro 20.0 vs 28.3 on MIMIC-III Full). Note that Motzfeldt's LoRA 1B LLM with label-wise attention matches PLM-ICD on MIMIC-III-50.
LLM coding has a precision problem and needs human review (Motzfeldt reconciler P 0.40; Yock/Eng 'selection is harder than verification'; Symphony full-code precision 24.6-66%; Akkhawatthanakun).

Expert re-annotation to check labels (MDACE 2023; MDACE-2025 with alpha 0.66), model-assisted expert audits finding large label error (Khadka 2026: 76.3% undercoding in MDACE, 29.7% error in CodiEsp), and manual review showing that many model 'false positives' are real under-coding (Edin et al. 2026 Danish cohort: 76-86% on three codes).
Evaluating an LLM coding agent against trained coders at natural prevalence and on an external site (Clinico, medRxiv 2026), though not by code rarity and not on a later year.
open_after_check: Choosing one answer per report among three coders (encoder, zero-shot LLM, retrieval-augmented LLM) with features of the proposed codes, chiefly their training count, over hundreds of codes. Not found in clinical coding: the nearest are L2D-Clinical (encoder-uncertainty features, 2-3 classes) and filter, audit or tool hybrids. Caveat: I could run no new keyword searches (shared budget exhausted), so neighbouring fields (general long-tail text classification, extreme multi-label routing) were not re-searched by me.

Fitting such a selector on one year, freezing it, and testing on a later year. No clinical LLM-coding paper found uses a temporal split; Clinico uses a different hospital in a later window, which is a site shift rather than a later-year test.

The false-positive load of LLM rare-code answers at true prevalence, turned into a review-queue size. Precision at natural prevalence exists only for all codes pooled (Clinico, Symphony); Yock/Eng's rare-bin precision (.317) comes from a stratified sample.
A training-size sweep (1k to 656k) of the rare/frequent crossover against several encoders and a LoRA LLM: not seen in clinical coding.

A single-label benchmark with hundreds of codes and expert or trained-coder labels, open to commercial APIs and released yearly, used for LLM-vs-encoder tail analysis. Clinical options fail on terms (MIMIC/MDACE), size (CodiEsp about 1,000 cases with a 29.7% audited error rate; MDACE-2025 61 encounters) or label quality. NEISS stays a candidate, but cases can carry up to three products, so it is not strictly single-label, and its terms and case counts are unverified. Only 100-case LLM studies were found (Nanda 2025 for product; Chakravarty 2026 for diagnosis only).

frames.thesis: LLMs are good on rare codes, but what that is worth depends on how rare the codes are. When every code counts equally, a frozen selector turns the LLMs' strength into a macro-F1 gain on a later year. It does this by checking how many training reports back the code each coder proposed, after the coders have answered. At real proportions (about 1 in 1,000), no rule turns that strength into rare labels that are mostly right. What it does give is a search aid that we can measure: it cuts the reading needed to find rare-code reports about 2-3 times against the encoder alone. We measure this in the terms used by technology-assisted review (TAR), and we show it on three report streams, one of which has labels assigned by trained coders rather than by the filer.
contributions: C1 (method, narrow): a selector that keeps one of three coders' answers per report (fine-tuned encoder, zero-shot LLM, LLM shown retrieved examples). It works after the coders answer, and its main input is how many training reports back the code each coder proposed. It is fitted on one year and frozen. On later years, on MAUDE and SDR (and NEISS if run), it beats the best single coder by about 0.03-0.06 macro-F1. It also beats the published routing methods head to head: a confidence cascade (Emer 2026; CMBS), a learned deferral model on encoder entropy and margin (L2D-Clinical 2026), an energy-gated cascade in the style of EnergyRoute, and a per-code precision/BKS table (the classical LCA counterpart, Woods 1997). Choosing per item between an encoder and an LLM is NOT claimed as new. The claim is that the proposed code's training support, used after the answers, adds to these baselines. If the BKS/per-code-precision baseline matches the selector, the paper says so and reports that simpler table as the method.

C2 (measurement, the strongest open item): a measured per-code false-naming rate for zero-shot and retrieval-prompted LLMs over a list of several hundred codes, on a stream at natural proportions where rare-code reports are about 1 in 1,198. The paper gives the base-rate account (a zero-shot LLM names a rare code on 1 in 45 to 1 in 100 ordinary reports) and a negative result tested on held-out years. Rules, prior or count correction, frequency-hint prompts, memory filters, LLM agreement, verifier vetoes and code-list repair all fail to give rare labels that are mostly right while keeping the finds, and only 219 of 552 rare reports are reached by any coder. The principle is published (Noren 2025; Srivastav 2026; Zhang COLING 2025 for prompts). What is new is the measurement at this prevalence across hundreds of codes, together with the frozen selector's behaviour there.

C3 (what 'using the strength' honestly means at natural rates): the coders' answers become a ranked read-first list, judged with TAR measures (gain curve, reads to reach recall r, WSS@r, a certified stopping rule). On MAUDE 2026, 200 of 552 rare reports are found in about 7,000 reads, against 16,000-17,000 for the encoder alone and about 240,000 at random. The paired gain of adding the LLMs to the ranking excludes zero. Ranking for human reading is NOT claimed as new (TAR; Bron 2024; Wang ECIR 2024; JMIR 2026 safety ranking). The open part is many codes pooled at about 0.08% prevalence, where the reader must also name the code, with the ranker frozen across years. TAR studies leave this regime out on purpose (Yang, Lewis & Frieder 2021 dropped RCV1 categories under 500 positives).

C4 (replication, labelled as such): prompted LLMs beat a fine-tuned encoder on codes with 1-5 training reports at every training size from 1k to 656k, and the encoder leads on codes with 21+ reports. This is reported as a replication in two new domains of a known result (Motzfeldt 2025; Yock/Eng EMNLP 2026; Martin ICHI 2026; Emer 2026). The added value is the training-size sweep and the later-year test, which those papers do not have.

C5 (labels): MAUDE and SDR codes are chosen by the filer and are described as such. Scores are called agreement with the filed code. A small expert-read MAUDE subset, aimed at the 'false' rare answers (as in Khadka IJMI 2026 and the Danish under-coding study), estimates how many of those answers are defensible. NEISS adds a stream whose code is assigned by a coder trained by the agency (CPSC), so the results do not rest only on filer labels.
datasets: MAUDE device-problem codes (main dataset; results exist). Train 2024 / dev 2025 / test 2026, 471 codes, natural rare share 1 in 1,198. Carries C1-C4 in full. Role in the paper: the hard, filer-labelled case. The manufacturer picks the code, FDA never re-codes it, and about a third of single-code reports share their text with a report filed under another code. The scores are therefore agreement with the filed code. Kept because the selector, natural-proportion and read-first results are already done and verified.

FAA SDR PartCondition (second dataset; results exist). About 290 terms, about 65k reports a year. Labels are much more self-consistent: 0.89% of same-text reports carry different labels, against 35% on MAUDE. Role in the paper: shows the selector holds with cleaner but still filer-chosen labels. Weak spots: synonyms (INOP, INOPERATIVE, FAULTY) and the change in how UNKNOWN was used in 2023-24. Rescoring with synonyms merged is CPU only.

CPSC NEISS product code on single-product cases (proposed third dataset; the one with trustworthier labels). About 805 codes, about 300k single-product cases a year, dated, public, de-identified, with no data-use agreement seen. A hospital coder trained by CPSC assigns the code, not a manufacturer; CPSC screens the data daily, corrects 9999 codes and re-reviews a portion of records every year. From a 23-code sample, roughly a fifth of codes have 1-5 cases a year, but the full tail is unverified. Nobody has published a frequency-binned, routing or natural-prevalence study on this code; only 100-case LLM pilots exist (Nanda 2025; Chakravarty 2026). It also answers the owner's 'it does not have to be failures' question, and coding automation is a live operational question there (NEISS-R from 2027). Weak points: the same coder writes the narrative and picks the code, and the manual requires the product to be named, so a keyword baseline and a subset with the code's own keywords removed are mandatory. There is no 2026 data until about April 2027, so the split is train 2023 / dev 2024 / test 2025. No explicit terms of use exist, so API use rests on the absence of restrictions.

Not used, with reasons. MIMIC-IV: the DUA blocks the Claude API without verified zero retention, there is no yearly split, and the rare split is already published there. USPTO CPC: no 1-5 tail at subclass level, and Emer 2026 already covers the ground. Bugzilla: routing labels, 13% of 2024 defects placed by Mozilla's own BugBug model, no licence. It could serve only as an optional prevalence contrast, since its rare share is 1.3-5%. CBP CROSS: about 6k rulings a year, the code is stated in the text, no bulk export.
new_work_needed: Head-to-head routing baselines on the saved MAUDE and SDR outputs: L2D-style deferral (encoder entropy, margin and text features), an encoder-energy gated cascade (EnergyRoute-like), a per-code precision / BKS lookup table fitted on 2024, and rank fusion. CPU only, 0 GPU h, $0 API, about 2-3 days of work, no downloads.

TAR framing of the read-first list: gain curves, reads to reach recall 0.3/0.5, and WSS@r. Baselines are two-phase TAR (logistic regression on TF-IDF), a simulated continuous active learning run over the coded subset, and an LLM-only ranking. Add a QuantCI or Delayed Countdown stopping rule with a recall interval. CPU only, $0, about 3-4 days. Uses the existing saved scores.
Tree-level scoring (IMDRF level 1 / 2 / leaf) and SDR rescoring with synonyms merged. CPU, about 1 day.

Expert-read MAUDE subset: about 200 reports, stratified to over-sample LLM rare answers that disagree with the filed code. Two readers plus an adjudicator; report kappa or alpha and the share of 'false' answers that are defensible. About 30-40 human hours; needs the owner's approval and readers. $0 API.

NEISS set-up: download the CPSC annual files for 2023, 2024 and 2025 by browser (tens of MB each, size unverified; owner approval needed). First confirm that 2025 has been released. About 1-2 days of cleaning: single-product filter, mapping retired and special-study codes, keyword baseline from the code names, and the subset with the code's own keywords removed. Verify the per-code tail before committing any further compute. This is a go/no-go gate.

NEISS encoder: class-balanced RoBERTa-large on about 300k 2023 cases, plus training-size sweep points. Roughly 15-30 GPU hours (estimate); GPU only with the owner's go-ahead, since the GPU is shared with Self-Play.

NEISS LLM coders: two open ~30B models, zero-shot and with retrieved examples, on a stratified sample of about 10-15k 2025 cases plus a natural-proportion slice of about 20-30k. The code-list prompt of about 800 codes dominates the length; cache it. Roughly 60-150 GPU hours per model pair (estimate). An Opus arm on more than about 1-2k cases would exceed the roughly $78 of remaining Claude credit (API credit expired 11-05). Either drop Opus on NEISS or use it on a small slice only and say so.

A follow-up literature search with a fresh web-search budget before any novelty sentence is written. Targets: learning-to-defer and multi-expert deferral with label-frequency features, rare-category detection with LLMs (2024-26), multi-issue e-discovery, EnergyRoute full text, and the unreadable EAAI/AEI/ESWA 2026 failure-text papers (Ding 115750, Hou 114403, Chhetri 105391, ESWA 131366, EAAI 114798). About 1 day, $0.

Writing changes: cite Martin ICHI 2026, EnergyRoute (Sci Rep 2026), L2D-Clinical, Noren 2025, Bron 2024, Yang/Lewis/Frieder 2021 and Woods 1997 (LCA). Soften the draft's 'has no counterpart' sentence (manuscript line 131). Rename the metric to agreement with the filed code. Paper edits stay on hold until the owner says go.
frames.closest_prior_and_gap: Routing. Emer et al. 2026 (arXiv 2601.23200 v2; patents; full text read) send the encoder's most uncertain 2-20% of items to a LoRA LLM, test on a later period, and get almost no full-set gain (0.412 vs 0.410 macro-F1). L2D-Clinical (arXiv 2604.13285; full text read) fits a logistic deferral model on BERT uncertainty for 2-3 classes. EnergyRoute (Sci Rep 2026; abstract only) is a tiered encoder / kNN / LLM router on 301 imbalanced classes, beating the encoder and a confidence cascade. All of these route on the encoder's confidence before any LLM answer. None uses the training support of the code each coder actually proposed, none picks among three coders' answers, and none freezes a selector on one year to compare it with a cascade by frequency bin on later years. Rare split. Motzfeldt 2025, Yock/Eng EMNLP 2026 and Martin ICHI 2026 already publish LLMs beating fine-tuned models on rare labels and a split of the work by frequency. Yock samples 50 notes per bin and Martin uses balanced 100/100 sets, so neither measures rare-label precision at real prevalence. Prevalence. Noren 2025 and Srivastav 2026 give the base-rate collapse as a principle, and Zhang COLING 2025 shows frequency hints in prompts are blunt, but only for 2-3 classes at several percent. Ranked reading. TAR has long owned ranked reading (Bron 2024 combines LLM judgements with active learning at 3.8% prevalence), and Yang, Lewis & Frieder 2021 explicitly drop categories below about 0.06%. The gap the paper can claim: answer-level selection on the proposed code's training support, frozen across years and compared head to head with confidence routing; a measured per-code LLM false-naming rate at about 1 in 1,000 over hundreds of codes, with tested fixes failing; and multi-code TAR at about 0.08% pooled prevalence. Caveat: the 'open' status of these items rests on searches that ran out of web-search budget, so it is plausible, not confirmed.
frames.reviewer_attack: "Every piece is known, and your labels are not ground truth. The rare/frequent split is published three times, encoder-LLM routing is published (Emer, L2D-Clinical, EnergyRoute), the base-rate problem is textbook, and the read-first list is TAR. On top of that, MAUDE codes are picked by manufacturers, so your 97% 'false' rare answers may be right." Answer. (1) The paper does not claim those pieces. It cites them as given and tests the one design choice they leave out: routing on the training support of the code each coder proposed, after the answers. It compares this head to head with their routing signals (confidence cascade, L2D-style deferral, energy gate, BKS per-code precision) on frozen later years, across two or three datasets and three LLMs. If the per-code-precision table matches the selector, the paper reports the simpler table, and the measurement contributions stand without it. (2) The natural-prevalence result is reported as agreement with the filed code. The expert-read subset gives an estimate with an interval for how many 'false' rare answers are defensible. NEISS, where a CPSC-trained coder assigns the code, shows whether the selector and the false-naming arithmetic hold when the labeller is not the manufacturer. Even if the subset shows that half the 'false' answers are defensible, precision stays far below a usable automatic label at 1 in 1,198, so the conclusion (rank, don't label) does not depend on the labels being perfect. (3) The TAR result is framed as measurement in the regime TAR leaves out, against TAR baselines and with a certified stopping rule, not as a new method. A second objection, specific to NEISS, is that the task is keyword lookup. The answer is a keyword baseline plus a subset with the code's own keywords removed.
frames.fit: If NEISS joins, the paper is no longer failure-only, so a general applied-ML venue fits best: Expert Systems with Applications (first choice), then Engineering Applications of AI, or Information Processing & Management for the TAR and measurement angle. Journal of Biomedical Informatics is a fit if MAUDE and NEISS are framed as product-safety surveillance. RESS or Part O fit only if the paper stays MAUDE + SDR and adds the downstream reliability angle (safety-signal or review-queue cost). These are journals only, matching the owner's route. ACL/EMNLP main is a poor fit, since that community has the clinical precedents and will see C1 as incremental.
frames.honest_odds: ESWA or EAAI with the head-to-head routing baselines, TAR measures and the label-honesty section: about 40-50% acceptance after one or two revision rounds. Without the new baselines it is about 20%, because reviewers will cite Emer, L2D-Clinical or EnergyRoute and call it incremental. JBI with MAUDE + NEISS: about 30-35%. RESS: about 20-25%, because of the change of domain and no downstream reliability model. NLP main tracks: under 15%. Main risks: (a) the per-code-precision/BKS baseline equals the selector, which shrinks C1 to a measurement paper; (b) the NEISS tail turns out thin, or the keyword baseline closes the LLM's tail gap, which makes NEISS a weak third dataset; (c) a scoop hidden in the unread 2026 EAAI/AEI/ESWA papers or the learning-to-defer literature. The novelty checks behind 'open' ran with the web-search budget exhausted, so treat every 'open' item as plausible until the follow-up search is done.

frames.thesis: Prompted LLMs beat fine-tuned coders on rare codes when every code counts equally, but in a natural report stream that advantage cannot be used to put labels on reports. A rare code turns up about once in 1,000 reports, and a zero-shot LLM names one on roughly 1 in 45 to 1 in 100 ordinary reports, so most of its rare answers are wrong. We measure where that limit sits for each coder and code, show it holds on two or three datasets with different base rates and label sources, and show that the advantage survives as ranking: the LLMs' answers cut the reading needed to find rare-code reports by 2 to 2.5 times compared with the fine-tuned encoder alone.
contributions: C1 (measurement, open per the prevalence and clinical checks): the first measured per-report false-naming rate of zero-shot and retrieval-prompted LLMs (Opus 5.5, Qwen, Gemma) over a list of several hundred codes in a natural stream where rare codes are about 1 in 1,198. With the matching recall, this gives the precision ceiling for rare answers. Existing work uses balanced or stratified samples (Martin 2026: 100/100; Yock/Eng 2026: 50 per stratum) or binary tasks at 1.6% prevalence or more (Nawrath 2026; Srivastav 2026). The Bayes principle itself is taken (Norén 2025, Drug Safety 2026) and must be cited as such. The new part is the measured rates and the finding that they stay put.

C2 (where the limit is, mostly cheap CPU work): a break-even analysis. For each coder, this is the false-naming rate it would need for its rare answers to be mostly right (on MAUDE about 40 to 266 times lower than now). Next to it goes a dose-response curve: precision of rare answers against rare-code prevalence, made by reweighting the natural pool and checked against datasets with different natural base rates (MAUDE about 0.08%; SDR and NEISS to be measured). The aim is a rule a practitioner can apply before deploying: from the base rate and a small sample of a coder's false-naming rate, predict whether its rare labels can be used.

C3 (negative result, with mechanism): none of the levers tried on the saved outputs crosses the limit while keeping the finds. Tried: a frozen per-coder selector, a confidence cascade, frequency and prior-correction rules, prompts with frequency hints (in line with Zhang et al. COLING 2025, at a prevalence 30 to 100 times lower), a filter on past reports, agreement between LLMs (in line with Sirago 2026), and count correction (fails because error rates shift between years, as Linder 2026 predicts). The mechanism is decomposed: base-rate arithmetic, manufacturer boilerplate that the LLM reads literally while the filer codes by habit, one defect in the code list, and a long scattered remainder. Also reported: only 219 of the 552 rare reports are reached by any coder.

C4 (what use remains): treat the long-tail advantage as a ranked read-first list, measured in technology-assisted-review (TAR) terms. Report gain curves, reads to reach recall r, and work saved over sampling (WSS@r) against two-phase TAR, continuous active learning and LLM-only ranking baselines, with a certified stopping rule (QuantCI or Delayed Countdown). Data: 200 of 552 rare reports in about 7,000 reads, against 16,000 to 17,000 with the encoder alone and about 240,000 at random. The ranking is frozen on 2025 and tested on 2026. TAR as a method is taken. Pooled recall-versus-reads over hundreds of rare codes at about 0.08% prevalence, where the reader must also name the code, is open: the TAR cost study drops RCV1 categories with fewer than 500 positives.

C5 (kept, but demoted to a supporting result): the frozen selector raises macro-F1 by 0.03 to 0.06 on a later year with three LLMs and two datasets, beating a confidence cascade, a frequency rule and a majority vote. It must be framed against EnergyRoute (Sci Rep 2026), L2D-Clinical and Emer 2026, and its only distinct element is the training support of the proposed code as a signal. It needs a per-code precision or behaviour-knowledge-space baseline, in the spirit of Local Class Accuracy (LCA, Woods 1997). Its role in the story is to show that the macro-F1 gain and the natural-proportion failure come from the same rare answers. Claim 2 (rare codes to LLMs, frequent codes to the encoder) is cited as known (Motzfeldt 2025; Yock/Eng 2026; Martin 2026; Emer 2026) and replicated across training sizes. It is not claimed as new.
datasets: MAUDE device-problem code, train 2024 / dev 2025 / test 2026 (primary). It has the lowest base rate (rare-code reports are 1 in 1,198) and all saved outputs from the three LLMs, so C1 to C4 already run here. Its weakness is that the filer chooses the code and nobody audits it. The score is therefore described as agreement with the reported code (note section 20.1), and a small expert-read subset is added (see new work).

FAA SDR PartCondition, same years (second dataset, already done). Its labels are far more consistent: 0.89% of reports share their text with a different label, against 35% on MAUDE. That makes it the control for 'is the limit just label noise?'. Its rare base rate at natural proportions still needs computing from saved outputs (CPU).

CPSC NEISS Product_1 on single-product cases (proposed third dataset; verdict medium; tail partly checked). The code is assigned by a CPSC-trained coder, not a manufacturer, with CPSC screening, an annual re-review and correction of 9999 codes. That is better than MAUDE on criterion b, though the coder also writes the narrative and no agreement figure is published. About 800 codes. About 300k single-product cases in 2024, and a sample of 23 codes suggests roughly 150 to 200 codes with 1 to 5 cases a year (unverified until the per-code counts are computed). Public, federal and de-identified; no explicit licence or LLM clause. Its roles: it varies the label source and the base rate; there is no published frequency-binned, routing or natural-prevalence study (only 100-case pilots by the Nanda group); and NEISS-R ends manual coding from 2027, which makes the 'automation versus people' question operational there. Constraints: the split must be train 2023, dev 2024, test 2025, because 2026 data arrive about April 2027. A keyword-lookup baseline and a subset where the narrative does not name the product are required, since the manual makes coders name every product in the narrative.

Mozilla Bugzilla Product::Component (optional contrast only). Rare pairs make up 1.3 to 5% of bugs, more than ten times MAUDE's share. That is useful as a high-base-rate point on the C2 curve. It is not a main dataset: the labels are routing decisions (13% of 2024 defects were moved by the BugBug model), the text leaks the answer, and there is no licence.

Not used: patents (no 1-5 tail at subclass level, and Emer 2026 already covers the comparison), MIMIC-IV (data-use agreement blocks the Claude API; only 3-year time bins; claim 2 already published there), CBP customs rulings (CROSS) (the text states the code; about 6k rulings a year). They are cited only as related work.
new_work_needed: Prevalence dose-response and break-even analysis (C2) on MAUDE and SDR from saved outputs: CPU only, about 1 to 2 days, no API, no downloads.

TAR framing (C4): gain curves, WSS@r, reads to recall r, baselines (two-phase TAR with logistic regression, continuous active learning simulated on the coded sample, LLM-only ranking) and a QuantCI or Delayed Countdown stopping rule with a random check sample. CPU only, about 3 to 4 days, using the stored 2025 and 2026 answers. Caveat: continuous active learning can only be simulated on the coded reports (the uniform sample plus all rare reports).

Selector baselines a reviewer will ask for (C5): per-code precision or behaviour-knowledge-space (BKS) table, Local Class Accuracy (LCA), L2D-Clinical-style deferral, and EnergyRoute-style tiers if feasible from saved encoder logits. CPU only, about 2 days.

Expert-read subset on MAUDE: about 200 reports, stratified over the coders' false rare answers, true rare answers and disagreements. Two readers plus an adjudicator; report Krippendorff's alpha against the filer code (MDACE-2025 or Khadka 2026 style). Human time 30 to 50 hours; no GPU or API. This is the decisive test of whether the precision ceiling is a property of the coder or of the labels. It needs the owner's approval and recruited readers.

SDR rare base rate and natural-proportion slice from saved outputs (CPU, about 1 day). If SDR test outputs at natural proportions do not exist, the open models must code a natural slice: GPU about 10 to 20 hours, with the owner's approval because the GPU is shared.

NEISS replication (optional third dataset). Downloads: CPSC yearly tab-delimited files for 2023 to 2025 by browser, tens of MB each (size unverified), with owner approval. Cleaning: 1 to 2 days (single-product filter, retired and special-study codes, keyword baseline from the code names). Encoder: RoBERTa-large on about 300k short narratives, about 6 to 10 GPU hours. Open-model coders: zero-shot and retrieval prompts on a stratified 10 to 20k test set plus a natural slice of about 20 to 30k, with prefix caching of the roughly 800-code list, about 40 to 80 GPU hours for two models. Opus: about $78 of credit is left, which is not enough for tens of thousands of calls, so on NEISS Opus is either dropped or run on a few hundred reports through agents. Human time: about 5 hours of spot-checks. Total about 2 to 3 weeks.

Writing: rewrite the draft around C1 to C4. Cite Martin, Feng & Peng (IEEE ICHI 2026), EnergyRoute (Sci Rep 2026), L2D-Clinical, Norén 2025 / Drug Safety 2026, Bron 2024, Wang ECIR 2024, Yang-Lewis-Frieder 2021, Akkhawatthanakun 2026 and Linder 2026. Soften the 'no counterpart' sentence about selection (manuscript.tex line 131). About 1 week, no compute.

Follow-up literature search with a fresh web budget before claiming C1 and C4 as open. These checks were cut short because the search budget ran out. Targets: learning-to-defer and multi-expert deferral, rare-category detection with LLMs, multi-issue e-discovery, LLM coding of occupation, OIICS and MedDRA terms at natural distributions, and the unread EAAI/AEI/ESWA abstracts (Ding 115750, Hou 114403, Chhetri 105391, ESWA 131366, EAAI 114798). Human or agent time about 1 day, no cost.
frames.closest_prior_and_gap: Yock/Eng et al. (EMNLP 2026): rare-versus-frequent split by training frequency with Claude Opus, but on 50 notes per stratum; the paper chooses not to sample at natural prevalence, and its rare-bin precision (.317) is measured at an inflated prevalence. Martin, Feng & Peng (ICHI 2026): LLMs beat RoBERTa on low-prevalence NVDRS circumstances, with rare circumstances routed to LLMs, but on balanced 100/100 test sets, so the precision collapse never appears. Norén et al. (arXiv 2510.04341; Drug Safety 2026): the Bayes principle for rare-event AI, but with no LLM, no list of hundreds of codes and no measured false-naming rates. Srivastav 2026 and Nawrath 2026: LLM precision collapsing at low prevalence, on binary tasks at 1.6% or more. EnergyRoute (Sci Rep 2026), L2D-Clinical and Emer 2026: per-item routing between encoder and LLM, by confidence, judged on macro-F1 only. Bron 2024, Wang ECIR 2024 and Yang/Lewis/Frieder 2021: LLM-plus-ranker TAR at about 3 to 4% prevalence on single binary topics. The TAR cost study drops categories with fewer than 500 positives in 804k documents. The gap: nobody has measured what the LLM long-tail advantage becomes in a natural multi-code stream at about 0.1% rare prevalence, why it fails (per-code false-naming rates that prompts, filters, agreement and correction do not move), where the break-even lies as prevalence varies, or how much of it survives as reading saved under TAR measures on a frozen later year. Caveat: the 'open' status rests on searches that ran out of web budget, so it has medium confidence until the follow-up search.
frames.reviewer_attack: Objection: "This is Bayes' theorem plus noisy labels. The MAUDE code is chosen by the filer, so your '97% false' rare answers may largely be correct LLM readings. Li H et al. 2026 found that blinded adjudicators sided with the LLM in 60.8% of disagreements. And TAR ranking is a known method." Answer, in three parts. (1) The principle is cited as known (Norén). What we add is the measured false-naming rates per code and coder over hundreds of codes, the break-even factor, and evidence that the rates do not move under the tested levers. (2) The label-noise question is settled empirically, not by argument. The expert-read subset gives the adjudicated share of 'false' rare answers. SDR's consistent labels (0.89% conflicting texts) and NEISS's CPSC-trained coder show whether the ceiling persists when the labels are cleaner. The break-even framing also says how many of the false answers would have to be label errors to change the conclusion (precision above 50% needs the false-naming rate to fall about 40 to 266 times), so a reader can judge the result against any audit rate. Honest risk: if the audit finds that most rare 'false' answers are right, the paper becomes one about MAUDE label quality, which is still publishable but a different paper. (3) TAR is adopted on purpose, with its own baselines and stopping rules. What is new is the measurement, not the method: pooled multi-code recall against reads at about 0.08% prevalence, frozen year to year, which TAR studies leave out.
frames.fit: Journals only, since the owner cannot present. Best fit for the 'limit plus what use remains' framing: Information Processing & Management (TAR and evaluation readership) or Journal of Biomedical Informatics (MAUDE plus NEISS as product-safety surveillance). Solid fallbacks: Expert Systems with Applications and Engineering Applications of AI, which publish LLM-versus-classifier evaluation work. RESS or Safety Science remain possible if the paper stays on MAUDE and SDR as safety and failure reporting and adds an operational angle (review-queue size per year, automation share at target agreement). RESS usually expects a downstream reliability model, which this framing does not have.
frames.honest_odds: With C1 to C4, the TAR baselines and the expert subset: roughly 40 to 50% at ESWA or EAAI, 25 to 35% at IP&M or JBI, 15 to 25% at RESS. Without the expert-read subset, take off about 10 points everywhere, because the label-noise objection stays unanswered. NEISS adds standing and a cleaner label source, but it does not change the odds much unless its per-code tail is confirmed. The main downside risk is a scoop in the follow-up search, most likely in learning-to-defer or rare-category detection with LLMs. A smaller risk is that the expert audit shows that most 'false' rare answers are right, which would turn the paper into one about MAUDE label quality. Novelty is narrow (a measurement-and-limits paper, not a new method), so careful positioning against Norén, Martin, Yock/Eng, EnergyRoute and the TAR literature carries most of the weight.

frames.thesis: On three report streams whose labels come from different kinds of coder (MAUDE device-problem codes picked by manufacturers, FAA SDR part-condition terms picked by operators, and NEISS product codes picked by CPSC-trained hospital coders), a selector frozen on one year keeps one coder's answer per report, choosing among a fine-tuned encoder, a zero-shot LLM and a retrieval-prompted LLM. It beats the best single coder, and also confidence and learned-deferral routing, on macro-F1 in a later year. At natural proportions, though, the LLMs' long-tail gain arrives almost entirely as false rare-code answers. The paper measures that cost code by code for the first time and turns the real finds into a ranked review list with a certified recall, instead of passing them off as automatic labels.
contributions: C1 (method, scoped narrowly): a per-report selector that judges each coder by the code it proposes, mainly by that code's training support, plus answer agreement, fitted on one year and frozen. It is tested on a later year of three corpora against every published routing form: a confidence cascade (CMBS, Emer), learned deferral on encoder uncertainty and text features (L2D-Clinical), energy-tiered encoder/kNN/LLM routing (EnergyRoute), a classical class-conditional baseline (a per-code precision table in the style of Local Class Accuracy, and a Behaviour-Knowledge-Space lookup), majority vote and a frequency rule. The claim is only what survives that comparison: that the proposed code's training support adds to these signals on a later year, shown by ablation and by frequency bin. The paper does not claim that per-item encoder/LLM choice is new, and the draft's sentence that training support 'has no counterpart' has to go.

C2 (measurement, the main new result): per-code false-naming rates of zero-shot and retrieval-prompted LLMs (Opus 5.5 and two open ~30B models) across hundreds of codes on natural streams where each rare code turns up about 1 in 1,000, on all three corpora. The same systems are also scored under the stratified protocol of Yock/Eng (EMNLP 2026) and the balanced protocol of Martin et al. (ICHI 2026), so the paper can show how far stratified evaluation overstates rare-code precision. The Bayes principle is published (Noren 2025, Srivastav 2026); the measured rates across hundreds of codes are not.

C3 (label regime as a variable): whether the encoder's head advantage and the LLM's tail advantage move when the label comes from a third-party trained coder (NEISS) rather than a filer's habit (MAUDE, SDR). This tests the exploration finding that the encoder partly learns manufacturer boilerplate (a 60-character template rule gets 0.53 at row level, against 0.87 for the encoder) on data where that shortcut should be weaker.

C4 (application, stated in technology-assisted-review terms): finding rare-code reports pooled over hundreds of codes at about 0.08% prevalence, where the reader must also name the code. It is reported as reads-to-recall, WSS@r and a certified stopping rule (QuantCI or Delayed Countdown) against two-phase TAR, an encoder-only ranking and an LLM-only ranking. The existing result (200 of 552 rare reports in about 7,000 reads, against 16-17k with the encoder alone) carries over. TAR studies leave this prevalence band out on purpose (Yang, Lewis & Frieder 2021 dropped RCV1 categories with fewer than 500 positives), so this is a measurement in a gap, not a new method.

Reused without new novelty claims: the training-size sweep (1k-656k) and the rare/frequent crossover, presented as a replication in failure and injury text of Motzfeldt 2025, Yock/Eng 2026, Martin 2026 and Emer 2026.
datasets: MAUDE, device-problem code, 471 codes (primary; existing 2024/2025/2026 runs reused). Role: largest stream and the natural-proportion test (1 in 1,198 rare). Label: chosen by the filer (about 96% manufacturers), never re-coded by FDA, about a third of single-code text shared with another code. The task is called 'agreement with the filed code' throughout. Keep it because its weakness is what C3 exploits.

FAA SDR, PartCondition, about 290 terms (second; existing runs reused). Role: replication in a second domain. Label: filer-chosen but highly consistent (0.89% same text with a different label, against 35% on MAUDE). The synonym-merge rescoring from note section 20 item 7 should be added.

NEISS Product_1 on single-product cases, about 805 listed codes (new third dataset). Role: label-regime contrast, since the code is assigned by a CPSC-trained coder with CPSC QC rather than by the maker, plus a non-failure domain, which answers the owner's 'does it have to be failures?'. Verified: about 302k single-product cases in 2024 (HF mirror counts); public annual files with no DUA; about 5 of 23 sampled codes had 1-5 cases in 2024, so roughly 150-200 rare codes a year (extrapolated, wide interval). Prior LLM work covers only 100-case pilots (Nanda 2025 HFES; Chakravarty 2026). Weak points: the same coder writes the narrative and must name the product, so a lexical baseline and a no-own-keyword subset are mandatory; Product_1 order is arbitrary, so the set is limited to single-product cases; no explicit terms of use; split train 2023 / dev 2024 / test 2025 only if the 2025 file is out (unverified), otherwise 2022/2023/2024. 2026 data will not exist until about April 2027.

Not used as main data: USPTO CPC (no 1-5 tail at subclass level, and Emer et al. 2026 already ran encoder vs LLM plus routing with a temporal split there; cite as closest prior). MIMIC-IV (the DUA blocks the Claude arm without verified zero retention, years are only 3-year bins, and the split is already published). Mozilla Bugzilla (routing labels, 13% of 2024 defects placed by the BugBug model, circular; at most a robustness appendix). CBP CROSS (about 6k a year, code stated in the text, no licensed bulk export).
new_work_needed: Check NEISS before committing (1 day, CPU): confirm the 2025 file is on cpsc.gov, then download one annual tab-delimited file (tens of MB, by browser; needs the owner's OK) and count single-product cases per code. Go/no-go rule: at least about 100 codes with 1-5 cases a year after dropping 9999/5555, special-study and retired codes. Human: 0.5 day.

NEISS preparation (2-3 days, CPU): single-product filter, code-version mapping with the comparability table, and stripping the age-sex prefix and 'DX:' tail. Build a code-name keyword baseline, BM25 against code names, and a 'no own keyword in text' test subset.

NEISS encoder (GPU, needs the owner's go-ahead, since the GPU is shared): class-balanced RoBERTa-large on about 300k cases, about 8-12 GPU-hours (estimate from the MAUDE runs' scale), plus a linear TF-IDF model on CPU. Skip the full training-size sweep on NEISS; one or two sizes are enough.

NEISS LLM coding: two open ~30B models, zero-shot and kNN-10, on a stratified test set of about 10k plus a natural-proportion slice of about 30k. Narratives are under 400 characters and the roughly 800-code list is a cacheable prefix. Rough estimate: 25-40 GPU-hours with prefix caching (vLLM). Opus 5.5 on a subset of about 2,000 reports; whether the remaining ~$30 covers it depends on cached-prefix pricing (check with the claude-api reference, not from memory). A natural-slice Opus run would need extra credit, probably low hundreds of dollars (unverified estimate).

New routing baselines on all three datasets (CPU, about 1 week): L2D-style logistic deferral (encoder entropy, margin, text length, boilerplate flag), a per-code precision/LCA table, BKS lookup over answer tuples, energy-tiered routing, and an ablation of the selector without training support. Needs saved encoder logits; if they were not saved, re-running inference costs 1-3 GPU-hours per dataset.

Stratified vs natural scoring (CPU, 2-3 days, reuse outputs): re-score every system under Yock-style 50/50/50 rarity sampling and Martin-style balanced sampling, next to natural proportions. Report per-code false-naming per 10k ordinary reports with exact-binomial intervals, and precision projected via Bayes as Noren 2025 recommends.

TAR framing (CPU, 3-4 days): gain curves, WSS@r, reads-to-recall at 50/75%, two-phase TAR with a logistic-regression baseline, and QuantCI/Delayed-Countdown stopping on a random check sample of unread reports. Calibrate on 2025 and apply to 2026 (MAUDE, SDR), or on dev and apply to test (NEISS).

Optional but strongly advised label check (human): one reader (the author), 100 MAUDE 'false' rare answers plus 100 NEISS ones, scored exact / defensible / contradicted, following the Khadka 2026 and Danish-cohort template. About 12-20 human-hours. A second reader on 50 items gives an agreement figure. Without it, C3 rests on provenance alone.
Writing and figures: 3-4 weeks. Total: about 2.5 months, roughly 40-60 GPU-hours, $30 plus optional extra credit, and 1-3 days of human reading.
frames.closest_prior_and_gap: Closest per-item hybrids: EnergyRoute (Sci Rep 2026, abstract only) routes encoder, kNN fusion and LLM over 301 imbalanced classes and beats both the encoder and a confidence cascade on macro-F1. Emer et al. (arXiv 2601.23200 v2, full text) route the 2-20% most uncertain patents to a LoRA LLM on a temporal split; the full-set gain is negligible (0.410 to 0.412 macro). L2D-Clinical (arXiv 2604.13285, full text) fits a logistic deferral model between BERT and an LLM on 2-3 classes. Classical Local Class Accuracy (Woods 1997) already judges a classifier by the class it outputs. The rare/frequent split is taken: Motzfeldt EMNLP-F 2025, Yock/Eng EMNLP 2026, Martin et al. ICHI 2026 (not yet in references.bib), Emer 2026. Taken outright: the ranked review list as TAR (Wang ECIR 2024; Bron 2024; Yang, Lewis & Frieder 2021), the base-rate principle (Noren 2025; Srivastav EMNLP-F 2026), and model-assisted label audit (Khadka IJMI 2026). The gap that survives all checks: (1) selection on the proposed code's training support across three coders, frozen on one year and compared head to head on a later year with confidence, deferral, energy and LCA/BKS routing by frequency bin. Nobody routes after the LLM answers on that signal, though the open-ness rests on searches that were cut short by the budget. (2) Measured per-code LLM false-naming over hundreds of codes at about 1 in 1,000, set against the stratified protocols used by Yock/Eng and Martin; none reports this. (3) Multi-code TAR at about 0.08% with certified stopping, a band TAR studies exclude. (4) The label regime (filer vs trained third-party coder) as a factor in the encoder/LLM gap. Also, no published frequency-binned encoder-vs-LLM study exists on NEISS product codes, MAUDE single-code leaf codes or SDR PartCondition.
frames.reviewer_attack: Strongest objection: "This is learned deferral or dynamic classifier selection with one more feature. EnergyRoute already routes encoder, kNN and LLM and beats a cascade; LCA judged classifiers by their output class decades ago. The rare-code collapse is just Bayes, which Noren and Srivastav already stated. And on MAUDE and NEISS the labels are either filer habits or keyword lookups, so the numbers do not mean much." Answer: (a) Every one of those methods is implemented as a baseline under the same frozen-year protocol, and the paper claims only the increment that training support adds in ablation. If that increment is not significant, C1 is demoted to 'the routing gain holds in failure and injury text' and the paper rests on C2-C4. (b) Bayes gives the form, not the magnitude. Measured rates (a zero-shot LLM names a rare code on 1 in 45 to 1 in 100 ordinary reports), set beside the same systems scored under the stratified protocols that recent EMNLP papers use, show by how much published rare-code precision is inflated. That is a quantitative correction the field lacks. (c) The labels are named for what they are ('agreement with the filed code'). NEISS adds a third-party coder label, the no-own-keyword subset and keyword/BM25 baselines answer the lookup objection, and the 200-item reading audit puts a number on how much of the 'false' share is label error.
