A secondary objection, 'NEISS is string matching', gets the same answer: if the LLM's tail gain vanishes on the no-keyword subset, report it, since it also tells readers where the LLM advantage comes from.
frames.fit: The order changes from the earlier route. Expert Systems with Applications or Engineering Applications of AI come first: both take multi-dataset method-plus-measurement papers and are not tied to failure framing, which matters once NEISS is added. Journal of Biomedical Informatics or JAMIA Open come next: two of the three corpora are US federal health surveillance streams (MAUDE, NEISS), and the review-queue and label-regime results suit surveillance readers. RESS or Part O are now third, viable only if the paper keeps SDR/MAUDE in front and adds a downstream reliability use, so they fit worse after the pivot. Safety Science is a fallback for the evaluation-heavy version. TACL (a journal, so no presenting) is a long shot if the stratified-vs-natural measurement turns out striking.
frames.honest_odds: Feasibility: about 70% that NEISS passes the tail check and its 2025 file is out; if not, train 2022 / test 2024 still works and costs only a year of recency. The GPU need is moderate but depends on the owner's go-ahead. Novelty risk: about 35-45% that the training-support increment over learned deferral or LCA is small or not significant on a later year. Then the paper becomes a measurement paper (C2-C4), which is still publishable but less in the spirit of 'LLMs win the tail'. Also, the prior-art searches for C1 and C2 were cut short by an exhausted search budget, so a scoop in learning-to-defer, XMC or occupation coding is possible (perhaps 15-25%). Acceptance after one major revision, with all baselines and NEISS done: roughly 45-55% at ESWA/EAAI, 35-45% at JBI, 20-30% at RESS. Without NEISS and the new baselines, i.e. the draft as it stands, judged against EnergyRoute, L2D and Martin 2026: below 25% anywhere good. Owner-facing truth: the strongest honest message is not that LLMs automate the long tail but that they find it, at a measurable review cost, and that the published evaluations hide that cost.

datasets_ranked.name: CPSC NEISS product code (Product_1, single-product cases only)
datasets_ranked.verdict: Best new candidate, medium. It is the only checked dataset that improves on MAUDE's labels and still has a real tail, but it is not a clean win.
datasets_ranked.why: Public, federal, de-identified, dated (Treatment_Date), about 300k single-product cases a year (302,324 in 2024 by the HF-mirror count), about 805 codes in the 2021 manual. A 23-code sample put 5 codes at 1-5 cases in 2024, which suggests roughly 150-200 rare codes a year. That figure is extrapolated, the interval is wide, and it needs the full count. Weak points: (1) the coder who writes the narrative also picks the code, and the manual requires every product to be named in the narrative, so many codes are close to keyword lookup; (2) Product_1 order is arbitrary when several products are involved, so only single-product cases can be used; (3) no 2026 data until about April 2027, so the split must be 2023/2024/2025 (whether the 2025 file is out is unverified); (4) no explicit terms of use and no LLM clause; (5) NEISS-R replaces manual coding from 2027.
datasets_ranked.who_labels: A NEISS hospital coder (hospital staff or a CPSC contract coder) who must first be trained by CPSC. The coder abstracts the ED chart, writes the short comment and enters the codes. Quality control: software edits at entry and after transmission, CPSC analysts screen the data the morning it arrives, CPSC replaces 9999 ('cannot find') codes with the right one, and a yearly visit re-reviews part of each hospital's records. No published agreement or error figure for the product code.
datasets_ranked.prior_work_there: Only small LLM pilots: Nanda et al. HFES 2025 (100 cases, ChatGPT-3.5 against LR/MLP on cause, product and diagnosis; abstract only) and Chakravarty, Ahmad & Nanda HFES 2026 (100 cases, diagnosis code; abstract only). Other NEISS NLP work targets other fields: helmet status (Burford JAMA Netw Open 2024; arXiv 2412.02173), diagnosis with 24 classes (Ye AMIA 2024), fall circumstances (Omaki Inj Prev 2023), body part. No frequency-binned, routing or natural-prevalence study of the product code was found. The scout's claim that a 2025 blog post picks product codes with gpt-4o-mini was checked and is wrong: those posts classify injury or body part.
datasets_ranked.what_it_would_buy: A third stream where the label comes from a trained third-party coder rather than the manufacturer. It answers 'it does not have to be failures' and puts the 'automation versus people' question in a real operational setting (CPSC is ending manual coding). It must come with a keyword or BM25 baseline against the code names and a test subset where the narrative does not contain the code's own keywords; otherwise reviewers will call it string matching.
datasets_ranked.cost: Download of 3 yearly CPSC files by browser (tens of MB each, owner approval needed; curl gets 403). 1-2 days of cleaning. Go/no-go gate: count single-product cases per code first. Encoder roughly 8-30 GPU-h, open-model coders roughly 25-150 GPU-h depending on sample size (agents' estimates differ). Opus only on a small slice with about $78 of credit left.

datasets_ranked.name: MAUDE device-problem code (existing)
datasets_ranked.verdict: Keep as the main dataset; its weakness is now part of the story.
datasets_ranked.why: All results already exist (selector, natural proportions, read-first list). Lowest base rate (rare-code reports are 1 in 1,198), which is what makes the measurement interesting.
datasets_ranked.who_labels: The filer, about 96% manufacturers. FDA never re-codes. No expert audit exists, and about a third of single-code reports share their text with a report filed under another code.
datasets_ranked.prior_work_there: MADE (ACL 2026, multi-label benchmark, temporal split, reasoning models better on rare labels), Li H et al. npj Digit Med 2026 (LLM re-coding; blinded adjudicators sided with the LLM in many disagreements), and a 2026 stapler-report prioritisation paper (binary seriousness, AUC only).
datasets_ranked.what_it_would_buy: Results already in hand. Scores must be called 'agreement with the filed code', ideally with a small expert-read subset.
datasets_ranked.cost: CPU only for the new baselines and TAR measures; 30-50 human hours for an expert-read subset.

datasets_ranked.name: FAA SDR PartCondition (existing)
datasets_ranked.why: Labels are far more consistent than MAUDE's: 0.89% of same-text reports carry different labels, against 35%. That makes SDR the control for 'is the limit only label noise?'.
datasets_ranked.who_labels: The filer (operator or repair station). Consistent but not independent.
datasets_ranked.prior_work_there: Only JASC-code work: Verhagen & Scott 2025 (LLM vs legacy NLP, abstract only) and Dela Peña et al. 2026 (Trans Inst Aviation; TF-IDF+SVM, conformal abstention with a review-required rule, chronological split, 4,430 events; abstract only). Nobody has published on PartCondition.
datasets_ranked.what_it_would_buy: Replication across domains with cleaner labels. Rescoring with synonyms merged (INOP / INOPERATIVE) is CPU only.
datasets_ranked.cost: CPU; the natural-proportion rare base rate still has to be computed.

datasets_ranked.name: Mozilla Bugzilla Product::Component
datasets_ranked.verdict: Weak as a main dataset; useful at most as a contrast at a higher base rate.
datasets_ranked.why: Counts checked live: 37,097 defects in 2024 over 633 pairs, about 210 pairs with 1-5 defects after admin buckets are dropped. Rare-pair bugs are 1.3-5% of bugs, more than ten times MAUDE's share, which makes it a different prevalence point. But the labels are routing decisions. 30.5% of 2024 defects changed component and 12.8% were moved by Mozilla's own BugBug model, so the labels are partly a model's output. Component words and source paths leak into the text (68 of 200 sampled summaries). No bulk dump, no licence found, and about 11% code churn per year.
datasets_ranked.who_labels: The reporter picks first. Triagers correct some, and the BugBug classifier moves others automatically above a threshold. No audit.
datasets_ranked.prior_work_there: Component and developer triage with fine-tuned encoders (Dipongkor & Moran ASE 2023, chronological split); LLM-RAG triage on Eclipse (Lajko ICSOFT 2026). BugBug itself is a production confidence cascade on this exact label. No frequency-binned LLM-vs-encoder study found.
datasets_ranked.what_it_would_buy: One high-prevalence point on a precision-vs-prevalence curve.
datasets_ranked.cost: About 37k REST calls a year plus cleaning; licence unclear.

datasets_ranked.name: US patents, CPC first symbol (USPTO-70k / HUPD / PatentsView)
datasets_ranked.verdict: Weak. Ground largely taken and no tail at the usual level.
datasets_ranked.why: The label is better than MAUDE's: a primary examiner must review and sign the classification at issue (MPEP 905.03(b), opened). But at subclass level there is no 1-5 tail: the rarest USPTO-70k subclass has 4 items over 12 years. Labels are natively multi-label, HUPD stops at 2018 and has a licence conflict (BY-SA tag, BY-NC-SA text), and the bulk download path has moved and returned 403. The main-group tail is unverified and would need thousands of codes in a prompt.
datasets_ranked.who_labels: Pre-grant classification partly by contractors (Commerce OIG: 19-27% error against a 10% contract limit, 2021-22); at grant, reviewed by the primary examiner. No agreement figure for the first symbol.
datasets_ranked.prior_work_there: Emer et al. arXiv 2601.23200 v2 (2026, full text read by checkers): encoders vs zero-shot, few-shot, RAG and LoRA LLMs, temporal split, routing of the most uncertain 2-20% to the LLM. Full-set macro-F1 is about unchanged (0.410 to 0.412), and a long-tail-trained encoder beats the LLMs, rare labels included. Also Jiang, Sun & Goetz ACL Findings 2026 (balanced 500 IPC subclasses).
datasets_ranked.what_it_would_buy: Little beyond a replication against Emer.
datasets_ranked.cost: Hundreds of MB to 125 GB of data; costly long-text prompts.

datasets_ranked.name: MIMIC-IV ICD-10 (principal diagnosis)
datasets_ranked.why: Codes come from billing coders, not the note writer, and the tail is real. But a credentialed DUA applies, and PhysioNet's 2025 guidance blocks sending notes to a commercial API without verified zero retention, so the Opus arm is in doubt. Dates fall only in 3-year bins, so no yearly split is possible. The task is natively multi-label (median 14 codes), and notes average about 1,500 words.
datasets_ranked.who_labels: Hospital billing coders. No audit for MIMIC-IV. MDACE (354 MIMIC-III charts) is the expert re-annotation, and Khadka IJMI 2026 estimates heavy under-coding there.
datasets_ranked.prior_work_there: The rare-vs-frequent split is published here: Motzfeldt EMNLP-F 2025; Yock/Eng EMNLP 2026 (rare micro-F1 PLM-ICD .227 vs CodeSeeker-Opus .560, 50 notes per stratum). Hybrids: Akkhawatthanakun Informatics 2026 (LLM audits PLM-ICD candidates); L2D-Clinical (2-3 classes).
datasets_ranked.what_it_would_buy: Only a replication of claim 2, under awkward terms.
datasets_ranked.cost: 1-2 weeks of credentialing; heavy GPU time for long notes.

datasets_ranked.name: CBP CROSS customs rulings (HTSUS code)
datasets_ranked.why: 222,344 rulings in total (CBP API), so roughly 6,000 a year on average. That is too small and almost entirely tail, so the encoder has no head to lead on. The ruling text states the code. Rulings often carry several codes, there is no official bulk export, and the code list is revised every year. ATLAS inputs were rewritten by GPT-4o-mini.
datasets_ranked.who_labels: CBP National Commodity Specialists: a third party to the importer, but the same person writes the text.
datasets_ranked.prior_work_there: ATLAS arXiv 2509.18400 (fine-tuned Llama vs GPT-5; no encoder baseline, no frequency analysis); HSCodeComp ACL 2026 (632 e-commerce items, not CROSS).
datasets_ranked.what_it_would_buy: Open ground, but in a setting where the comparison barely makes sense.
datasets_ranked.cost: Scraping or an unlicensed mirror; 1-2 weeks of cleaning.

synthesis.is_there_a_better_dataset: Not clearly. No checked dataset beats MAUDE and SDR on every criterion. The only real improvement on the label question is CPSC NEISS (product code, single-product cases). There a CPSC-trained hospital coder, not the manufacturer, picks the code under daily CPSC screening and a yearly partial re-review. It is public, dated and large (about 300k single-product cases a year), and the tail looks real (about 5 of 23 sampled codes had 1-5 cases in 2024). Nobody has published a frequency-binned, routing or natural-prevalence study of that code; only two 100-case LLM pilots exist. Its limits are serious. The same coder writes the narrative and must name the product in it, so a keyword baseline and a no-own-keyword subset are mandatory. 2026 data will not exist until about April 2027. There are no explicit terms of use. No agreement figure is published. The full per-code tail still needs one download to confirm. The other candidates are worse. In patents a long-tail encoder beats the LLMs, Emer 2026 already routes between them, and the subclass level has no 1-5 tail. MIMIC has DUA limits on the Claude API, 3-year date bins, and the split is already published. Bugzilla labels are routing decisions, partly made by Mozilla's own model. CBP rulings number about 6k a year and state the code in the text. About ninety further datasets were ruled out, mostly because the filer picks the label (CFPB, procurement CPV/PSC, arXiv), labels are machine-assigned since 2022 (MeSH), data are restricted (occupation coding, VetCompass, SEER), or the code list is short. On the owner's worry that 'nobody uses MAUDE': MADE (ACL 2026) and Li H et al. (npj Digit Med 2026) show it is used. What it lacks is trustworthy labels, not standing. Coverage caveat: the shared web-search budget ran out early in this run. Most agents worked through PubMed, Crossref, arXiv and direct page fetches, so a missed dataset is possible, especially in non-English official statistics and in occupation and injury coding. I did not reopen sources myself, except to confirm the 'no counterpart' sentence at paper/manuscript.tex line 131.

taken: LLMs beat fine-tuned coders on rare codes and lose on frequent ones, with the work split by frequency: Motzfeldt EMNLP-F 2025; Yock/Eng EMNLP 2026 (per-bin, with Claude Opus 4.6); Martin, Feng & Peng IEEE ICHI 2026 (NVDRS, balanced 100/100, per-label hybrid; NOT in references.bib); Emer arXiv 2601.23200 (patents). Claim 2 is a replication.

Choosing per item between a fine-tuned encoder and an LLM, including with a learned logistic deferral model: L2D-Clinical arXiv 2604.13285 (2-3 classes); CMBS arXiv 2408.09629; Emer 2026 (uncertainty routing, temporal split, full-set gain about zero); EnergyRoute Sci Rep 2026 (encoder / kNN / LLM tiers over 301 imbalanced classes, beats the encoder and a confidence cascade; abstract only); TRACER 2026; Nie et al. ICML 2024.
The confidence cascade we use as a baseline is itself a published method (CMBS, Emer, BugBug in production) and must be cited as one.

Judging a classifier by the class it outputs: Local Class Accuracy (Woods et al. 1997, confirmed through the DESlib documentation). The draft's sentence at manuscript.tex line 131, that training support 'has no counterpart' in dynamic selection, is too strong and should be softened.
The base-rate collapse of precision at low prevalence, including for LLM classifiers: Norén et al. 2025 / Drug Safety 2026; Srivastav et al. EMNLP-F 2026.
Frequency hints in prompts steer LLM output bluntly and inconsistently: Zhang, Hangya & Fraser COLING 2025 (3 classes, prevalence of a few percent).
Count correction fails when error rates shift: Linder et al. 2026 (multicalibration).

LLMs over-name codes when they generate freely, and an LLM or trained verifier over a classifier's candidates restores precision: LLM-codex (ML4H 2023); Akkhawatthanakun Informatics 2026 (recall not reported).

A ranked read-first list judged by recall against reading is technology-assisted review (TAR), which also covers LLM plus ranker (Bron 2024; Wang ECIR 2024; LGAR 2025), a ranker frozen on earlier data and applied to a later stream (Cochrane RCT Classifier 2021; two-phase TAR, Yang, Lewis & Frieder 2021), and ranked triage of safety reports (JMIR Med Inform 2026; FDA CBER VAERS 2011; Lareb 2023; GSK MLIT 2026).
An automatic share plus a manual share, with rare codes failing first: BLS autocoder; Marucci-Wellman 2017 (explicitly routes 'rare, emerging' narratives to people); ONS SIC/SOC; Norwegian census.
LLM agreement or majority vote does not fix errors, and errors are correlated across models: Sirago 2026 (hospital incident reports).
Model-assisted expert audits that find many 'false positives' are real label errors: Khadka IJMI 2026; Danish 1.8M-patient cohort (76-86% of flags confirmed on review); MDACE-2025.
LLM-based work on SDR JASC codes with a temporal split and conformal 'review-required' abstention: Dela Peña 2026; Verhagen & Scott 2025.
open: A selector that judges each of three coders by the training support of the code it proposed, after the answers, frozen on one year and compared head to head on later years with confidence, deferral, energy and per-code-precision (LCA/BKS) routing, by frequency bin. Not found anywhere. It is open only as an increment over those baselines, which have not yet been run.

A measured per-code false-naming rate of zero-shot and retrieval-prompted LLMs over hundreds of codes in a natural stream where rare codes are about 1 in 1,000, with a set of fixes tested on held-out years and failing. Published studies use stratified (Yock: 50 per bin) or balanced (Martin: 100/100) samples, or binary tasks at 1.6% prevalence or more.
Showing how much stratified or balanced evaluation protocols overstate rare-code precision, by scoring the same systems under natural, stratified and balanced protocols.

Recall against reads pooled over hundreds of rare codes at about 0.08% prevalence, where the reader must also name the code, with a certified stopping rule and a ranker frozen across years. TAR studies leave this band out on purpose (Yang, Lewis & Frieder 2021 dropped RCV1 categories with fewer than 500 positives).
Any frequency-binned LLM-vs-encoder study on MAUDE single-code leaf codes, SDR PartCondition or NEISS product codes.
The label source (filer versus trained third-party coder) as a factor in the encoder/LLM gap.
uncertain: Every 'open' item rests on searches cut short by an exhausted web-search budget and rate-limited APIs. Not searched or under-searched: learning-to-defer and multi-expert deferral with label-frequency features, rare-category detection with LLMs (2024-26), multi-issue e-discovery, extreme multi-label classification with LLM rerankers, LLM occupation, OIICS and MedDRA coding at natural distributions.

Five 2026 venue papers known by title only could hold part of a scoop: Ding EAAI 115750 (LLM-augmented hierarchical failure-text classification), Hou EAAI 114403, Chhetri AEI 105391, ESWA 131366 (benchmark of 4,100 rare-event models), EAAI 114798.
EnergyRoute details (routing signal, splits) come from the abstract only; the full text should be read before positioning against it.
Whether training support adds anything once a per-code precision or BKS table is a baseline. This is the main threat to claim 1 and it is an experiment, not a search.
The NEISS per-code tail, the 2025 file release and the terms of use.

framings.name: Limits and what use remains (measurement-first; the 'reality' lens)
framings.thesis: Prompted LLMs beat fine-tuned coders on rare codes when every code counts equally. In a natural stream (rare codes about 1 in 1,000) that advantage cannot be turned into automatic labels, because a zero-shot LLM names a rare code on about 1 in 45 to 1 in 100 ordinary reports. The paper measures this limit per coder and code, shows where break-even would be as prevalence changes, shows that no tested fix crosses it, and shows the advantage survives as ranking: 2-2.5 times fewer reads to find rare-code reports than with the encoder alone, measured in TAR terms. The selector's macro-F1 gain is a supporting result.
framings.needs: CPU only for the core: a precision-vs-prevalence curve and break-even factor on saved outputs (1-2 days), TAR measures with two-phase TAR, continuous-active-learning and LLM-only baselines plus a QuantCI or Delayed Countdown stopping rule (3-4 days), LCA/BKS, L2D and energy baselines for the selector (2 days). Strongly advised: an expert-read MAUDE subset of about 200 reports, two readers plus an adjudicator (30-50 human hours), because otherwise 'the labels are wrong' stays unanswered. NEISS optional. A follow-up literature search (about 1 day) before writing novelty sentences. New citations: Martin ICHI 2026, EnergyRoute, L2D-Clinical, Norén, Bron, Wang ECIR 2024, Yang/Lewis/Frieder, Woods 1997, Linder 2026.
framings.risk: Narrow novelty (a measurement paper, not a method). It goes against the owner's wish to 'use the strength' for automation, since the honest message is 'LLMs find the tail, people confirm it'. If the expert audit shows most 'false' rare answers are right, it becomes a paper on MAUDE label quality. Possible scoop in the unsearched learning-to-defer or rare-category literature. Agents' odds: about 40-50% at ESWA/EAAI with the TAR baselines and the expert subset, about 10 points lower without the subset.

framings.name: Three label sources (pivot: MAUDE + SDR + NEISS, selector plus measurement)
framings.thesis: On three report streams whose labels come from manufacturers, operators and CPSC-trained coders, a selector frozen on one year beats the best single coder and every published routing form on later-year macro-F1. At natural proportions the LLMs' tail gain is almost all false rare answers. The paper measures that cost code by code for the first time, shows how stratified evaluation hides it, and turns the true finds into a ranked list with certified recall.
framings.needs: Everything in framing 1, plus the NEISS go/no-go check (confirm the 2025 file, count single-product cases per code; at least about 100 codes with 1-5 cases a year), 2-3 days of NEISS preparation with a keyword/BM25 baseline and a no-own-keyword subset, a RoBERTa-large encoder (GPU, owner's go-ahead), open-model coders on a stratified plus natural sample (roughly 25-150 GPU-h; agents' estimates differ), Opus only on a small slice, and rescoring under natural, stratified and balanced protocols. About 2.5 months in total.
framings.risk: Most work and the most dependencies (GPU shared with the owner's Self-Play, browser download approval, a credit limit for Opus). The NEISS tail may be thin, or a keyword lookup may close the LLM's tail gap. About 35-45% risk that training support adds nothing significant over the LCA/BKS or deferral baselines, which demotes the selector. Highest ceiling if it works: agents' odds 45-55% at ESWA/EAAI and 35-45% at JBI. It also answers 'does it have to be failures?'.

framings.name: Selector first, honestly scoped (the 'strength' lens)
framings.thesis: The LLMs' rare-code strength is worth what the prevalence allows. Judged with every code counting equally, a frozen selector that checks the training support of each proposed code, after the answers, converts the strength into a later-year macro-F1 gain over the best coder and over published routing methods. At natural rates, no rule gives mostly-correct rare labels; the strength becomes a measured search aid.
framings.needs: Same CPU baselines as framing 1 (L2D-style deferral, energy-gated cascade, per-code precision/BKS table, rank fusion), TAR framing, IMDRF tree-level scoring and SDR synonym rescoring, the expert-read subset, and NEISS as an optional third dataset. Rewrite: claim 2 labelled as a replication; drop the 'no counterpart' sentence.
framings.risk: It leads with the claim most exposed to prior art (EnergyRoute, L2D-Clinical, Emer, LCA). If the BKS or per-code-precision table matches the selector, the headline collapses and the paper falls back to framing 1 anyway. Agents' odds: about 20% at ESWA/EAAI without the new baselines, about 40-50% with them. Closest to the owner's original aim and to the current draft.

synthesis.recommendation: Do framing 1's core now, on MAUDE and SDR, using only CPU and saved outputs. In order: (a) run the baselines that decide claim 1, namely a per-code precision / BKS table fitted on 2024, an LCA-style class-conditional accuracy, L2D-style deferral on encoder entropy and margin, and an energy-gated cascade, plus an ablation of the selector without training support; (b) put the read-first list in TAR terms (gain curve, reads to recall r, WSS@r, two-phase TAR and LLM-only baselines, a QuantCI or Delayed Countdown stopping rule); (c) compute the precision-vs-prevalence curve and the break-even factor; (d) score the same systems under the stratified (Yock) and balanced (Martin) protocols to show how much they inflate rare-code precision. If (a) shows that training support adds a significant increment, the paper can lead with the selector (framing 3 or 2). If not, it leads with the measurement (framing 1) and the selector becomes a supporting result. Separately, ask the owner to approve the NEISS go/no-go check: one browser download of a yearly CPSC file and a per-code count. Add NEISS only if it passes and the GPU can be had, and always with the keyword baseline. Before writing any novelty sentence, run a follow-up literature search with a fresh budget on learning-to-defer, rare-category detection, multi-issue e-discovery, the EnergyRoute full text and the five unread EAAI/AEI/ESWA 2026 papers. Paper edits stay on hold until the owner says go. When they resume, cite Martin ICHI 2026 and EnergyRoute, call the scores 'agreement with the filed code', and soften manuscript.tex line 131. Venue order shifts toward ESWA/EAAI (or JBI if NEISS joins), with RESS/Part O only if the paper stays on failure data and adds an operational angle.
synthesis.plain_summary: 다시 찾아봤지만, MAUDE와 SDR보다 모든 면에서 나은 데이터셋은 없었습니다. 그나마 나은 후보는 미국 소비자제품안전위원회(CPSC)의 NEISS(응급실 제품 사고 기록)입니다. 여기서는 제조사가 아니라 CPSC가 교육한 coder가 제품 코드를 붙이고, 매일 검사합니다. 1년에 약 30만 건이고 코드는 약 800개이며, 드문 코드도 꽤 있어 보입니다. 다만 같은 coder가 글도 쓰고 코드도 고르며, 글에 제품 이름을 꼭 쓰게 되어 있어서 '단어 찾기' 문제라는 비판을 받을 수 있습니다. 2026년 데이터는 2027년 봄에야 나옵니다. 특허, MIMIC, Bugzilla, 세관 판정 데이터는 이미 남이 했거나, 드문 코드가 없거나, 이용 조건이 맞지 않았습니다. 이미 남이 한 것: 'LLM은 드문 코드에, encoder는 흔한 코드에 강하다'는 결과는 최소 세 편이 있고, 그중 Martin 2026은 초안에 없으니 꼭 인용해야 합니다. encoder와 LLM 사이에서 보고서마다 고르는 방법(EnergyRoute, L2D-Clinical, Emer)과, 사람이 읽을 순서 목록(TAR라는 분야)도 이미 있습니다. 아직 아무도 안 한 것: 제안된 코드의 학습 건수로 세 coder 중 하나를 고르고, 한 해에 고정해서 다음 해에 시험하는 것입니다. 실제 비율(약 1/1,000)에서 LLM이 드문 코드를 얼마나 잘못 붙이는지를 코드별로 잰 사람도 없습니다. 그래서 기여는 '자동 라벨'보다 '측정과 한계, 그리고 찾기 도구'가 가장 안전합니다. 선택기가 새로운 기여가 되려면, 코드별 정확도 표 같은 단순한 기준보다 나아야 합니다. 이 실험은 CPU만으로 며칠이면 됩니다. 초안의 "counterpart가 없다"는 문장(manuscript.tex 131행)은 너무 강하므로 고쳐야 합니다. 이번 검색은 중간에 검색 한도가 끝나서, '아무도 안 했다'는 판단은 아직 확정이 아닙니다. 논문을 쓰기 전에 한 번 더 확인 검색이 필요합니다.
untried_methods: Per-code precision / Behaviour-Knowledge-Space lookup table fitted on 2024 (classical class-conditional selection; Woods 1997 LCA): the baseline that decides whether training support adds anything. CPU.

Learned deferral on encoder entropy, top-2 margin and text features (L2D-Clinical 2026), and an encoder-energy tiered router (EnergyRoute, Sci Rep 2026), as head-to-head baselines. CPU if the encoder logits were saved, otherwise 1-3 GPU-h per dataset.

LLM as auditor of the encoder's top 10-15 codes (Akkhawatthanakun 2026; LLM-codex 2023), measuring rare recall as well as precision. This is unlike the binary veto already tried. Needs one LLM pass on a subset.
Constrained LLM choice among encoder or retrieved candidates for uncertain reports only (Emer 2026; filter-then-rerank). One LLM pass on a subset.
Agent-trace precision signal: whether the rare code is named early or by both the zero-shot and the retrieval run (suggested but untested by Yock/Eng 2026). CPU on existing outputs.

TAR baselines and measures: two-phase TAR with TF-IDF logistic regression, simulated continuous active learning on the coded subset, gain curves, WSS@r, and certified stopping (QuantCI, Yang/Lewis/Frieder 2021; Delayed Countdown, Lewis 2026). CPU.
Diversity-aware ranking with diminishing returns per code (multiclass active search, Nguyen & Garnett), so the list is not filled by a few boilerplate codes. CPU.

Grouped certification of automatic acceptance (clustered conformal prediction, Ding 2023; Available Guardrails 2026), pooling rare codes by IMDRF level 1. Expect few groups to certify, which itself answers 'can automation replace people'. CPU.
Conformal prediction sets for the long tail with a prevalence-adjusted score (Ding, Fermanian & Salmon 2025/26) on the encoder, with the LLM choosing inside the set. Needs encoder softmax on 2025.
Split-conformal 'review-required' abstention with a stated coverage (Dela Peña 2026). CPU.
Multicalibrated count correction conditioned on text cluster or boilerplate (Linder 2026), and prediction-powered inference for yearly rare-code counts with valid intervals (Angelopoulos 2023). CPU.

Label-efficient evaluation under extreme imbalance by adaptive importance sampling (Marchant & Rubinstein KDD 2021), instead of a uniform sample in which each report stands for about 164. Needs a new labelling budget.
Prompt variants that Zhang et al. COLING 2025 found steadier than giving the true distribution: telling the model the classes are balanced, or a feedback prompt. Opus re-ask on the prompt set.
Online or monthly refitting of the selector (TRACER flywheel; Nie et al. ICML 2024), compared with the frozen 2024 selector on 2026. CPU.
Model-assisted expert label audit aimed at the 'false' rare answers (Khadka IJMI 2026; Danish cohort; MDACE-2025), reporting Krippendorff's alpha against the filed code. Human time.
Rescoring under the stratified (Yock) and balanced (Martin) protocols next to natural proportions, with precision projected via Bayes (Norén 2025). CPU.

Reporting balanced accuracy and macro-recall next to macro-F1 (Collot EACL 2026). Also reporting the automation share at a target agreement level and the manual share needed to reach it (BLS autocoder, Marucci-Wellman 2017). CPU.
owner_decisions: Which message the paper carries: 'LLMs find the long tail and people confirm it, at a measured cost' (framing 1), or keep trying to lead with the selector (framing 3). The evidence favours the first unless the LCA/BKS baseline experiment comes out in the selector's favour.
Approve the NEISS go/no-go check: one browser download of a yearly CPSC file (tens of MB) to count single-product cases per code, after confirming the 2025 file is out.
If NEISS passes: approve GPU time on the shared machine (roughly 30-150 GPU-h) and decide whether Opus runs on a small NEISS slice only, given about $78 of credit left.
Whether to fund an expert-read MAUDE subset (about 200 reports, 30-50 human hours, two readers plus an adjudicator). Without it the 'labels are wrong' objection stays open.
Whether to allow a follow-up literature search with a fresh web budget before any novelty sentence is written.
When to lift the hold on paper edits, which include citing Martin ICHI 2026 and EnergyRoute, renaming the metric to agreement with the filed code, and softening manuscript.tex line 131.
Venue order: ESWA/EAAI first (or JBI if NEISS joins) instead of RESS first.

errors: EnergyRoute is misdescribed. The synthesis read only the abstract and lists its full text under 'uncertain'. I opened the full text (Europe PMC PMC13315699, Jang, Kim, Nam, Yong, Lee, Lim; KISTI/KRIBB; Sci Rep 16:19697, Apr 2026). It is closer to our work than the synthesis says: (a) it reports results by class-frequency group (Fig. 2), with the largest gains on tail classes; (b) its macro-F1 gain over the fine-tuned encoder is 0.738 to 0.778, the same size as our +0.03-0.06; (c) it beats a FrugalGPT confidence cascade (macro 0.701) and replicates on WoS (0.770 to 0.804, cascade 0.758); (d) its LLM tier gets retrieved neighbours, backfilled from the parent category for tail classes, which is our retrieval coder. So the novelty-map item 'compared by frequency bin ... Not found anywhere' is wrong for the frequency-bin part. What stays different: EnergyRoute routes on encoder energy before any LLM answer and fuses rather than selects; I saw no frozen later-year test (no split statement found); and there is no natural-prevalence analysis. Its data are available only on request from KRIBB. The authors are Korean, so Korean reviewers may well know it.

NEISS code count. The synthesis gives 'about 805 codes' as fact. The evidence conflicts: agent 1 parsed 1,114 PROD codes from NEISS-formats.xlsx, the scout's unverified figure was about 885 current codes, and agent 2's 805 is a regex over the 2021 manual that includes special-study and out-of-jurisdiction codes. The 150-200 rare-code extrapolation inherits that denominator problem. The sample is also 24 values, not 23 (two of them are zeros that may be retired codes).
'About 96% manufacturers' (MAUDE filers) is stated as current. The exploration notes (line 240) attribute it to Kavanagh 2019 on 1997-2018 data and say explicitly that it is not the current share.
Li H et al.: 'blinded adjudicators sided with the LLM in many disagreements' appears nowhere in the evidence provided.

'CPSC is ending manual coding', given as an operational motivation, goes beyond the source. The NEISS-R release (as summarised by agent 1) says the release does not state how products or narratives will be coded after 2027.

'About ninety further datasets were ruled out' counts many entries that rest on memory, snippets or unopened pages (FDA 510(k), MeSH automation, NFIRS remarks, USCG/EMSA/CAA MOR, ATSB, MSHA). Those are untested, not ruled out. The two MeSH entries in the evidence even disagree on whether the automation claim is verified.
overclaims: Every 'open' novelty item (training-support selector, natural-prevalence false-naming measurement, TAR at 0.08% pooled prevalence, nothing on PartCondition) rests on agents whose WebSearch budget was exhausted before or near their first query. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited and the arXiv API came back empty. My own WebSearch calls in this check were also refused. The synthesis does flag this in 'uncertain', but the plain_summary and the framings still treat 'nobody has done X' as the basis for the contribution.

NEISS 'only two 100-case LLM pilots exist' is not established. Google Scholar, ACL Anthology, IEEE and AMIA full text were not searched. Vichare et al. 2024 report 90.47% top-1 accuracy on unspecified 'injury codes' from NEISS (abstract only), and these could be product codes. Divya Venkatesh 2024 used 120,000 pre-labelled narratives of unknown source.

'NEISS improves on MAUDE's labels' overstates it. The same coder writes the narrative and chooses the code, the product word must appear in the text, and no agreement figure exists. NEISS is better on who chooses the code, not shown to be better on consistency. The synthesis does not propose the cheap same-text/different-code check that was used to compare MAUDE (35.2%) with SDR (0.89%).
'The tail looks real' rests on 24 codes counted on an unofficial HF mirror while the counting API was failing. It was not checked against CPSC files.
Agents' acceptance odds (40-50%, 45-55%, about 20%), the 35-45% risk figure and the GPU-hour ranges (8-30, 25-150) appear as findings, but none comes from any opened source. They are guesses.

'Claim 2 is a replication' is stated more firmly than the evidence supports. Prior work covers ICD (multi-label notes, stratified samples), NVDRS (balanced binary per-circumstance) and patents (where a long-tail encoder reverses the result). The training-size sweep and single-label short-report setting are listed as open elsewhere, so 'mostly replicated, with an unreplicated sweep' is more accurate.
missing: EnergyRoute full text: it now has to be the main head-to-head baseline for claim 1, and its frequency-group figure has to be compared with ours. Also a check of whether it uses a temporal split; I found no split statement by grep.

Learning-to-defer and multi-expert deferral with label-frequency features, rare-category detection with LLMs, and XMC with LLM rerankers. All three are named as the likeliest scoop locations, and none was searched.

Non-English and Korean sources. The owner is Korean, and EnergyRoute shows Korean public-research classification work exists. Korean MFDS device adverse-event reports, Japan PMDA malfunction reports, Australia TGA DAEN device reports, Health Canada MDI and UK MHRA were not considered as MAUDE-like streams that might be regulator-coded.
Whether the NEISS 2025 file is out. I opened the CPSC data page on 2026-11-11: it lists no years and no terms of use, and says only that a year 'generally' appears in April. This is still unverified.

A same-text/different-code consistency check on NEISS, and a keyword/BM25 pilot on a small NEISS sample before any go/no-go decision. Without these, the label-quality and string-lookup risks stay hypothetical.
The five 2026 EAAI/AEI/ESWA papers known only by title (Ding EAAI 115750 and others) were never read.
The natural-proportion rare-code base rate for SDR, which is needed for the precision-vs-prevalence curve, is noted as not yet computed.
No check that 'Edin et al. 2026' is the author group of the Danish 1.8M-patient study (abstract only, authors not recorded) before it is cited.
critic.weakest_link: The synthesis says the selector is new ('judges each coder by the training support of its proposed code, after the answers, compared by frequency bin; not found anywhere'). That rests on prior-art searches whose web budget was gone. The synthesis also judged EnergyRoute from its abstract alone. Its full text reports tail-class gains by frequency group, a macro-F1 gain of +0.04 over the encoder (same size as ours), a win over a confidence cascade, and a retrieval-augmented LLM tier. So the remaining novelty is only the signal: the training support of the code each coder proposes, used after the answers, rather than encoder energy before them, plus a frozen later year. That increment is untested against LCA/BKS or per-code-precision baselines.
critic.verdict: The synthesis's direction is sound: lead with measurement and the limits, run the LCA/BKS, deferral and energy baselines before claiming a selector, and treat NEISS as conditional. But it overstates how open the selector ground is and how good NEISS is. On reading the full text, EnergyRoute (Sci Rep 2026, Korean authors) already shows a three-tier encoder/kNN/retrieval-LLM router with frequency-group tail gains of similar size and a win over a cascade. Claim 1 is therefore an increment at best, and the paper must compare against EnergyRoute directly. On NEISS, the code count (805 vs 1,114), the tail and the 2025 release are unverified, prior LLM product-code work may exist (Vichare 2024), and the label is better on who chooses the code but not shown to be more consistent. Several numbers in the synthesis are guesses (odds, GPU hours) or lack sources (the 96% filer share is old data; the Li H adjudication claim is not in the evidence). Every 'nobody has done it' needs a real search with a fresh budget before it goes into the paper. I opened: arXiv 2605.21845 abstract page (Martin et al.; ICHI 2026 acceptance confirmed in the comments), the CPSC NEISS data page (2025 status unconfirmed, no terms), and the EnergyRoute record and full text via Europe PMC (PMC13315699). My web searches were refused because the budget was used up.
